title: Mindlink
pitch: The idea is simple: stop searching and start connecting
about_excerpt:
The idea is simple: stop searching and start connecting
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 



 
 Inspiration
Research tools help people find information, while chat tools help people ask questions. However, neither makes it easy to see how ideas, evidence, notes, and decisions connect. 

 We were inspired to build MindLink as a shared thinking space for humans and AI. The goal is simple: 

 Stop searching. Start connecting. 

 We wanted to create a tool that helps users understand research papers in simple language, challenge assumptions, discover relationships, and turn information into better decisions. 

 What it does
MindLink transforms thinking and research into an interactive visual canvas. 

 Users can: 

 Explore questions with AI-generated thoughts.
Compare optimistic and pessimistic perspectives.
Explore multiple future paths.
Search real research papers through OpenAlex.
Add papers, notes, Markdown files, paper files, and images.
Convert research into claims, evidence, methods, risks, gaps, contradictions, and questions.
Connect related thoughts with animated neural links.
Explain selected ideas in simple language.
Build a research story map.
Listen to an audio brief.
Generate images for thoughts.
Ask different AI roles for perspectives, including Investor, Mentor, Domain Expert, Future You, and Devil’s Advocate.
Zoom, move, edit, pin, and delete thoughts.
Lock decisions after reviewing possible outcomes.
Interact with the canvas through WebMCP tools.
MindLink does not just store information. It maps understanding. 

 How we built it
MindLink was built with: 

 Next.js
React
TypeScript
Tailwind CSS
Zustand
Groq AI
OpenAlex
WebMCP
Lucide React
FFmpeg for demo media creation
The application uses a visual canvas where every thought is represented as a node. Nodes contain metadata such as type, source, trust level, author, and relationships. 

 The Research Desk provides a focused workspace for finding papers, adding user context, explaining ideas, creating story maps, and generating audio briefs. 

 We used OpenAlex to retrieve real academic papers from the web. Research results are added to the canvas with source links and confidence indicators so users can distinguish evidence from interpretation. 

 WebMCP exposes MindLink actions to compatible AI agents, including starting a session, adding thoughts, expanding ideas, challenging assumptions, reading the canvas state, locking decisions, and finding research papers. 

 Challenges we ran into
One major challenge was designing a canvas that remained useful as more thoughts and connections appeared. We needed to make relationships visible without overwhelming the user. 

 We also had to handle uncertainty responsibly. AI-generated research explanations can sound confident even when evidence is weak, so we added source labels, trust levels, and clear distinctions between evidence, interpretation, risks, and open questions. 

 Another challenge was combining multiple interaction types in one workspace: research search, file input, visual mapping, audio, images, AI roles, decision-making, and WebMCP. We focused on keeping the canvas as the central experience while moving research tools into a collapsible sidebar. 

 Finally, we had to make the demo reliable even when an AI API was unavailable. We added fallback responses so the core research experience could still be demonstrated. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of
We are proud that MindLink turns a research question into a connected visual experience instead of another chat transcript. 

 Our key accomplishments include: 

 Building a working human + AI thinking canvas.
Adding real research paper retrieval through OpenAlex.
Creating a dedicated Research Desk workspace.
Adding animated neural links between ideas.
Supporting paper explanations with evidence-oriented node types.
Adding audio briefs and visual story mapping.
Adding WebMCP tools for AI-agent interaction.
Preserving human control through editing, challenging, source inspection, and decision confirmation.
Creating a polished hackathon demo with narrated video and visual documentation.
What we learned
We learned that useful AI products are not only about generating better answers. They are also about helping users understand where an answer came from, how reliable it is, and what should happen next. 

 We learned that visual structure can make complex research easier to understand. Separating a paper into questions, methods, claims, evidence, limitations, contradictions, and gaps gives users a more useful mental model than a single summary. 

 We also learned that human control is essential. The best experience is not AI making decisions alone, but AI helping people see possibilities, challenge assumptions, and make more informed decisions. 

 What's next for MindLink
Next, we plan to make MindLink a complete personal research memory system. 

 Planned improvements include: 

 Full PDF text extraction and document parsing.
OCR for scanned papers and research images.
Persistent research libraries beyond browser storage.
Semantic search across personal notes and papers.
Automatic citation and reference graph generation.
More advanced paper diagrams and concept maps.
Better source passage and page-level citations.
Multi-paper contradiction and consensus detection.
Personalized research podcasts with multiple AI voices.
Story-based video generation from research maps.
Zotero, Obsidian, and Markdown export.
Collaborative research workspaces.
The long-term vision is for MindLink to become a living map of a person’s knowledge: a place where papers, ideas, questions, evidence, and decisions continuously connect and grow.

title: Runbook Studio
pitch: Procedures that people and agents write, run and improve together. When a step no longer matches reality, the run records it, and the agent turns that into a fix.
about_excerpt: Procedures that people and agents write, run and improve together. When a step no longer matches reality, the run records it, and the agent turns that into a fix. Like Comment Story Updates A procedure held as structured data. Each step carries an instruction, a check saying what proof looks like, and an optional condition. Inspiration We run a small agency and a SaaS product on our own infrastructure, so we live on written procedures. Onboarding a client, restoring a backup, rotating a credential. They get written once, carefully, and then the software underneath them changes. A tab is renamed, a field moves, a step becomes somebody else's job. Within months a good portion of the document is wrong. What struck us is why that happens. The moment you discover a procedure is wrong is precisely the moment you cannot fix it. You are mid-task, under time pressure, and correcting the document is somebody else's job. So you work around it silently and move on, and the next person hits the same wall. WebMCP suggested a way out. If the procedure is something an agent can read and edit while you are standing in front of it, then finding the error and fixing it stop being separate jobs. What it does Runbook Studio holds a procedure as structured data rather than prose. Every step has a title, an instruction, an optional check stating what proof looks like, and an optional condition that sends the run to a different step when something is already true. Because the steps are data, three things become possible in one place. Write it with the agent. Ask it to split a vague step, add checks, reorder, or add a condition, and watch the document rearrange. Every change the agent makes is marked on the page. Run it with the agent. A run walks the steps in order, honouring conditions. At each step you confirm the check, or you record a blocker saying what you found instead. Improve it from the run. The blocker is pinned to the step that failed. Afterwards, the agent reads it and amends that step to match reality. That loop is the point. Documentation that gets better every time somebody uses it. The model is domain-neutral. Three examples ship with the app: onboarding a client into a CRM, restoring a database from a backup, and a cooking recipe. How we built it Next.js and TypeScript, client-side state, no database, no authentication. Self-hosted on our own infrastructure behind nginx-proxy. The only server-side component is an optional route that proxies to an OpenAI-compatible endpoint for the built-in agent, rate limited and turn capped. 13 tools are registered on document.modelContext, covering the full lifecycle: reading the runbook, editing steps, setting checks and conditions, running, recording blockers, and turning blockers into amendments. Design decisions worth naming: Tool descriptions are the interface: they are written for a model to read, not a developer. We tested selection accuracy by giving the raw getTools() output to models with no other context and checking which tools they chose for real instructions. Descriptions were tuned until selection was reliable across independent models. The annotations are used properly. readOnlyHint on read tools, untrustedContentHint wherever user-written content flows back to the model. Chrome's budgets are respected: names under 30 characters, descriptions under 500, parameter descriptions under 150, and an output guard that trims oversized responses with a hint to use a narrower tool instead. Tools stay same-origin. exposedTo is unset, so no cross-origin frame can call them. Registration takes an AbortSignal: the execution-time signal is treated as optional, since it is not supplied in the Chrome build we tested against. The app also ships with its own agent, so it needs no browser flag and no ChatGPT to try. A built-in harness discovers the page's tools with getTools() and runs them with executeTool(), either manually or by sending a sentence to a model that chooses the tools itself. With no model configured, manual mode still works with zero setup. Verification was done against Chrome for Testing with native WebMCP, driving executeTool through Playwright and asserting on the resulting DOM, so no tool is reported working on the basis of code inspection alone. Challenges we ran into The API is new and the documentation moves. Older material uses navigator.modelContext; current Chrome uses document.modelContext. The API is undefined outside a secure context, which makes several obvious testing approaches fail silently rather than loudly. Steering a model reliably. Given only tool descriptions, a model would sometimes re-read every step, propose a change instead of making it, or keep editing after finishing. We fixed this with server-side guards rather than by making the tools more forgiving, because the tools have to behave correctly for any agent, not only ours. We could not test in ChatGPT's in-app browser. Our development machine is old enough that it is capped at a Chrome version predating WebMCP, and it cannot run the ChatGPT desktop app at all. So we never saw our own app inside the environment the judges will use. We compensated rather than hoped. Every tool was verified against Chrome for Testing 152 with native WebMCP, headless on our server, driving executeTool through Playwright and asserting on the resulting DOM. We separately tested tool-selection accuracy by giving the raw getTools() output to models with no other context, checking they chose the right tools for real instructions before we relied on the descriptions. The constraint turned out to be productive. Because we could not lean on ChatGPT, we built the app its own agent instead, which means anyone can try it with no browser flag, no desktop app and no API key. That is a better product than the one we would have shipped with easier hardware. Failure has to be as easy as success. If recording a blocker were harder than confirming a step, people would confirm and move on, and the loop would never close. Both controls sit together, same size, one click apart. Accomplishments that we're proud of The loop actually closes. A blocker recorded during a run becomes an amendment to the document, and the procedure is measurably more accurate afterwards than it was before somebody used it. Every tool was individually verified as firing and changing the page, not assumed correct from reading the code. The whole app is operable by keyboard, agent changes are announced through a live region, and it works with no browser flag at all. What we learned Naming is not cosmetic when a model is one of the readers. We renamed "branch" to "condition" throughout the interface, because "branch" is developer language borrowed from version control and told a first-time reader nothing. The tool kept its original name for the model. The two audiences did not want the same word. We also found that the work we did on semantic structure, accessible names and live-region announcements serves agent legibility as much as assistive technology. Both consume the page as structure rather than pixels. Building well for one turned out to be building well for the other. What's next for Runbook Studio Multiple checks per step, richer conditions, and shared runbooks so a blocker recorded by one person amends the procedure for everybody. Built With css docker javascript next.js nginx playwright typescript webmcp Try it out runbook.landingpad.digital github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I set the direction and scope, decided what the product needed to be, and reviewed every iteration of the interface. I made the calls on how checks and conditions should read to someone seeing them for the first time, which led to renaming "branch" to "condition" in the interface while keeping the original name for the model. I wrote and recorded the narration. My first time building against WebMCP, and the most interesting part was discovering how much the wording of a tool description matters when a model is the one reading it. title: Agent Search Console
pitch: SEO for the agentic web to help website owners understand, measure, and improve how effectively AI agents can discover, understand, and operate their websites.
about_excerpt:
SEO for the agentic web to help website owners understand, measure, and improve how effectively AI agents can discover, understand, and operate their websites.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 I am a technical SEO, so I spend a lot of time thinking about how machines understand websites: search crawlers, rich result parsers, AI assistants, and now agentic browsers. Technical SEO has always been about making the web more readable to non-human users. 

 That made WebMCP immediately exciting to me. Instead of an agent guessing how to use an SEO interface from buttons, screenshots, and page text, the site itself can expose structured SEO tools directly. Agent Search Console came from that idea: what would an SEO tool look like if it was built for both humans and agents from the start? 

 What it does 

 Agent Search Console is a WebMCP-powered technical SEO toolkit. 

 A human can paste a public URL and generate a technical SEO report. The app checks indexability, schema, robots.txt, sitemaps, redirects, HTTP headers, headings, meta tags, broken links, and SERP snippet signals. It then turns those checks into a readable report with scores, findings, raw evidence, and a prioritized action plan. 

 An agent can call the same functionality through WebMCP. Instead of scraping the UI, the agent can call tools like generate_seo_report , check_indexability , check_schema , or check_robots_txt and receive structured results it can use for follow-up work. 

 How we built it 

 The app is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS. 

 The SEO checks run on server-side API routes that safely fetch public URLs, parse crawler-visible HTML and headers, and return structured JSON. The full report generator runs the core checks together and creates an executive summary, section scores, detailed findings, raw checker output, and an agentActionPlan . 

 For WebMCP, the app registers browser tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . The WebMCP surface is intentionally capped at ten tools: one full report generator plus focused technical SEO checkers. The app also exposes static discovery JSON at /webmcp.json and /.well-known/webmcp.json . 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was the steep learning curve around WebMCP itself. The standard is new, and it changes how you think about a web app. I had to stop treating the UI as the only product surface and start thinking about the agent interface as a first-class experience. 

 Another challenge was output quality. SEO tools often dump raw data, but agents need structured, specific, actionable evidence. A lot of the work went into making the outputs useful: clear statuses, scores, findings, metrics, raw results, and prioritized next steps. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 I am proud that this became a genuinely passionate project, not just a wrapper around a demo API. 

 Agent Search Console has a real product direction: technical SEO tools at the core, a human-readable report experience, and an agent-readable WebMCP interface. It shows how SEO workflows can become more collaborative when humans review strategy and agents handle structured diagnosis, evidence gathering, and follow-up tasks. 

 I am also proud of keeping the tool surface focused. Instead of exposing too many generic tools, the app centers on a small set of practical technical SEO checks that map to real SEO work. 

 What we learned 

 I learned what WebMCP really is: not just another integration format, but a way for websites to describe what agents can actually do. 

 The most important shift is that agents should not have to guess. A good WebMCP app gives agents clear tool names, clear input schemas, safe execution boundaries, and useful structured outputs. That makes the web feel less like a visual maze for agents and more like a set of intentional capabilities. 

 I also learned that agent-facing output design matters as much as human UI design. If the result is vague, too raw, or poorly structured, the agent cannot do much with it. 

 What's next for Agent Search Console 

 Next, I want to scale Agent Search Console into a production-grade, comprehensive technical SEO product. 

 That means deeper crawling, richer schema validation, rendered-page analysis, historical reports, project tracking, issue monitoring, exports, and integrations with real SEO workflows. I also want to expand the WebMCP side so agents can not only diagnose issues, but help create implementation briefs, compare reports over time, and coordinate SEO fixes with developers and content teams.

title: Askew
pitch: Point at what looks wrong. Say four words. Get a measured answer, and a safe fix.
about_excerpt: Point at what looks wrong. Say four words. Get a measured answer, and a safe fix. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Measured findings: spacing, radius, and contrast, with evidence Apply confirmation: the human's click is the only write boundary Real write, real HMR reconnect: settled measurements confirm the fix Hover pinned without the pointer: a state a screenshot can't show Inspiration Every frontend session with a coding agent hits the same wall. The agent writes a page, I open it, and something is off — but I can only say "this looks cheap." So I screenshot it, paste it into a chat, and the agent guesses. It cannot see that the padding is 13px while thirty-one other surfaces use 20px . It cannot measure a 3.1:1 contrast ratio from a JPEG. It has never seen the hover state, because a screenshot cannot hold one. The browser knows all of this. It just had no way to say it. What it does Askew is a development-only Vite plugin that turns a running React app into a shared debugging surface for a browser AI agent. Click one element in your live app. Tell the agent something vague — "this looks cheap." The agent reads the real runtime truth through WebMCP: the computed cascade, the design scale the page is actually rendering, the measured contrast ratio, and how many visible instances share that source. It stages three Tailwind alternatives. Hovering A/B/C morphs the real component in place. Nothing has been written. You click Apply. One static class string changes in source, Vite HMR reconnects the selection, and the change is undoable. Two sentences and two clicks. No screenshots, no rebuilds. How WebMCP makes it possible Every Askew tool had to pass one test: it must return state that exists only in this browser tab, right now, and is unavailable from any repo, API, screenshot, or MCP server. Four things Askew reads that nothing else can hand an agent: Live DOM selection — what the human pointed at, one second ago Computed cascade — the resolved outcome of every competing declaration, not the source declarations Runtime design scale — spacing, radius, and colour frequencies derived from the rendered page, because tailwind.config is aspirational and the DOM is the truth Held interaction state — :hover and native focus, pinned and measured without a pointer An agent with perfect repo access is useless here. That is the whole argument. The design decision I am most pleased with: file writes are not an agent capability. The four tools inspect, diagnose, and stage. askew_stage_variants returns sourceWritten: false . Only the human's Apply click in Askew's own UI crosses the write boundary. Tool descriptions are the only channel for steering an agent whose system prompt you never see, so they are written as instructions — diagnose before proposing, never invent a finding when Askew reports uncertainty, warn when multiple visible instances share a source. How I built it npm workspaces, strict TypeScript. The plugin is apply: "serve" , so it does not exist in production — production-build.test.ts runs a real vite build and asserts that no instrumentation, endpoint, or capability header survives. Element-to-source identity comes from code-inspector-plugin with its editor server disabled. React 19 removed _debugSource , which quietly broke every click-to-component tool built on fiber inspection, so compile-time attributes were the only reliable route. The write path is contained by construction: the client never sends a filesystem path, only a sourceId resolved against an in-memory index of already-transformed modules, then realpath -canonicalised, root-contained, extension-gated, schema-closed, and applied as a one-for-one token replacement that must still match the full expected class string or fail 409 and write nothing. Challenges Page JavaScript cannot force :hover . That is a DevTools capability. Askew parses direct hover: utilities and applies the equivalent declarations inline, then measures. It resolves literal colour values only — anything else returns an explicit UNSUPPORTED_STATE rather than a confident no-op, because a wrong measurement is worse than a declined one. A false positive is worse than a missing finding. A dominant design value requires at least three samples and no tie. Contrast requires a resolvable opaque background or it reports ambiguity. A healthy element is reported as consistent, not silently skipped. A public write endpoint. The capability token is served to every visitor, so it is not authentication. I accepted that early and made containment carry the security model instead: an unprivileged secret-free process, two allowlisted files, an explicit token allowlist, rate limiting, and automatic baseline restore. What I learned Scope discipline is the whole game. The spec named thirteen things I would not build — multi-select, general CSS attribution, breakpoints, group-hover , AST mutation — and holding that line is why one path works end to end instead of six paths working halfway. What's next Design-token file writing so fixes become the system rather than one-off patches, and broader source-shape support beyond static single-line className literals. AI usage disclosure Built with OpenAI Codex — this hackathon's sponsor — used throughout planning, PRD/spec iteration, implementation, test writing, deployment hardening, and live browser verification. Claude Code independently exercised the running golden path and identified selection/actionability gaps; those findings were reproduced and fixed. Gemini then performed a separate architecture and edge-case review, whose valid color parsing, token validation, selection, and HTTP-status findings were verified against the code and incorporated. I made the product, scope, security, and submission decisions and reviewed the resulting changes; the assistants accelerated implementation and acted as independent code reviewers. Notes for judges The hosted demo at https://askew.xpworx.com is a deliberately writable, disposable, single-user development environment. It restores itself on startup, after three idle minutes, and from the visible Reset Demo button. If two people explore at once, changes will conflict and fail stale rather than merge — press Reset Demo and try again. The video is the authoritative uninterrupted proof. video_transcript_excerpt: Ask you. Point at what looks wrong. Every time an AI-generated interface looks a little bit wrong, the usual fix is screenshot it, paste it into a chat, and hope the agent guesses right. It usually doesn't, because a screenshot can't carry what the browser already knows. This is Ask you, a WebMCP tool running inside a real dashboard. I select the AI confidence card, and Ask you reads its live source, its computed styles, and how many other elements are just like it. Clicking analyze, it measures three real problems. The padding is 13 pixels while the rest of the page uses 20. The corners don't match the surrounding cards. And the supporting text sits under the 4.5 to 1 contrast a screen reader test would require. These are measurements, not guesses. Now the agent stages three token-level fixes through WebMCP. Hovering a direction morphs the real card immediately. No clone, no reload, and nothing written to disk yet. I pin the direction I want and click apply. Only this human click crosses the right boundary. The exact source file updates. Hot module reload reconnects the same element, and the change is undoable with one click. Here's the moment a screenshot can't show at all. I ask Ask you to hold this button's hover state without touching it. It measures the exact style a real hover would trigger live with no pointer anywhere near it. And reset demo returns the whole page to its starting state for the next visitor. The current selection, the computed cascade, the live design scale, a held interaction state. None of that exists in a screenshot or a repository, only in this browser tab right now. That's why this had to be WebMCP.

title: CommandCanvas
pitch: A shared spatial workspace where people and agents turn rough thinking into structured, attributable output on the same live canvas.
about_excerpt: A shared spatial workspace where people and agents turn rough thinking into structured, attributable output on the same live canvas. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Meetings produce sketches, decisions, tasks, and commitments, but the useful deliverable is often reconstructed afterward in another application. CommandCanvas lets the meeting itself produce structured output. People, hands, collaborators, voice, and ChatGPT work against the same live spatial objects. Instead of sending an agent a stale transcript, CommandCanvas gives it bounded capabilities over the canvas everyone is using. What it does CommandCanvas is an infinite collaboration canvas built from semantic objects rather than untyped pixels. A participant can create notes, boards, schedules, sketches, diagrams, charts, tables, decisions, actions, and meeting packets; arrange them spatially; and see who changed what. The central workflow starts with rough human thinking. A participant draws a multi-stroke sketch while explaining it, then asks the agent to make it usable. CommandCanvas preserves the original, creates a separate structured result beside it, records provenance, and adds an immutable receipt. The result is not limited to architecture: the same system supports flowcharts, generic diagrams, bar, line, and pie charts, tables, boards, and written summaries. Every input follows one path: Hands / voice / pointer / collaborator / WebMCP ↓ validated capability ↓ canonical mutation ↓ revision + receipt + Supabase sync This lets a hand gesture, a remote collaborator, and ChatGPT change the same durable workspace without creating separate sources of truth. Mutations are visible and attributable. Destructive actions are recoverable. An agent may prepare a meeting packet and stage a send request, but the human host must approve the packet and authorize the external action. WebMCP Leverage WebMCP is the product boundary, not an integration badge. CommandCanvas registers a concise Site Tools catalog with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . A supported ChatGPT host can read the current canvas and selection, create or update semantic objects, organize work, use shared history, transform selected material, prepare a packet, and request a staged send. Each tool has a strict schema, read/write annotations, cancellation support, lifecycle cleanup, phase requirements, role checks, revision guards, and compact results. Registration can remain stable or change by phase behind one feature flag, while execute-time authorization stays identical in both modes. The agent never receives camera frames, database credentials, the user's ChatGPT credential, or authority to approve an email send. WebMCP makes CommandCanvas meaningfully better because selection, object identity, room revision, collaborator activity, packet approval, and receipts are live application context. ChatGPT acts against the same objects the participants can see and manipulate rather than a detached export. Execution CommandCanvas uses Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Zustand, Zod, and a custom DOM/SVG spatial canvas. Pointer, touch, stylus, voice, and hand input converge on one intent model. Stable object changes use expected revisions; high-frequency cursor and movement previews remain ephemeral. Supabase Postgres stores rooms, objects, receipts, packet snapshots, and send requests. Supabase Presence represents connected participants. Broadcast carries cursors, revision notices, and participant-bound small-room WebRTC signaling. The no-signup judge preview creates a bounded temporary authenticated identity only after entry; durable rooms use six-digit email OTP. Browser hand input uses local MediaPipe landmarks in a worker and keeps frames on the device. It implements index-finger drawing, pinch-to-grab, two-hand resize and canvas zoom, open-palm pan, minimize, recoverable side-edge trash, and visible interaction states. Pointer, touch, keyboard, typed command, and voice equivalents remain available. Optional in-page Live Voice uses gpt-realtime-2.1 through a user-owned API project key and a narrower capability catalog. The production release completed a real controlled provider chain from spoken transcription through a create_board function call, visible board creation, and a voice receipt. A separate production provider test rasterized a sketch to PNG, sent it to an image-capable OpenAI model, validated the structured result, and preserved the source beside the generated diagram. The current release also passed 1,723 automated tests across 164 files, responsive production acceptance at nine viewport sizes, two independent browser contexts sharing Supabase Presence, cursors, durable mutations, and receipts, controlled browser-to-browser WebRTC media, and native Chrome 153 WebMCP discovery, lifecycle, and cancellation. Potential Impact The gap between discussion and follow-through appears in planning, teaching, design review, research, technical interviews, and team decision-making. CommandCanvas turns live spatial work into reusable objects while the context and participants are still present. Rough notes can become decisions and actions. A sketch can become a chart or diagram. The room can become a reviewable packet. Because the system is domain-neutral, it can support a student drawing a study model, a team mapping a launch, or an analyst sketching a chart. Creativity & Ambition The memorable interaction is not gesture control or generation alone. It is a shared semantic world in which a person can draw with an index finger, explain the idea aloud, receive a structured result, physically reposition it, watch a collaborator modify nearby work, and let ChatGPT continue through explicit capabilities. Human, collaborator, voice, and WebMCP actions appear in one receipt stream. Preserving the rough source matters. It makes the transformation understandable, inspectable, and reversible instead of hiding the human contribution behind a generated replacement. Challenges and lessons The hardest problem was maintaining one trustworthy state model across fluid previews, durable collaboration, agent tools, undo, and consequential external actions. Spatial input became more reliable when gestures produced the same small intents as a pointer instead of owning separate business logic. Agent actions became safer when registration was treated as discoverability, while every execution still rechecked current room authority and state. We also learned to separate evidence boundaries. A green source test does not prove a physical hand, real email delivery, or a ChatGPT-hosted Site Tool call. Native Chrome 153 has verified the deployed registration and lifecycle behavior; the exact ChatGPT built-in-browser invocation and final named-device hand rehearsal remain required recording gates and will not be claimed from other evidence. Try it Open the temporary no-signup judge preview at https://commandcanvas.vercel.app/demo . It needs no signup, login form, password, third-party account, API key, or configuration for the core canvas path. The public preview intentionally reports packet delivery as preview-only rather than claiming an email was sent. title: Verdiqt
pitch: Verdiqt is an agent-native web app that runs a SaaS idea through a real evidence trial: it gathers live signals, scores the idea across six judges, and returns a Build, Pivot, or Kill verdict.
about_excerpt: Verdiqt is an agent-native web app that runs a SaaS idea through a real evidence trial: it gathers live signals, scores the idea across six judges, and returns a Build, Pivot, or Kill verdict. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI made building software cheap. It did not make building the right software cheap. People now ship a SaaS product in a weekend, and find out at launch that nobody wanted it. Verdiqt moves that painful discovery to before you write the first line of code. You put your idea on trial, and a court decides whether it deserves to live. What it does You file a case: your SaaS idea in a sentence, or a link to a public GitHub repo you already built. Then the courtroom goes to work, and you watch every step happen live: The case file. The court reads your idea and writes it up: who it's for, what problem it solves, what to search for. The investigation. Real research across five real communities : Hacker News, Reddit, GitHub, Stack Overflow, and Product Hunt. Every finding appears on screen with a link to its source, and every source reports honestly: gathered, failed, or empty. If the first search comes back thin, the court automatically widens its search. The deliberation. Six AI judges each take one question: "Is the pain real? Is anyone actively looking for this? Who already exists? Who would pay? Can you reach these people? Can you build it fast enough?" Each judge delivers their score the moment they finish, you literally watch the bench board fill in, one verdict at a time. The ruling. A presiding judge reads the entire case file and rules: BUILD, PIVOT, or KILL —> with a score out of 100, the reasoning behind every number, and exactly one recommended next step (a real, cheap test you can run this week). A full trial takes about a minute. And if you refine your idea and try again, the court remembers: the evidence you marked as important and the previous ruling follow your case, so every iteration builds on the last. How we built it Zero cash out of pocket. The whole product runs on free tiers and hackathon credits: one small server runs the website and the research pipeline, the AI judges run on free model APIs, and when one provider's daily quota runs dry, the court automatically switches to a backup provider mid-trial and keeps ruling. Constraints became design: the court paces itself under rate limits, shows its deliberation while it works, and never wastes a token. The model argues; the code rules. Anti-hallucination isn't a prompt, it's enforced in code. Judges may only cite evidence the court actually gathered: invented citations are stripped automatically, and a high score that loses its citations gets capped. When public evidence is thin, the judge is allowed to use domain judgment but the ruling must say so, out loud, in the rationale. Uncertainty is never dressed up as certainty. Privacy without accounts. No sign-up. Your browser gets an unguessable key; only its fingerprint is stored. Your cases are yours, anyone else asking for them gets an identical "not found.", don't worry. Challenges we ran into Running a multi-stage AI pipeline on free tiers meant treating every token and every request as scarce... the wait-and-retry pacing, the provider failover, and the one-at-a-time trial queue all exist because of it. And WebMCP is new enough that the tool contract itself was a design problem: we learned that the workflow belongs inside the tool descriptions, so agents teach themselves the journey. Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete, evidence-cited validation trial in about a minute. A deliberation you can actually watch. A surface that serves two audiences at once... humans get a courtroom, agents get a toolbox, and each can see the other working. What we learned Never think you have enough time to build something. What's next for Verdiqt GitHub sign-in to put your whole repo graveyard on trial at once, re-trials over time to watch a verdict change as markets move, and Reddit's expanded API access for even deeper community evidence. These are the Graphs got by setting the parameters as in the Image Nirnay-Parameters 1 b and 1 a These are the Graphs got by setting the parameters as in the Image Nirnay-Parameters 2 b and 2 a Home page After changing some parameters (Random parameters part B) Home page After changing some parameters (Random parameters part A) These are the test results that shows all passed 46/46 Inspiration We spend a lot of time in control systems coursework, and tuning a controller is a strange kind of work: it is entirely about numbers, but you do all of it by staring at pictures. You drag a gain, you squint at a step response, you decide the wobble looks a bit better, you drag again. When we started reading the WebMCP spec, the first thing we wanted to know was what an agent could actually do on a page like that. The answer turned out to be almost nothing, and the reason was specific enough to be interesting. A step response, a Bode plot and a root locus are drawn on an HTML <canvas> . A canvas is coloured pixels. There is no text under it, no DOM, nothing to scrape. Hand a vision model a screenshot of a step response and ask for the overshoot and you get "roughly 25%" — a guess read off pixel positions. You cannot tune a controller on "roughly". The entire task is hitting a number like "under 10%", and 12% and 18% call for opposite corrections. So this was not a case of an agent being clumsy with a UI. The information the agent needed did not exist anywhere it could reach. It only existed as floating point numbers inside the running program. That felt like the sharpest possible answer to "why WebMCP?", so we built the page around it. What it does Nirnay is a control-system design bench. You pick a plant, drag sliders for the three PID gains, and three plots redraw instantly — step response, Bode, and a root locus / pole-zero map. On the right there is a scoreboard: every performance metric with a green PASS or red FAIL chip against design targets you set yourself. The page exposes eight WebMCP tools, so an AI agent in the same page can read the exact simulation numbers and tune alongside you. The important part is that there is one shared state behind everything. The sliders and the agent's tools write to the same place. When the agent changes a gain, the sliders physically move, the plots redraw and the scoreboard updates while you watch. You can grab a slider back mid-conversation and the agent's next reading reflects it. Neither side is driving a copy of the other's world. There is also an agent activity log on the page that prints a line every time a tool is called, so a human watching the screen can see exactly what just happened and why. The page opens in a deliberately failing state — 50.6% overshoot against a 10% target, three of four specs red. That is on purpose. It gives the agent something real to fix instead of a victory lap. The eight tools Five read, three write. Read: get_system (full current setup), run_step_response (exact overshoot, rise time, settling time, steady-state error), get_frequency_response (gain and phase margins, crossover frequencies), get_pole_zero_map (closed-loop poles, damping, and how far the gain can be pushed before instability), evaluate_design (score against targets, and what is still failing and by how much). Write: set_controller_gains , set_plant , set_design_spec . Three design decisions shaped how well this actually works: Every write tool returns the full measured result. set_controller_gains does not reply "done". It replies with the new overshoot, settling time, margins, pole positions and a pass/fail verdict. The obvious design is write-then-read, two calls per attempt. Returning the measurement with the write halves the round trips, but the real reason is that it keeps the agent anchored to a measurement instead of to its own prediction of what those gains would do. Agents are good at confidently predicting the wrong outcome. No tool ever returns a bare OK. Every response carries numbers the agent can check itself against. That is what lets it notice a change made things worse and back it out, rather than marching in the wrong direction. Bad input gets a sentence, not a stack trace. Pass a string where a number belongs and you get Error: Kp must be a finite number, got a string. A crashed tool call teaches an agent nothing. A sentence naming the mistake lets it retry. Read tools are marked with readOnlyHint so the browser does not interrupt with a confirmation prompt on every measurement, which matters a lot once the agent starts iterating. How we built it Everything runs in the browser. No server, no backend, no libraries, no build step — plain JavaScript files the browser loads directly. That was a deliberate choice: one deployable artifact, one failure point, and nothing between the plot and the tool that could make them disagree. The numerics, roughly in layers: Polynomial arithmetic as the base, since transfer functions are ratios of polynomials. Durand–Kerner for root finding, which chases all roots simultaneously. Roots sitting exactly at zero stall it, so those get peeled off first. RK4 integration for the step response, running twenty times finer than it records so the stored curve is smooth and trustworthy. Bisection to locate the gain and phase crossover frequencies exactly, rather than reporting the closest point on a sampled grid. Root locus by sweeping gain and matching each root to its nearest previous position, so drawn branches follow one root smoothly instead of jumping where two roots pass close together. Tool registration sits behind a feature check, so in a browser without WebMCP the page is simply a complete engineering tool with no agent. Nothing breaks and nothing looks broken. Who built what Nirnay was built by two of us. Challenges we ran into The bug that the cross-check caught. The gain at which a system goes unstable can be computed two entirely different ways: from the root locus, tracking roots in one mathematical space, and from the frequency response, tracking phase in a completely different one. They share no code. We wrote a test asserting they agree. They did not. The root locus said 6, the frequency path said 6.0577. The root locus was right. The bug was a rare edge case in the frequency path: the search grid happened to land exactly on the answer, which broke an assumption the refinement step depended on. We would never have found that by looking at a graph. Both curves looked fine. It is exactly the kind of quiet wrongness that makes a tool useless to an agent, because the agent has no way to sanity-check what it is handed — it will act on 6.0577 with total confidence. Testing before implementing. The test suites were written independently of the implementation and check against answers known from theory, not from our own code: closed-form textbook formulas for second-order overshoot and peak time, matched to within 0.5%, and classic worked examples whose margins can be derived by hand. 46/46 numerics tests and 111/111 browser tests pass from a fresh clone. Testing the browser half. Node cannot test browser behaviour, so there is a second suite that loads the real page markup, fakes the WebMCP connection, and checks the things that only exist in a browser: that all eight tools register, that each describes its inputs properly, that read tools are correctly marked read-only, that bad input produces a readable error, and that when a tool changes a gain, the sliders on the page actually move. That last assertion is the entire human-and-agent premise in one line. Learning the platform. A few things cost us time and are not obvious from the spec alone: it is document.modelContext , not navigator.modelContext , which many older examples still use. Tools registered inside iframes are not discovered, even same-origin, so everything has to live on the top-level page. The declarative HTML form API is not supported yet, so registration is JavaScript only. And WebMCP is a secure-context feature, so opening the file over file:// silently gives you no tools at all. Writing descriptions the agent actually reads. Our first pass had terse tool descriptions and the agent kept reaching for generic browser control before listing site tools. Tightening the input schemas — real descriptions on every property, additionalProperties: false — was what made it go straight to the right tool. What we learned Th

title: Rolequiry
pitch: Interview the job before it interviews you.
about_excerpt: Interview the job before it interviews you. Like Comment Story Updates AI job-search tools helped me find roles that looked like a fit. But that fit was still being inferred from the same job description I was trying to understand. Is this actually the work I think I am applying for — and should I let an AI decide that from the JD alone? I did not want another fit score. I wanted to do due diligence on one job. That is Rolequiry : a candidate-side investigation workspace that separates what an employer has stated from what a candidate still needs to know. A second official source can corroborate a published “50% travel” figure while the lived travel cadence remains unresolved. And because the agent and the page share the same case through WebMCP, changing a priority in the UI — without telling the agent — can cause Rolequiry to recompute the case and return a different investigation target on the next check. Inspiration Rolequiry started from a problem I kept running into in my own job search. AI could already help me discover jobs, compare a JD with my background, and prepare an application. But that still did not tell me whether the job itself was what I thought I was applying for. A job description is written to explain what the company wants from a candidate. It is much worse at answering what the candidate needs to know before investing years of their career in the role. “Ownership” might mean real authority over architecture and implementation, or accountability for delivery while important decisions still require approval elsewhere. “50% travel” tells me the published requirement, but not whether that means regular weekly trips, short launch spikes, or long consecutive stretches onsite. I have used this workflow on real technical roles I was personally evaluating, not only on the synthetic fixtures used to make the demo repeatable. What I kept finding was: A JD could answer the literal question and still leave the decision question unresolved. That became the core idea behind Rolequiry: Supporting an employer's written claim is not the same as resolving the candidate's uncertainty. Most career tools help you get the job. Rolequiry helps you investigate whether the job is worth getting. A bad fit is expensive for both sides. If candidates understand the job better before joining, they can make a better decision — and employers are less likely to hire someone who expected a different job. What it does Rolequiry is a candidate-side due diligence tool for investigating a job before committing to it. A candidate gives an agent a career summary and a job description. The agent turns the posting into testable claims and proposes the few decision variables that seem most important. The candidate confirms or changes those priorities. From there, Rolequiry keeps the case: what the employer said, what the candidate cares about, what evidence has been found, what is still unknown, and which unanswered question is worth investigating next. The output is a persistent pre-offer decision record : what is sufficiently resolved, what still blocks the decision, why it remains unresolved, what evidence is attached to each claim, and which question should be taken to a recruiter, hiring manager, or team member next. A posting can say “50% travel is expected.” That settles the published number. It does not tell you whether that means weekly trips, launch spikes, or long consecutive onsite stretches for this particular team. Rolequiry deliberately does not produce a fit score or tell the candidate to accept or reject an offer. The model can interpret and research; the candidate keeps the judgment. Why WebMCP An agent can already read a job description and produce a fit analysis. That was exactly the limitation I wanted to get past. If the final career judgment should not live only inside a model answer, the candidate needs inspectable state they can change: confirmed priorities, employer claims, evidence, unresolved questions, and the next investigation target. With WebMCP, the page and the agent work against the same Rolequiry case . Fastest proof Ask “What should I investigate next?” Change Travel → CRITICAL directly in the page UI. Do not mention the change in chat. Ask “Check again.” On the next check, Rolequiry recomputes from shared case state and returns a different investigation target. When the agent finds evidence, it writes that evidence back to the active claim instead of leaving it buried in conversation history. Rolequiry owns the confirmed priorities, typed claims, evidence provenance, derived uncertainty, authoritative next probe, and decision dossier. This problem is especially visible in forward-deployed engineering, solutions engineering, enterprise AI, and technical deployment, where similar titles can hide very different expectations around travel, coding share, technical authority, and concurrent workload. How I used AI ChatGPT was used for product reasoning, adversarial review, interaction design, and early live workflow testing. One early test exposed a bad UX: the user had to understand internal claim IDs and tool order, and a claim-name mismatch could leave the case without an active probe. I changed the normal interaction to: Analyze → confirm → investigate A later live routing test exposed a more important failure: the model re-ranked the app-selected Travel probe because the posting already stated a 50% travel figure. I changed select_decision_changer so the returned target is explicitly app-owned and authoritative, added claim kind, status, and authority coverage to its response, and pinned that scenario as a regression. I then repeated the live-site routing flow with Grok 4.6 through OpenCode: 4/4 scored PASS pre-hardening, and 2/2 PASS on the current hardened contracts. How I used Codex Codex was used throughout implementation, refactoring, debugging, testing, and WebMCP contract changes. The application intentionally keeps the important decision math out of the model: coverage, unresolvedness, tension, status, ranking, and dossier generation are app-derived. Key features Candidate-confirmed priorities and app-owned next probe — the model does not get to silently choose what matters. Shared UI/agent state through WebMCP — a UI change can alter the next investigation target without being restated in chat. Written claims stay separate from lived-experience uncertainty — another official source can repeat “50% travel” while the actual cadence remains materially ambiguous. Evidence provenance and employer-domain authority checks — mismatched or uncheckable employer sources stay visible but out of the decision math. Persistent decision dossier — unresolved blockers become concrete questions routed to a recruiter, hiring manager, or team member. How I built it The basic loop is: claim → candidate priority → active question → evidence → what is still unknown Eight page-native WebMCP tools on /case share the same CaseStore as the UI. deriveCase computes coverage, unresolvedness, tension, status, probe eligibility, and ranking. deriveDossier turns those claims into case-level progress, remaining decision blockers, and an interview question pack. WebMCP is registered page-natively through document.modelContext . There is no remote MCP server. The connected agent keeps the raw career narrative and performs external research; Rolequiry stores only the structured decision state it needs. Employer-official research earns authority only when the source domain matches the posting’s organization. Mismatched and uncheckable sources stay recorded and visible, but they never enter coverage or tension. Rolequiry does not independently authenticate authorship or page contents. Verification I keep deterministic browser evidence separate from model-facing evidence. 169 tests across 24 files — all passing 13-step deterministic browser journey — PASS across all 8 /case WebMCP tools Current hardened contracts — 2/2 model-facing PASS on September 3 Pre-hardening contracts — 4/4 scored model-facing PASS on September 2 A poisoned cross-domain EMPLOYER_OFFICIAL / CHALLENGES write is flagged without changing authority coverage, tension, or the materially ambiguous state One additional September 2 run is explicitly unscored because its research turn stalled. Full eval details are in the public repository. How to test it No login is required. Open https://rolequiry.com/case in ChatGPT’s in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled. 20-second shared-state test Ask “What should I investigate next?” Change Travel to CRITICAL directly in the page UI. Do not mention the change in chat. Ask “Check again.” Rolequiry should recompute from shared case state and return a different investigation target. For the full flow, give the agent a career summary plus a real job description and say “Analyze this role for me.” Confirm or revise the proposed priorities, ask it to investigate the selected probe, then ask “Where does the decision stand?” The demo video u

title: Seigyo
pitch: Seigyo lets browser agents investigate production incidents, correlate live evidence, propose safe recoveries, obtain exact human approval, execute actions, and verify recovery through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Seigyo lets browser agents investigate production incidents, correlate live evidence, propose safe recoveries, obtain exact human approval, execute actions, and verify recovery through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Production incident response is fragmented. Operators jump between monitoring dashboards, logs, deployment records, service maps, runbooks, and customer reports while an outage continues to affect users. AI agents can help investigate this information, but recovery introduces a serious safety problem. An agent should not make a production change simply because it found a likely cause. A human must understand and approve the exact intervention. Seigyo explores a better collaboration model: the agent investigates and verifies, while the human keeps control of consequential actions. Seigyo is the Japaese word for control. What it does Seigyo is a human-governed incident investigation and recovery console powered by WebMCP. A browser agent can use structured tools exposed directly by the application to: List and inspect incidents Query service metrics Search operational logs Review deployments Map service dependencies Correlate evidence and identify likely causes Prepare a specific recovery proposal Execute an approved intervention Verify recovery against the customer path Reverse an intervention when necessary Every tool call is shown in an animated Agent Console using clear activity labels such as “Searching logs” and “Verifying recovery.” Before a recovery action can run, Seigyo presents the human with the exact action, target, evidence, expected effect, risk, and expiry. Approval grants permission only. The agent must still call the execution tool and then verify the result. MyShop is a connected storefront used to demonstrate the complete customer impact loop. A faulty checkout release creates a real incident in Seigyo. After the agent investigates and the human approves the recovery, the storefront becomes healthy and the customer can complete the same purchase. The storefront is only one example. The same interaction model can support infrastructure operations, security response, data systems, internal platforms, and other environments where agents need structured access with human control. Why WebMCP WebMCP allows the visible application and its agent interface to exist together. Instead of making the agent interpret screenshots or rely on hidden automation, Seigyo exposes explicit tools with typed inputs and structured results. The operator can continue using the normal interface while the agent works through the same live environment. This makes the interaction clearer for both sides: The agent receives reliable operational data. The human can see what the agent is doing. Approval happens inside the relevant application. Recovery remains bound to the exact incident and action. The agent can verify whether the customer-facing problem was actually fixed. This kind of live, browser-native collaboration would be difficult to deliver through a traditional dashboard alone. How we built it The Seigyo and MyShop interfaces are built with React, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS. The operations API runs on Cloudflare Workers. Persistent environment state is stored in a SQLite-backed Cloudflare Durable Object, which provides a serialized boundary for incidents, services, deployments, metrics, logs, approvals, executions, carts, and orders. WebMCP tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool . Each tool has a defined input schema and an asynchronous execution callback connected to the operations API. Shared TypeScript contracts and Zod schemas keep the browser tools, interfaces, and backend aligned. WebSockets distribute operational changes so Seigyo and an already-open storefront remain synchronized. Recovery approvals are short-lived and bound to the operator session, proposal, action, and current causal state. Execution is idempotent, stale approvals are rejected, and completed interventions produce verifiable recovery records. The environment models connected services and causal behavior. Correct interventions restore the affected customer path, while unrelated actions do not magically resolve the incident. Challenges we faced The hardest challenge was designing human approval without turning it into a decorative confirmation button. Approval had to authorize one precise action while keeping execution and verification under the agent’s control. We also had to keep multiple browser surfaces synchronized, preserve the customer’s cart during an outage, prevent stale or replayed approvals, and make repeated demonstrations deterministic without deleting operational history. Another challenge was presenting service dependencies clearly across different screen sizes. The topology now calculates every connection from the measured card positions instead of relying on fixed SVG coordinates. Accomplishments We built an end-to-end incident story that starts healthy, introduces a checkout regression through a new release, exposes the resulting customer failure, supports evidence-based agent investigation, requires exact human approval, executes a reversible recovery, verifies multiple healthy samples, and ends with a successful customer purchase. The normal interfaces remain usable without WebMCP, while WebMCP adds a structured collaboration layer for agents. What we learned The strongest use of WebMCP is not simply giving an agent more buttons. It is giving the agent a precise operational contract while keeping important human decisions visible and enforceable. We also learned that recovery should be measured from the customer path, not merely from whether a command returned successfully. What's next Next, Seigyo could connect to real monitoring, deployment, ticketing, and change-management systems. The same approval and verification model could also support security response, database operations, infrastructure maintenance, and other high-impact workflows. title: CueMend
pitch: A WebMCP rehearsal room where humans protect dramatic beats, agents exhaustively repair caption timing, and every committed WebVTT track is revision-bound and verifiable.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP rehearsal room where humans protect dramatic beats, agents exhaustively repair caption timing, and every committed WebVTT track is revision-bound and verifiable. Like Comment Story Updates Icon MCP demo Inspiration Caption timing is both mechanical and artistic. Software can detect overlapping captions, reading-rate problems, missing speakers, and visual collisions, but it cannot decide whether an audience laugh, lighting reveal, silence, or actor's breath carries artistic meaning. CueMend explores a better division of responsibility: let the computer perform exhaustive, inspectable checking while the stage manager retains artistic judgment and final authority. It is designed around small theatres, school productions, and live-event teams that need systematic caption checks without handing the meaning of a performance to an optimizer. What it does CueMend opens a fictional 32-second rehearsal containing ten caption cues and seven independently reproducible timing issues. Through WebMCP, a compatible browser agent can: inspect the exact rehearsal state and revision; audit caption overlap, minimum gaps, duration, reading rate, speakers, protected beats, and reserved screen regions; ask CueMend's deterministic browser engine to evaluate all 3^8 = 6,561 bounded candidate tracks; stage up to three zero-conflict alternatives without changing the active captions; preview or discard an exact proposal; commit only the plan explicitly selected and approved by a human; run a post-commit deterministic re-audit; export editable WebVTT plus a SHA-256-bound evidence certificate. The 6,561 figure is the exact search space of this demo: eight adjustable cues, each with three authored repair variants. It is not a universal theatre number, and the engine never invents or rewrites dialogue. The signature interaction begins when the cheapest proposal crosses Jon's optional final breath. The stage manager decides that the breath matters and protects it in the visible UI. CueMend increments the workspace revision, reports an additional conflict, and makes the old proposal stale. An attempt to use the old revision receives a structured STALE_REVISION refusal. The agent must inspect the new state and replan under the human's updated constraint. After the human selects and approves one exact plan, a temporary commit capability appears. The commit is bound to the approved plan, current revision, protected beats, profile, and digest. After it is used, mutation tools retire. The finished rehearsal reaches revision 3 with zero conflicts under the named demo profile. Why WebMCP matters CueMend remains usable as an ordinary web application, but WebMCP turns it into a shared, state-aware collaboration surface for humans and agents. Without WebMCP, a browser agent would otherwise have to infer domain state from the DOM, automate brittle coordinates, or depend on a CueMend-specific integration. With WebMCP, the page exposes domain-level tools over the same live state the person sees: exact cue IDs, locks, revisions, alternatives, structured errors, and safe next actions. Tool availability follows the real authority state: a fresh workspace exposes inspect, audit, and stage tools; a current proposal adds preview and discard; a stale proposal cannot be previewed or committed; the commit tool appears only after a person approves the exact artifact; after commit, mutation capabilities disappear and verification becomes available. This means the human does not merely click a cosmetic approval button. A human decision changes the optimization problem, invalidates previous agent work, and changes which capabilities the page exposes to the agent. Without WebMCP, CueMend is a caption-checking and repair application. With WebMCP, it becomes a standardized, tab-bound workspace where repetitive work can be delegated to a compatible browser agent without surrendering artistic decisions. How we built it CueMend is a dependency-free static application built with semantic HTML, responsive CSS, and native JavaScript ES modules. A deterministic engine audits interval, duration, reading-rate, speaker, protected-beat, and reserved-region constraints. It enumerates the exact 6,561-candidate demo search space and ranks valid tracks by: number of changed cues; total timing movement; semantic changes such as speaker or position; a stable lexical key for deterministic output. A shared command layer owns revision validation, proposal and plan digests, human-only operations, idempotent request IDs, session-bound commit receipts, and structured error recovery. The ordinary UI and WebMCP handlers call this same command layer and update the same visible artifact. The page registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . Registrations are retired with AbortSignal when the capability inventory changes. Every consequential handler repeats runtime validation because schemas and annotations are not treated as security boundaries. Web Crypto produces SHA-256 digests, and Node's built-in test runner verifies the engine, authority model, and dynamic tool lifecycle without third-party packages. Challenges we ran into The hardest design problem was making human approval substantive instead of decorative. The person needed to change the actual optimization problem by protecting an artistic beat, while the system needed to invalidate an in-flight proposal reliably and explain the recovery path clearly. The evolving WebMCP API also required a careful distinction between registration-lifetime cancellation and execution cancellation. CueMend registers or retires tools only when the available capability set changes, while revalidating all important state immediately before mutation. Another challenge was keeping every numerical and accessibility-related claim auditable. CueMend names its exact demo profile, reports the number of candidates evaluated, preserves dialogue, and displays its limitations instead of implying universal caption compliance. Accomplishments that we're proud of A human decision causes a real agent replan, not a cosmetic approval step. The deterministic engine evaluates every candidate in its disclosed finite search space. A stale proposal cannot be previewed, approved, or committed after a human changes a protected beat. Commit is bound to the selected plan, current locks, profile, revision, and SHA-256 digest. One request ID can apply a change at most once and returns the same receipt if replayed. The final artifact is editable WebVTT rather than a result trapped inside a chat. The visible application remains fully usable when WebMCP is unavailable. The complete native WebMCP journey was repeated three times from a clean reset in Chrome 151, with ten native calls per run and a genuine stale-revision refusal each time. What we learned The most useful WebMCP tools are small domain verbs over live, visible state. Tool count matters less than clear preconditions, explicit postconditions, recoverable errors, and meaningful authority boundaries. Dynamic tool registration becomes especially valuable when it mirrors real authority: the agent should not even receive a commit capability until a person has approved the exact artifact. We also learned that a strong agent experience does not require hiding the application behind chat. Human and agent interfaces can operate on the same state, with every transition remaining visible, reversible before approval, and verifiable afterward. What's next Future versions could add real WebVTT import, user-authored production profiles, venue-specific safe areas, rehearsal-note exchange, and integration with existing caption playback systems. Those extensions would preserve the same principle: automation proposes and proves mechanical changes, while production teams retain control over artistic intent. Important limitations All dialogue and production details in the built-in rehearsal are fictional and rights-safe. The CueMend Demo Theatre Profile v1 is a transparent demonstration profile, not a universal WCAG, broadcast, venue, legal, accessibility, or artistic standard. CueMend does not claim to certify accessibility or replace professional caption review. No generative model runs inside the submitted application; its repair engine is deterministic and local to the browser.
