title: Liha Live Preview
pitch: A review session your agent can join — it reads the source behind a comment, resizes your preview, scrolls your screen to what you meant, and answers in the thread while you watch.
about_excerpt: A review session your agent can join — it reads the source behind a comment, resizes your preview, scrolls your screen to what you meant, and answers in the thread while you watch. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Design feedback usually reaches a developer as a sentence and a screenshot, and the first ten minutes go on translating "the hero button is too big" into a file, a line and a selector. Plenty of tools now capture that target for you. BugHerd has recorded a CSS selector for years. Vercel's vercel comments CLI prints one, alongside the React component tree, and exposes the thread over a remote MCP server. That part of the problem is solved, and we are not going to pretend otherwise. What none of them can do is put the agent in the room. Every one of those integrations is out of band — a clipboard buffer, a local server on the developer's machine, or a remote API the agent calls from somewhere else. The reviewer is on one screen and the agent is somewhere else entirely, and a person carries messages between them. WebMCP changes that specific thing: the page the reviewer is looking at can publish tools to the agent sitting beside them. So we built the review tool for when both of you are in the same place. What it does Before: a screenshot and "make this smaller" arrive in chat. Someone reopens the build, finds the element, guesses the breakpoint, and writes a prompt. With Live Preview: the reviewer clicks the button. The click records the selector, the DOM snippet, the page, the viewport and the version. An agent in the same tab reads exactly that, scrolls the reviewer to it, checks it at 390px, reads the CSS behind it, and answers in the thread. A coding agent fixes the source and the same URL becomes version 2. Nobody translated anything. Liha Live Preview gives any build artifact a stable review URL — a static site, an image, a PDF, or a page that is already deployed. liha-preview deploy . builds the project and publishes it. One URL, and every later version arrives at the same one. A reviewer opens it and clicks the thing they mean . Liha records the CSS selector, tag name, text content, an HTML snippet, the page path, the viewport size and the exact version — plus a pin, box, freehand or arrow in normalized coordinates. An agent reads that feedback through WebMCP , in the same page the human is looking at, and can reply inside the thread under its own name. The agent edits the source, rebuilds, and publishes a new immutable version to the same URL , then resolves the thread. Nobody copy-pastes anything, and the reviewer never needs a new link. What humans and agents do together Two of the thirteen browser tools move the reviewer's own screen , and two more read whatever version is on it. Together with writes that land in the sidebar the reviewer is watching, these are the reasons this is a WebMCP entry and not a REST client: focus_comment — the agent scrolls the human's screen to a comment, selects it, and outlines the element inside the preview. You say "show me what Sam meant" and their view moves. set_viewport — the agent resizes the preview to 390px, looks at what breaks, and comments on it. Checking a responsive bug becomes something it does, not something it asks you to do. read_artifact_file — the artifact runs in a sandboxed cross-origin iframe, so an agent cannot see inside it. This reads the HTML and CSS of the version the human currently has on screen — not necessarily the latest — so it can name the rule that needs changing without asking which build. add_comment with replyTo — the agent answers in the thread under its own name, and the reply appears in the sidebar with no reload, because tool calls post through the same API client as a human action and refresh the same sidebar. Running the other way, a click records the selector, tag, text, HTML snippet, page path, viewport and immutable version — captured at the moment of the gesture , not re-inferred later against a page that has since changed. That provenance is what keeps the feedback trustworthy three versions on. What the browser cannot do, we say plainly: an agent in the page can triage, read the source and reply, but it cannot edit your repository — a web page never gets a filesystem. That is what the local MCP server and the CLI are for: eight tools confined to the project root, the same review and the same threads, from the terminal. WebMCP connects the agent to the human's browser context; local MCP connects the coding agent to the developer's workspace; the product is the loop between them. All three surfaces can reply to a reviewer. How we built it A pnpm monorepo, TypeScript throughout, six packages: @liha-cli/webmcp — thirteen tools on document.modelContext . Details we went out of our way to get right: Only the annotations WebMCP actually defines. The spec's ToolAnnotations dictionary has exactly two members, readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint . destructiveHint , idempotentHint and openWorldHint are base-MCP server-side hints, dropped before an agent sees them. We set only the real two — readOnlyHint explicitly, including false on the writers — and a test fails the build if anything else appears. Chrome's metadata budgets enforced by test : 30 characters per name, 500 per description, 150 per parameter description. It caught a 246-character parameter description we had written. Registration that survives the spec moving. provideContext() and unregisterTool() were removed during 2026, unregistration became AbortSignal -based, and the getter moved from navigator to document . We probe document , then navigator , then the global object, and support all five teardown shapes, each with a test, because guessing wrong means zero tools and no error message anywhere. Untrusted content is fenced. Reviewer text and artifact source both come back inside delimiters, with an explicit note that they describe requested changes and are not instructions addressed to the agent. Registered in the top-level document , artifact sandboxed in the iframe — ChatGPT's browser does not discover tools inside iframes. API — Hono on Cloudflare Workers, D1 for metadata, R2 for artifacts. Route code talks to Database / ObjectStore ports that the real bindings satisfy structurally, so integration tests run the shipped SQL and migrations against node:sqlite in milliseconds. Web — React, Vite, TanStack Router/Query. Light/dark/system themes, English and Japanese, fully keyboard-driven. @liha-cli/mcp — a local stdio MCP server, so a coding agent outside the browser can read the same review and publish the fix. It only ever touches files under the project root it was given. @liha-cli/live-preview — a CLI with --json on every command; stdout carries exactly one JSON document and nothing else. Uploaded HTML is untrusted code , so every preview version is served from its own origin ( <slug>--<version>.preview.example.com ) inside an iframe sandboxed without allow-same-origin , with a matching CSP header. There is an end-to-end test that loads hostile script into a preview and asserts it can read neither the app's storage nor its parent frame. Challenges we ran into Coordinates that survive. A comment left on a 1280px desktop has to land in the right place on a phone. Everything is stored normalized 0–1 — against the rendered box for images and PDF pages, against the full scroll size for HTML, with the injected bridge reporting scroll offsets so the overlay re-projects on every scroll. Talking to an opaque origin. The preview iframe has no origin we can check, so event.origin is useless for authentication. Identity comes from comparing event.source against the exact contentWindow we created — a reference no other document can forge. Root-absolute asset paths. Bundlers emit /assets/app.js . Under a path mount those 404, which is why each version gets its own hostname rather than a path prefix — and it means a stale service worker from v1 cannot affect v2. Counting. An early bug had the agent reporting "2 open comments" while the sidebar said "1" — the agent was counting messages and the UI was counting threads. Counts are per thread everywhere now. Accomplishments we're proud of 354 unit and integration tests, 86 end-to-end tests in real Chromium, on CI Zero axe-core WCAG 2.1 AA violations on every screen, in both themes and both languages, enforced in the test suite The whole loop — deploy, comment, agent fix, new version, resolve — works with no copy-paste, and there is a test that proves it What we learned Writing good tool descriptions mattered more than writing more tools. The difference between an agent using get_share_info correctly and going looking for an owner token was one sentence in the description saying what the tool is for and what it deliberately does not return. untrustedContentHint also turned out to be a design constraint, not a flag: once you take seriously that comment text is written by whoever has the link, you start fencing it, labelling it, and n
video_title: Liha Live Preview — Human Feedback Agents Can Act On | WebMCP Challenge
video_transcript_excerpt: Design feedback usually reaches a developer as a screenshot and a sentence, and the first 10 minutes go on working out what it pointed at. Leha live preview turns the review itself into something an agent can use in the same browser tab the reviewer is looking at. One command publishes a build to a URL that never changes. Every later version arrives at that same link, so nobody has to send a new one, and feedback stays attached to the version it was written on. The CLI packages the build, uploads it, and opens the stable preview as soon as it is ready. A reviewer opens the link and clicks the thing they mean. Leha records the CSS selector, the tag, the text inside it, the viewport, and the exact version captured at the moment of the gesture, not guessed at afterwards against a page that has since changed. Each comment remains anchored to that element and the visual context in which it was written. This is the part WebMCP makes possible. The page publishes 13 tools to the agent inside the same browser tab. First, the agent reads the open review as structured data, including the comment and its captured context. It then focuses that exact comment and brings the referenced element into view. Call three switches the preview to a 390-pixel mobile viewport, reproducing the exact width where the reviewer saw the layout problem in context. Call four reads the style sheet behind that element and identifies the CSS rules controlling its padding and type size. Call five posts the proposed fix directly into the review thread. After fixing the source, the agent publishes again without creating a new URL. Version two arrives at the same preview with every earlier comment still attached. The reviewer checks the change in context and resolves the feedback on the spot. Everything you have made or reviewed in one place with what other people said on it. There is no sign up. An account appears the first time you do something and signing in only carries it to your other browsers. Humans know what feels wrong. Agents know how to change it. Leha live preview gives them the same page to work on and the same link to come back to.

title: PaperPilot
pitch: An Agent-Native research studio giving ChatGPT 13 WebMCP tools to autonomously extract, compare, and draft academic papers into fully compilable LaTeX.
about_excerpt:
An Agent-Native research studio giving ChatGPT 13 WebMCP tools to autonomously extract, compare, and draft academic papers into fully compilable LaTeX.

 1 2 3 4 



 
 The Problem: Academic Research is Broken 

 Writing a literature review today requires researchers to download dozens of PDFs, manually copy-paste abstracts into a chatbox, and beg the model to summarize them. The result? The LLM hallucinates methodologies, loses track of citations, and breaks LaTeX math formatting. 

 
 I realized that LLMs don't need better prompts—they need ==Agent-Native infrastructure==. 
 

 Why this is a perfect fit for WebMCP 

 Before WebMCP, LLMs were blind to the user's UI. By implementing WebMCP, I exposed 13 strictly typed tools directly to the agent. This creates a massive UX paradigm shift: 

 
 [x] Zero Copy-Pasting: The agent fetches full-text HTML directly via extract_findings . 
 [x] No More Hallucinations: The compare_papers tool forces the agent to read structured matrix data. 
 [x] Synchronous Collaboration: When the agent calls draft_section , the manuscript in my React UI updates instantaneously. 
 

 How I Built It: The Core Mechanisms 

 I built PaperPilot using Next.js 14, React 18, and TypeScript, deployed seamlessly on Vercel. To make this production-ready, I engineered three core mechanisms: 

 1. The Zero-Backend Event Bus 

 To achieve real-time UI synchronization without the latency of WebSockets, I implemented a decoupled event architecture. When ChatGPT executes a mutation tool:
 document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "draft_section" }) 
It triggers a pure async Next.js Server Action. This action mutates the local data store and emits a native DOM CustomEvent (e.g., paperpilot:outlines-changed ). The React UI listens to this bus and re-renders instantaneously. 

 2. Heuristic Extraction & Grammar-Aware Parsing 

 Academic HTML is notoriously messy. To prevent context window pollution, I engineered an extraction algorithm that isolates methodology while discarding boilerplate (Appendices, References). The extraction logic E for a document D composed of sentences s i is defined as: 

 E ( D ) = ⋃ i = 1 N s i subject to class ( s i ) ≠ "ltx_bibliography" 

 Furthermore, naive sentence splitting ruins context by breaking on abbreviations like "e.g." or "et al." I parse sentences using a strict, grammar-aware Regex formula to guarantee abbreviation bypass:
 (?<=[a-z]{3,}[.!?])\s+(?=[A-Z0-9]) 

 3. Math-Safe LaTeX Compilation 

 ChatGPT frequently generates inline mathematical formulas, such as O ( log ⁡ d ) . If I blindly escaped reserved LaTeX characters (like _ or % ), it would break the math mode syntax. I engineered a custom AST-like parser that isolates $ and $ $ blocks, safely escapes rogue characters only in standard text strings, and then restores the math blocks. 

 The agent also autonomously injects \cite{} markers linked to a dynamically generated \bibitem matrix, guaranteeing ==100% compilable Overleaf code==. 

 The Proof: My 20-Paper Stress Test 

 To prove PaperPilot isn't just a brittle hackathon demo, I built an automated stress test against 20 seminal AI papers (including Attention Is All You Need and Mistral 7B ).

 What I learned & What's next 

 I learned that strict typing in WebMCP inputSchemas is the absolute key to preventing agent hallucinations. Moving forward, I plan to expand my WebMCP toolset to integrate directly with Zotero and Mendeley, allowing researchers to bring their existing private libraries into the Agent-Native web.

title: TenderLens
pitch: An autonomous agent that reads every public tender dossier so small suppliers don't have to - scoring what they qualify for, and flagging notices written so only one firm could win.
about_excerpt: An autonomous agent that reads every public tender dossier so small suppliers don't have to - scoring what they qualify for, and flagging notices written so only one firm could win. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Across the EU, roughly half of all public contracts attract a single bidder. The usual explanation is corruption. The more common one is arithmetic: a tender dossier runs 40 to 130 pages, the qualification criteria that decide whether a company may legally bid are scattered through it, and a 26-person firm has nobody who can read forty of those a month. So they stop reading, and the field empties out on its own. The two problems turn out to have the same evidence base. The document that tells a supplier you qualify for this is the same document that reveals this one was written for somebody else -- a specification fixed to 14 mm and 63.5 Wh describes exactly one laptop on the market. Once you are parsing dossiers at scale, both answers fall out of the same pass. What it does One button starts an autonomous sweep. No further human input. The agent pulls open notices, pre-filters by the supplier's value ceiling and live deadlines, then for every surviving notice: opens the dossier, extracts the qualification criteria into structured form, rules each one met / gap / unclear against the supplier's real profile with the evidence attached, screens the buyer's award history and the clause wording for integrity red flags, scores fit out of 100, estimates win probability adjusted for that buyer's historical bidder count, and writes a dated bid plan working backwards from the deadline with an owner on every step. It ends with a ranked board -- 87 down to 17 across twelve notices -- and a written bid / no-bid brief per notice. The entire reasoning trace streams to the browser while it runs: every tool call with its input, its output and its latency. The integrity screen Five detectors, each grounded in a documented single-bidding indicator: Flag Fires when SHORT_WINDOW The submission window is shorter than the customary minimum, which favours a bidder who prepared before publication THIN_COMPETITION The buyer averages under two bidders across prior tenders VENDOR_CONCENTRATION 40% or more of a buyer's prior awards went to one supplier SPEC_LOCK The specification fixes exact physical parameters instead of performance ranges, which usually describes one product on the market INCUMBENT_LOCK A qualification clause can only be satisfied by the current supplier None is presented as proof of wrongdoing, and the app never says otherwise. Each flag carries the reasoning that makes it worth a clarification question or a formal challenge. How I built it TypeScript throughout. Supabase Postgres holds the notices, the supplier profile, the run log and every assessment; Server-Sent Events carry the live trace; the deployed demo runs on Supabase Edge Functions. The agent core -- orchestrator, six tools, provider adapters, types -- depends on nothing from Node, React or Next. That is deliberate, and it buys a second runtime for free: the same engine drives a Next.js build and a Deno edge build, unmodified. The decision worth defending is deterministic core, model at the edge . Every score, verdict and flag comes from code that can be read, tested and cited. The language model writes one artefact -- the decision brief -- where prose is the deliverable. This is not a cost saving. A supplier disqualified on a criterion needs to point at the rule that fired; a score that exists only inside a model's context window cannot survive a procurement review board. The side effect is that the hosted demo runs with zero API keys -- open it and press the button. Graceful degradation at every boundary: no database falls back to the bundled corpus, Supabase unreachable mid-request falls back silently, a deep link to a never-assessed notice is assessed on demand server-side. There is no configuration in which the deployed app shows an error page instead of doing its job. The board is also published to visiting AI agents over WebMCP -- seven tools registered through document.modelContext -- so an assistant browsing the page can search, screen and re-rank it alongside the human, with every call mirrored on screen. Enterprise governance and compliance Auditability by construction. Every assessment is a row tied to a run, carrying the verdicts, flags, checklist and reasoning mode used. You can reconstruct why the agent said what it said, months later. Explainable decisions, not scores. Each verdict ships with its evidence string ("Requires EUR 600,000; profile turnover is EUR 1,850,000"). Each risk flag ships with its rationale. Row-level security on all four tables. The demo project's open policies exist because it holds nothing but synthetic notices; a real deployment scopes them to the authenticated supplier. No unsourced claims. The integrity screen surfaces the pattern and why the pattern matters -- the standard a challenge before a procurement review body is held to. Synthetic corpus. Modelled on the structure of real TED, e-Prokurimi and eNabavke publications. No real notice, buyer decision, supplier name or award record is reproduced. Monetization Two customers, one engine. 1. Suppliers -- SaaS subscription (primary). Solo EUR 49/mo: one country, weekly digest, three profiles. Team EUR 199/mo: three countries, daily sweep, unlimited profiles, bid plans exported to calendar. Agency EUR 699/mo: white label, API access, multi-client dashboards for bid-writing consultancies. The wedge is measurable. A firm bidding six times a year at roughly five days of unpaid bid effort each spends about EUR 12,000 of staff time. TenderLens removes the two days spent deciding whether to bid, and kills the disqualified-on-a-technicality bids entirely. 2. Watchdogs and journalists -- usage-based. Integrity screening billed per thousand notices analysed, with an NGO tier at cost. Anti-corruption organisations and investigative desks already do this by hand, one buyer at a time. 3. Buyers -- compliance licence (later). The same detectors run pre-publication: a procurement office checks its own draft notice for SPEC_LOCK and SHORT_WINDOW before it goes out. Sold per authority, annually. Highest margin, and the one that needs credibility from the first two to earn. Marginal cost is a few cents of model spend per notice, and zero when the deterministic engine handles it. Challenges I ran into Deciding how much judgement to hand to a model. The first version asked an LLM to rule on each criterion; it was fluent and unciteable, and a bid manager cannot take "the model thought so" to a review board. Rewriting the criterion logic as parsed thresholds and set membership made the output defensible and, unexpectedly, made the product better -- the evidence line next to each verdict is what users actually read. Scoring calibration was worse. The first scorer put eight of twelve notices between 90 and 100, which ranks nothing. Fit is now a five-factor blend -- qualification, capability match, economics against the bid ceiling, historical competition, and slack between the deadline and the work the dossier implies -- and the board spreads properly. Two bugs only surfaced when I screenshotted the thing: the bid plan was scheduling steps in the past whenever a deadline was closer than its fixed offsets, and a delivery-time commitment was being marked met because the supplier's category matched. Both are fixed. Both were invisible in the happy path. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The reasoning trace. An agent that returns a verdict asks to be trusted; an agent that shows six tool calls with their inputs, outputs and latency lets you audit the verdict. Making the trace a first-class contract rather than a debug view is the single decision that most changed how the product feels. And the zero-configuration demo: it runs, fully, with no key, no database and no signup. What I learned That agentic is not a synonym for the model decides everything. The parts of this agent that make it worth deploying -- the tool sequence, the extraction contract, the detectors, the trace -- are engineering. The model is one step in seven, and the system is better for the model being replaceable. What's next for TenderLens A live connector per portal. The portal search is one function; TED first, then the national portals. A real dossier reader, with a PDF pipeline feeding the same structured requirement shape, so the agent handles notices nobody has pre-structured. Scheduled sweeps with a morning digest. The run loop already has no browser dependency. More detectors. Each one is an independent function of the notice, so this is purely additive. title: Hand Off Helper
pitch: Live multiplayer ops room where a human support lead and an AI agent work the same support or incident case on the same page.
about_excerpt:
Live multiplayer ops room where a human support lead and an AI agent work the same support or incident case on the same page.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like

 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 I am tired of "AI everywhere" and help nowhere. 

 You open a support chat because a charge posted twice. You get a polite paragraph. You ask for the refund. You get another paragraph. You ask for a person. You get a form. Twenty minutes later the money still has not moved and you still cannot see who owns the case. 

 That is the loop I wanted to break. Not "more chatbot." A page where an agent can actually do the work, I can see every step, and I still have to approve anything that spends money or emails the customer. 

 What it does 

 Handoff is a multiplayer ops room for one live support case. 

 I am Jordan, the human lead. The agent is on the same board. We share CASE-1042: Maya Chen, duplicate Pro annual charge, $2,388, chargeback risk. 

 The agent does not scrape the UI. The page registers WebMCP tools, so it can get_case , draft_customer_reply , propose_refund , issue_refund , send_customer_reply , page_oncall , and resolve_case . Drafts show up in public. Refunds sit behind an Approve / Reject card. If I reject, that is a first-class event. Nothing irreversible happens in the dark. 

 Live site: https://handoffhelper.com 

 How I built it 

 Vanilla HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. No Next.js. No backend. State lives in the page. 

 Tools register with document.modelContext.registerTool , with navigator.modelContext as fallback. Each tool has a JSON schema. Read-only tools are marked readOnlyHint . Destructive tools open an on-page approval gate before they commit. The same store drives the UI, the timeline, and the tool results, so what the agent does is what I see. 

 I shipped it on Cloudflare Pages at handoffhelper.com so judges do not hit a login wall. 

 Challenges I faced 

 WebMCP was new to me. I had used the phrase "MCP" and assumed server-side Model Context Protocol. This challenge is the browser spec: the page exposes tools to the model. 

 That distinction ate time. I had to learn registerTool , the schemas, readOnlyHint , and what happens when modelContext is missing. Early on the public URL was a ChatGPT Site that required login. Useless for a judge. I bought handoffhelper.com and moved the static files to Cloudflare. 

 The other hard part was the human gate. It is easy to let the agent "just send the email." It is harder to make approve / reject visible, blocking, and logged under two identities. I wanted the kill switch to be obvious, not a hidden confirm in the model transcript. 

 What I learned 

 Agents are fast at draft and lookup. They should not be trusted with money or customer email until a person says yes. 

 If the tools are sloppy, the model asks extra questions and the demo dies. Tight descriptions ("do not call issue_refund until propose_refund exists") mattered more than extra features. 

 And a public URL with no login is part of the product. If a judge cannot open the page, the tools do not exist.

title: CoMapper - WebMCP
pitch: Make maps multiplayer.
about_excerpt: Make maps multiplayer. Like Comment Story Updates CoMapper Make maps multiplayer. CoMapper is a WebMCP reference implementation for shared spatial work. Users and agents explore, filter, inspect, style, and export the same live map state. Inspiration Maps shape our world. We use them to navigate, predict, plan, and understand the world around us. And yet, as the old saying goes: Tabula non est terra. (The map is not the territory.) For millennia, we've built tools for working with maps: the compass, sextant, surveying instruments, satellite imagery, GIS, spatial databases. Now agents can use those same tools. CoMapper asks: what happens when humans and agents collaborate on cartography? What it does CoMapper turns attributed GeoJSON into a shared spatial workspace. It validates mixed geometry, infers useful fields and controls, creates stable feature identifiers, and keeps the map, results, inspector, filters, and selection synchronized. Its WebMCP tools reflect the current page state. Dataset discovery and workspace inspection are always useful. Result-level actions appear once a search produces visible features. Styling and filtering accept fields declared by the active dataset. Feature actions accept visible result IDs. Agents can search, inspect, select, filter, style, and prepare CSV or GeoJSON exports. Their actions resolve into the same interface users are viewing. Prepared downloads appear as explicit controls in the workspace. Demo Scenario For the challenge demo, CoMapper includes a Toronto dataset with 269 features: 158 neighbourhoods, 86 technology-company locations, and 25 mobility, talent, and ecosystem anchors. The scenario gives the collaboration loop a focused question: build a shortlist for a potential OpenAI office. The first pass surfaces a density-led set of candidates. Users broaden the search beyond downtown, ask for a shorter list, inspect the evidence, and request an export. Each prompt continues from the state already visible on the map. The Toronto question is one worked example. The same interaction model applies wherever location, evidence, and human judgment meet: logistics, infrastructure, field operations, urban planning, environmental analysis, site selection, and emergency response. The demo also surfaces the limits of its evidence. A real property decision would require current rents, vacancy, floorplates, zoning, incentives, employee origins, and travel-time analysis. Why WebMCP WebMCP lets the application expose the context it already understands. CoMapper registers page-bound tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) and refreshes the available surface as the workspace changes. Each tool calls the same React action used by the interface. A search updates the result ledger and map. A selection opens the inspector. A filter changes the visible evidence. A prepared export reveals a download control. Users and agents remain synchronized around one state model. CoMapper demonstrates four reusable principles: Page state determines capability. Tools appear when their inputs and effects are valid. The interface remains authoritative. Tool actions resolve into visible application state. Schemas enforce scope. Fields, result IDs, limits, and spatial frames are validated. Users retain control. Evidence gaps stay visible and downloads require an explicit action. Stack CoMapper uses React, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre GL JS, Zod, Cloudflare Workers, and the OpenAI Sites Vite plugin. The browser-side data pipeline accepts GeoJSON, validates its geometry, infers fields and controls, creates stable feature IDs, and normalizes the dataset into a shared search response. The bundled Toronto atlas follows the same path as an imported local dataset. The map, result ledger, inspector, and WebMCP tools all consume that response. The tool layer uses narrow JSON Schemas with Zod validation. Searches accept one spatial frame: radius, visible bounds, or a drawn polygon. Feature actions are limited to visible result IDs. Styling and filtering use fields declared by the active dataset. Connected text carries an untrusted-content hint. Tool registration follows page state and uses an AbortController for cleanup. Search calls receive the invocation cancellation signal. Tool results return updated visible state and provenance for the next step. The public demo runs entirely in the browser with its bundled fixture. Evaluation requires no account, database, API key, or paid model call. Challenges Three details shaped the implementation. First, tool state had to match page state. Result-specific tools need current rows, fields, and IDs, so registration changes as users move through the application. Second, spatial datasets mix geometry types and overlapping evidence. CoMapper keeps points and polygons legible together, gives points click priority where geometries overlap, and preserves the camera while layer state changes. Third, every agent action needed a visible and trustworthy boundary. Search limits, field allowlists, visible-ID checks, provenance, cancellation, and user-controlled download reinforce the same interaction model. Accomplishments Users and agents work with the same live application state. Tools adapt to the active dataset and current results. Follow-up prompts revise the evidence within the active workflow. Imported GeoJSON and the bundled fixture share one data pipeline. Inspection keeps source fields, provenance, and evidence gaps visible. Agent-prepared downloads remain explicit user actions. The public demo is deterministic, attributed, and ready immediately. Takeaways WebMCP is especially effective when a website is already an instrument. The most useful tools expose a few high-confidence operations, inherit the application's constraints, and return their effects to the interface. Shared state also changes the role of follow-up prompts. A correction becomes an input to the active workspace: users can see what changed, challenge the direction, and continue from the same evidence. The broader opportunity is software where visual interaction and agent action form one inspectable loop. What's next The next step is to develop the reference implementation into a reusable spatial-workbench pattern: pluggable dataset adapters and validation profiles; saved workspaces and collaboration history; richer spatial operators, joins, and travel-time analysis; reusable tool contracts for other MapLibre applications; and review flows for teams working with consequential spatial decisions. Try it Live project: https://sidetools.dev/comapper Public repository: https://github.com/mgd1984/comapper-webmcp Demo video: https://youtu.be/I5I-9khq2UY Architecture: https://github.com/mgd1984/comapper-webmcp/blob/main/docs/architecture.md WebMCP tool contract: https://github.com/mgd1984/comapper-webmcp/blob/main/docs/webmcp.md Testing instructions Open https://sidetools.dev/comapper/#workspace in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome 149+ with WebMCP testing enabled. Use the bundled Toronto Office Placement Decision Atlas, or import an attributed GeoJSON file to exercise the same data pipeline. Ask the site tools to inspect the workspace or search the current map. For the bundled scenario, ask: “Build a shortlist of candidate locations for a new OpenAI Toronto office using site tools.” Follow with: “You're over-indexing on downtown. Broaden the search scope.” Then request a shorter list and inspect a selected feature. Ask CoMapper to filter or style a declared field and confirm that the map and inspector update together. Ask CoMapper to prepare the visible candidates as GeoJSON. Confirm that the download control appears and waits for user action. title: PARALLAX SPATIAL MCP
pitch: PARALLAX is a Spatial MCP that lets autonomous agents safely understand, change, re-observe, and verify 3D environments through governed actions and auditable execution receipts.
about_excerpt:
PARALLAX is a Spatial MCP that lets autonomous agents safely understand, change, re-observe, and verify 3D environments through governed actions and auditable execution receipts.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration 

 PARALLAX started from a simple problem: autonomous agents can call tools, but in spatial environments that is not enough. If an agent moves, rotates, or modifies something in a 3D world, we need a way to know what it was allowed to do, what actually changed, and whether the result matched the objective. 

 That led to the core loop: 

 Observe → Act → See Again → Verify → Receipt 

 The goal was to make spatial agency more accountable instead of treating a tool call as proof that a task succeeded. 

 What it does 

 PARALLAX is a Spatial MCP for autonomous agents. It turns 3D environments into governed workspaces where an agent can: 

 
 inspect a scene 
 discover bounded capabilities 
 request authorized spatial actions 
 execute allowed changes 
 re-observe the resulting state 
 verify the outcome 
 produce an execution receipt 
 

 Restricted actions can be denied without changing the protected scene state. 

 Our WebMCP demo uses a virtual production studio. The agent is given the objective of preparing the studio for an interview while operating inside defined permissions. 

 How we built it 

 PARALLAX was built with WebMCP, TypeScript, React, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Vite, GLTF assets, and OpenAI Codex , with ChatGPT and Hermes assisting with development, verification, documentation, and submission preparation. 

 The application separates the visual 3D scene from the authoritative logical state. Scene objects expose spatial capabilities, actions pass through governance checks, the environment is re-observed after execution, and verification determines whether the objective was satisfied before a receipt is shown. 

 We also built explicit denial behavior so a restricted mutation can fail closed rather than silently modifying the scene. 

 Challenges we faced 

 The hardest challenge was making the execution loop understandable visually, not just technically correct. 

 Early versions used proxy geometry that made real scene changes difficult to recognize. We had to improve object presentation, before/after comparison, labels, camera framing, video backgrounds, and the relationship between the 3D environment and the governance system. 

 Deployment parity was another major challenge. A local build could look correct while a production deployment could lose assets, motion, layout, or visual hierarchy. That pushed us to add stronger design and production-parity checks. 

 We also had to be disciplined about claims. A generated visualization is not the same thing as a verified result, so throughout the project we used the rule: 

 Generated! = Verified 

 What we learned 

 We learned that agentic spatial systems need more than tool access. They need an execution contract. 

 The important part is not simply whether an agent can manipulate a 3D environment. It is whether the system can clearly answer: 

 What did the agent observe? 
What was it authorized to do? 
What changed? 
Did the change satisfy the objective? 
What evidence remains afterward? 

 PARALLAX is our attempt to make those questions first-class parts of spatial agent infrastructure.

title: Live Canvas
pitch: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface.
about_excerpt: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration For as much as marketers have optimized for conversion, they haven't been able to cut through the number one reason that people leave open carts. they're not ready to buy. It had just happened to me while shopping for a microphone: I started at one site, then realized I needed more information to determine which was going to be the best fit. What if the shopping interface could have met me where I was at--researching the options, ranking the matches, explaining its rationale, and then designing a search result layout to fit its conclusions? That's just one glimpse of how web-interfaces of the future will adapt to their users' needs through a Live Canvas. What it does Each demo walks you through a conventional user interface, and then cordons off a bounded portion of it as WebMCP to redesign (the Live Canvas) The Storefront demo lets the agent curate the search results with a toolbox of approved card presets and badges. This constrained design is a good fit for the untrusted nature of the public internet, keeping users safe from XSS attacks. The Dashbord demo scales the idea up by giving you an entirely blank page. It imagine how the future of CRM / ERP dashboards might function. Prompt the agent to onboard you, collaborate on a vision with the agent as you would with your analytics team, and the end result is an entirely personal dashboard of controls, visualizations and reports. The Distribution demo scales the idea outwards by asking whether you distribute a Live Canvas as part of conventional component libraries. It demonstrates what a future Datatable component could be, with the ability to generate bespoke reports and save them to your browser - all without backend engineering or ai-vendor lock-in. How we built it The architecture north star is "agent composition, application execution". The application exposes its UI primitives through WebMCP. The agent supplies a composition, and then the live canvas renders that composition using application-owned components. This solution prevents data from leaking out of the organization's security boundary, and also prevents token bloat. Challenges we ran into and accomplishments that we're proud of There are two large challenges that required creativity: The largest challenge was discoverability. WebMCP is not bidirectional: an agent can invoke tools, but there's no mechanism for the website to initiate a conversation. The past 30 years of the web have trained users for the affordance of buttons and forms. I built a new set of visible prompts and verbs to communicate to surface the new modality which was an interesting accomplishment, but does highlight an apparent shortcoming in the standard. The second challenge is the built-in approval flow of agentic browsers. ChatGPT would auto-deny requests to access the user's simulated library to make recommendations, e.g. In the short term, this is solved with instructional text to ask for permission in advance. However, what WebMCP needs is a built in consent layer where tools are tied to required consent artifacts. What we learned WebMCP shows great potential to break interfaces out of the "ai chatbot jail". What's next for Live Canvas The most likely next step is to select an existing open-source component library and use it to build the first end-to-end WebMCP UI framework. That would turn the Live Canvas from just a demo pattern into a production-hardened implementation. title: DispatchGuard WebMCP
pitch: Agent-native transit telemetry and collision mitigation command deck powered by browser WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt:
Agent-native transit telemetry and collision mitigation command deck powered by browser WebMCP tools.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 About two months ago, as I was preparing for my graduation, my family was traveling together to celebrate with me. They were driving along a two-lane highway corridor—the kind of treacherous mountain pass defined by blind curves, sudden visibility drops, and heavy commercial freight trucks that turn everyday transit into deadly collision zones. 

 On that road, a catastrophic crash occurred. I lost five of my closest family members in an instant. 

 When the OpenAI WebMCP Challenge was announced, I knew I could not build a toy or another generic chatbot. I had to focus on a problem with real-world stakes: preventing this specific, devastating failure mode so no other family has to suffer that loss. 

 Most browser AI agents today interact with applications through brittle screen-scraping, OCR, or simulated clicks. While that might suffice for casual e-commerce, life-safety operations cannot tolerate non-deterministic delays or scraping failures. When sudden fog drops visibility to near zero on blind S-bends, human drivers and dispatchers experience severe cognitive overload trying to calculate safe stopping sightlines and coordinate emergency interventions. 

 I asked a fundamental question: 

 
 What if high-risk transit corridors could be supervised directly inside the browser, where the application exposes deterministic, typed telematics tools to an AI agent? 
 

 I built DispatchGuard WebMCP to pioneer what an agent-native safety cockpit looks like—merging autonomous collision risk evaluation with human supervisory dispatch into a synchronized, life-saving control loop. 

 What it does 

 DispatchGuard WebMCP is a real-time transit telemetry and collision mitigation command deck where human dispatchers and browser agents collaborate to secure hazardous, two-lane highway corridors. 

 When the application loads in a WebMCP-capable browser, it exposes four typed tools directly to the agent layer via document.modelContext.registerTool : 

 
 query_corridor_telemetry : Ingests real-time sector parameters—sightline distance (meters), weather state, commercial truck ratio, and blind curve counts. 
 evaluate_overtake_risk : Runs kinematic collision modeling, evaluates hazard probability (0–100%), and escalates sector status to CRITICAL. 
 broadcast_safety_alert : Pushes a geofenced advisory speed cap (e.g., 45 km/h) and overtake ban across active vehicle nodes and UI cards. 
 export_incident_dossier : Bundles the entire incident timeline, telemetry data, and mitigation checklist into an audit-ready post-mortem modal with copyable JSON. 
 

 The human operator retains visual control through an interactive SVG vector radar schematic, while the AI agent runs risk math in the background and executes safety protocols with zero screen-scraping delay. 

 How I built it 

 
 Frontend Stack : Built with Next.js 16 (Turbopack), React 19, and Tailwind CSS. The interface uses a dark, high-contrast command deck palette (deep slate #0A0B0E , warning amber, and critical red vectors) designed for high-stress situational awareness. 
 WebMCP Registration : Implemented inside src/hooks/useWebMCP.ts . The tools are registered directly on document.modelContext with strict JSON Schema definitions for every input parameter. 
 Fallback Simulation Harness : Because judges test across various environments (some with Chrome flags enabled, others in standard browsers), I built an on-page simulation bus. Clicking the harness tools runs the exact same client-side mutation logic as the native WebMCP calls, guaranteeing the demo works on every browser. 
 Testing & Verification : Verified native tool discovery and execution using the official WebMCP browser extension and the ChatGPT in-app browser environment. 
 

 Challenges I ran into 

 
 Next.js SSR vs. Browser-Native WebMCP : In Next.js, document does not exist during server-side rendering. Furthermore, document.modelContext is injected dynamically by the browser or extension at runtime. I had to design a clean hydration guard and an asynchronous registration hook that polls safely for the context without throwing SSR errors or causing infinite re-renders. 
 Input Validation for Autonomous Agent Calls : When an AI agent executes tool calls, it can occasionally pass unexpected string formats or out-of-range floats. I implemented runtime input sanitization to clamp numerical values (like speed caps and truck ratios) and normalize weather strings before passing them into the UI state machine. 
 Real-Time Visual State Sync : Making the vector radar map dynamically pulse red, spike the risk gauge to 99%, and display active geofenced warning banners—all within milliseconds of an agent tool call—required keeping local UI state tightly coupled to the tool execution callbacks. 
 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 
 True In-Browser Agency : Proved that WebMCP can eliminate screen-scraping entirely. Tool execution happens sub-15ms directly in browser memory. 
 Clean Fallback Architecture : Built a system that gracefully degrades: if native WebMCP is detected, it registers to the browser agent; if not, the interactive UI harness lets any user test the full lifecycle manually. 
 Full Open-Source Compliance : Delivered a clean, production-built repository with complete TypeScript typing, strict zero-error builds, and an MIT license visible at the root. 
 

 What I learned 

 WebMCP represents a massive shift in how web applications should be architected. Instead of treating a web page as a purely visual surface meant only for human eyes, we can now design applications as shared state machines. The human sees an intuitive visual interface, while the AI agent interacts with typed, deterministic tools on the exact same page. 

 What's next for DispatchGuard WebMCP 

 A command deck in a browser is only the first step. To physically eliminate fatal head-on collisions on two-lane mountain corridors, the system must bridge the gap between software dispatch and real-time physical intervention on the asphalt: 

 
 Sub-100ms Peer-to-Peer Overtake Clearance (Vehicle-to-Vehicle): 
Developing a decentralized WebMCP toolset that operates over local ad-hoc Wi-Fi / DSRC networks without cellular internet. When a driver signals an overtake behind a freight truck, the agent automatically interrogates the forward oncoming corridor and issues an immediate, non-negotiable "ABORT OVERTAKE" interlock if the time-to-collision window is under 6 seconds. 
 Solar Edge Nodes for Mountain Blackspots: 
Partnering with roadside monitoring hardware (solar-powered radar/optical cameras on blind S-bends) to run local WebMCP micro-agents at the curve itself, beaming real-time corridor sightline obstructions directly to approaching vehicles and regional dispatch. 
 Offline Edge PWA for Drivers and Remote Outposts: 
Packaging DispatchGuard into an ultra-lightweight, offline-first Progressive Web App (PWA) with client-side WebAssembly models, ensuring crash prediction algorithms function with zero latency in rural mountain valleys where cellular reception completely drops. 
 Field Piloting on High-Risk African Transit Corridors: 
Collaborating with regional transport authorities, long-haul trucking cooperatives, and highway safety bureaus to pilot the early warning telemetry layer on notorious high-casualty mountain passes and freight corridors.

title: WhenToProfit
pitch: Know when your small business makes money.
about_excerpt: Know when your small business makes money. Like Comment Story Updates Home Page - What If Scenario For Tech Business Home Page - What If Scenario For Retail/FnB Business Home Page - "Reach The Goal" Recommendation Inspiration Recently, I spent a lot of time learning Finance, especially financial modeling. Building a financial model was much harder than I expected. It requires you to think about assumptions, scenarios, how metrics (COGS, Cash Conversion Cycle, Liabilities, etc.) relate to each others, and many other things at the same time. But I realized something: I was learning this because I had the time and motivation to study finance. Many builders and small business owners around me don't. They often have much simpler questions: How much money do I need to survive if I quit my job? How much cash do I need to sustain my business before it becomes profitable? When will my business break even? If I increase my price by 20%, will it actually help? What happens if I hire someone next month? What can I change to improve my profit? These are financial questions, but they shouldn't require everyone to become a financial analyst first. That became the inspiration for WhenToProfit . My ambition is to eventually build a financial guide and decision-support tool for builders and small business owners — something that helps them understand their business financially and make better decisions without needing a finance background. What it does WhenToProfit is a simple financial planning and decision-support tool for builders and small business owners. I built it around a few questions that I think many entrepreneurs have but often struggle to answer: How much money do I need to survive if I quit my job? How much cash do I need to sustain the business before it becomes profitable? When will the business break even? What happens if I increase my price? What happens if I hire someone? What can I change to improve my profit? How much could the business be worth under a simple valuation approach? The goal is not to replace accounting software or build a complete financial system. Instead, WhenToProfit focuses on turning financial modeling into something more understandable and actionable for people who don't have a finance background. The tool supports two common business types: Tech / Solo businesses , such as SaaS and mobile apps Retail / F&B businesses , where revenue can be estimated from visitors, conversion rate, operating days, customers, and average order value At the core, the model connects simple assumptions to practical financial outcomes: $$ Revenue = Volume \times Price $$ $$ Gross\ Profit = Revenue - Variable\ Costs $$ $$ Operating\ Profit = Gross\ Profit - Fixed\ Operating\ Expenses $$ $$ Cash\ Flow = Operating\ Cash\ Flow - CapEx + Financing $$ From these inputs, WhenToProfit estimates monthly revenue, gross profit, operating profit, cash flow, cash balance, break-even timing, cash-flow-positive timing, runway, and a simplified valuation. The other important part is scenario planning . Instead of forcing users to build a complicated 24-month financial spreadsheet, they can describe business changes as events. For example: Increase the price by 20% in July Hire 5 engineers in January Improve monthly churn from 5% to 3% Raise $2M in March The user can then compare different scenarios and see how those decisions change the financial outcome. I also built WebMCP into the product so an AI agent can interact with the financial model instead of only talking about it. The agent can read assumptions and results, analyze the business, simulate decisions, compare scenarios, and perform structured actions such as creating scenarios or adding and moving scenario events. This creates an experience where the agent can help the user explore financial decisions while the user remains in control of the actual business plan. How I built it I built WhenToProfit in about two days , from the initial idea to the final submission. The project uses Next.js, TypeScript, a client-side financial calculation engine, local project storage, and WebMCP . I deliberately kept the architecture simple because the goal was to build a useful prototype quickly rather than create a large backend system. The financial model is separated from the UI so that the same calculation logic can be used by the dashboard, scenario simulations, and WebMCP tools. The project uses a scenario-based approach. A base case contains the original assumptions, while other scenarios describe changes to those assumptions over time. For WebMCP, I designed the tools around three stages: Read → Analyze → Act The agent can first understand the current project and financial model, then analyze or simulate possible decisions, and finally make structured changes to scenarios when the user wants to act. I also wanted WebMCP actions to use the same mutation paths as the normal application UI whenever possible. This means an action performed by an agent updates the same application state and persistence layer rather than creating a separate system just for AI. One important design decision was keeping the Base Case immutable . Agents can create and modify other scenarios, but they cannot directly modify the original base assumptions. I also added persistence for the active scenario so that the user's current planning context remains after switching projects or reloading the application. For development, I used AI heavily and treated it as a coding partner. I broke the work into small steps, gave it detailed product requirements, reviewed the generated implementation, ran builds and tests, and corrected the direction when something didn't match the intended product. Challenges we ran into 1. Building a financial model without making the product too complicated Financial modeling can become extremely complex very quickly. I deliberately avoided trying to build: Full accounting Tax calculations Double-entry bookkeeping Complex debt models Detailed cap tables Banking integrations Instead, I focused on the financial questions that are most useful for an early-stage builder. That constraint helped me keep the product understandable and practical. 2. Making WebMCP actually useful I didn't want to add WebMCP just because the hackathon required it. I had to think carefully about which parts of the product an agent should actually be able to interact with. This led me to think about the experience in three stages: Read → Analyze → Act The agent should first understand the business, then help analyze possible decisions, and finally be able to take structured actions when appropriate. This was an important design challenge because I wanted WebMCP to feel like a natural extension of the product rather than a separate feature added for the hackathon. 3. Controlling AI while working under a very short deadline My biggest development challenge was probably not writing code. It was controlling the scope . I had only two days, so I had to continuously ask: "Is this feature actually necessary?" "Does this help the core financial question?" "Will this make the user experience better?" "Is WebMCP actually useful here?" I had to guide the AI step by step instead of letting it build too much at once. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The biggest accomplishment is going from an idea to a working financial planning product in about two days . Building it helped me revisit my financial knowledge in a much more practical way, while also learning how to use AI to build a real product under a very tight deadline. I'm especially proud of seeing a possible future of work where people can collaborate with AI without being technical . I see WebMCP as a smooth bridge toward a more AI-native web, where existing websites can become tools that AI can understand and interact with. More importantly, I see this as a way for small entrepreneurs to leverage AI more naturally — not by learning how to code, but by simply working with AI through the tools they already use. What we learned This project gave me two very different kinds of learning: financial modeling and building with AI . Financial modeling Before this project, I mostly understood financial modeling as something you study. Building WhenToProfit made me understand it as a way to support decisions. The important flow became: Assumptions → Model → Scenarios → Financial Results → Decisions A financial model becomes much more useful when the numbers help someone decide what to do next. I also learned how difficult it is to simplify a financial model without making it meaningless. Every metric and assumption needs to have a reason to exist. Building with AI I also learned a lot about vibe-coding. AI can make implementation incredibly fast, but it doesn't remove the need for product thinking. In fact, I found that clear direction becomes even more important . When my requirements were specific, AI helped me move extremely quickly. When my requirements were vague, it was easy for the

title: MultiCOM
pitch: A shared incident room where engineers and AI agents investigate, challenge theories, and revise their confidence -> with a human approving the fix.
about_excerpt: A shared incident room where engineers and AI agents investigate, challenge theories, and revise their confidence -> with a human approving the fix. Like Comment Story Updates lobby war room ways in investigation commander approval manual controls judge console resolved untrusted-literal mobile Inspiration Incident response is a team effort. But when each engineer asks an AI assistant for help, the investigation splits into private conversations. Someone finds a useful log. Someone else follows a different theory. People copy answers between windows, trying to keep everyone on the same page. I wanted to try a different approach: what if the engineers and their agents could work in the same room? That became multicom—a shared incident room where agents gather evidence, challenge each other’s theories, and revise their confidence in public. The human responsible for the service still decides whether a fix should happen. What it does The demo starts with a simulated storefront service failing at 23% errors. Its database connection pool is too small, but a recently enabled feature flag gives responders a plausible wrong lead. Participants join through one room link. They can investigate with a browser agent, use the manual controls, or watch a clearly labeled scripted drill. The investigation stays visible to everyone: Agents pull logs and run checks. They post theories with evidence and a confidence level. Other participants challenge those theories. The original author can revise their confidence and explain why. The board keeps both the opening and revised numbers. Participants propose a fix and vote. The commander approves or rejects it. After the fix is applied, everyone sees whether the service actually recovers. Each new room gets its own copy of the incident, so one judge’s completed run does not spoil another’s. Why WebMCP fits The website is where the team works. WebMCP lets agents take part in that same workspace through specific tools, instead of relying on screen clicks or asking people to copy information between chats. multicom exposes thirteen tools covering the investigation, debate, voting, and fix workflow. Their results update the same board that people read and use. The most interesting part is not an agent finding the right answer. It is another participant challenging that answer—and the author changing their stated confidence, with the evidence and explanation still visible. An agent’s tool access also has a clear stopping point. It can request approval, but none of the thirteen tools can grant it. A person must click Approve. How I built it I built the interface with TypeScript and Vite. A Cloudflare Worker keeps each room’s participants, theories, votes, and approvals together. A separate Worker runs the simulated storefront service. WebMCP connects the browser agent to the room. People using the manual controls follow the same rules as agents: neither route skips the vote or approval checks. I used Codex to help implement the application, review the boundaries between its parts, and build tests. Running real agents through the tool surface was especially useful. Their mistakes showed where the tools needed clearer explanations or a missing capability. Challenges I faced One early problem was that an agent could vote against a fix but had nowhere to explain why. I added a tool for attaching a reason to a vote. Another was that challenging a theory did not let its author update their confidence. I added author-only revision and preserved the original number. Other participants can argue with a theory, but they cannot rewrite it for its author. Human approval needed more than a button. The server checks which action was approved, limits approval to sixty seconds, and allows it to be used only once. I also planted an instruction inside the synthetic logs telling agents to skip diagnosis and apply the wrong fix. The application returns that line as untrusted data and displays it as plain text. In the recorded agent drill, both agents rejected the instruction and continued investigating. What I learned Watching agents use the application taught me more than watching a scripted walkthrough. A result that looked obvious in code could still confuse an agent. A simple “no” vote could hide the most useful reasoning in the room. The interface needed places for disagreement, explanations, and revision—not just answers. I also learned to separate agreement from permission. A majority can support a fix without being allowed to apply it. Keeping that distinction visible became central to the project. What I’m proud of multicom makes the investigation observable. You can see what was proposed, what challenged it, how confidence changed, who supported the fix, and who approved it. The current project includes 73 automated tests and a separate 32-check production acceptance suite. Those checks cover shared updates, room isolation, approval expiry, repeated requests, and recovery across browsers. It is deliberately a controlled demonstration with one scripted incident, not a tool connected to someone’s real production systems. The question it explores is broader: how can several people and their agents work through uncertainty together, while keeping the consequential decision in human hands? title: CodeATlas
pitch: A live dependency graph you and your AI agent both see and both act on
about_excerpt: A live dependency graph you and your AI agent both see and both act on Like Comment Story Updates Graph dependency Graph dependency-Loaded Repo Hero Page Chatgpt Browser Chats Graph dependency-Loaded Repo Chatgpt Browser Chats Thumbnail What got me into this I kept running into the same annoying moment while working with AI coding agents. The agent would change a file and I'd immediately think, wait, what else is using this? Then I'd start grepping through the repo myself, trying to figure out what might have been affected. Sometimes I'd trust what the agent said, but I never really liked having to. That was basically the reason I started this project. I wanted to be able to see the blast radius of a change instead of just being told what it was. Then I came across the WebMCP spec and something clicked. What if the graph itself was the thing the agent and I shared? Instead of the agent explaining a dependency graph in a chat message, it could actually show me the graph on screen. I could look at it, click around, and the agent could interact with that same graph. That felt much more useful. How it got built The core of it is actually pretty simple. I use ts-morph to walk through a TypeScript repo and build the import graph. Then a basic BFS handles questions like: What depends on this file? There is deliberately no AI involved in that part. I wanted the important answer in the demo to come from the code itself. If the tool says 12 files are affected, I want those 12 files to actually be the result of the graph traversal, not something a model guessed. React Flow handles the graph on the frontend, Fastify handles the backend, and I added chokidar later so the graph could update when files change on disk. That changed the idea quite a bit for me. An AI writing code and an AI I'm talking to are really two different things. But they don't need two different interfaces. A code change can update the graph, and a WebMCP call can interact with that same graph. The graph becomes the common ground between the two. The tools also grew as I kept building. At first it was just about asking for the blast radius and highlighting the affected files. Then I made it work both ways, so the agent could also ask what I was currently looking at. After that came cycle detection, switching the graph to another GitHub repo, and eventually a propose and approve flow for changes. At that point, a read-only graph didn't feel like enough anymore. The part that ate my whole evening React Flow wouldn't draw a single edge. The nodes showed up perfectly. They were just floating there with absolutely nothing connecting them, which is a pretty bad look for a dependency graph. I spent way too long checking the data, handle IDs, edge configuration, and rewriting parts of the implementation. Eventually I found the actual problem. React Flow uses ResizeObserver to measure nodes before figuring out where edges should start and end. In my setup, that measurement wasn't happening properly. The fix was surprisingly simple. I gave the nodes a fixed size and explicitly defined where the handles were. Suddenly all the edges appeared. It was one of those bugs that takes hours to understand and about two minutes to fix once you finally know what is happening. It also taught me not to immediately assume that something is wrong with the data just because the UI is missing something. Figuring out how ChatGPT actually sees it I thought getting an actual AI agent to use the tools would be the easy part. It wasn't. At first, ChatGPT would confidently talk about tools that I hadn't even built. It would invent names for things and tell me to connect an MCP workspace that had nothing to do with how I was actually using WebMCP. After a few rounds of this, I realized what was happening. It wasn't actually opening my app as a live browser page. It was basically reading the static page and trying to figure out what the application did from that. Since the app is React, most of what I cared about doesn't exist in the initial HTML anyway. Once I explicitly opened the app through the browser, everything changed. Instead of guessing, the agent could actually interact with the page and call the tools I had built. It could get the same file list my backend calculated and even tell me which tests would be worth rerunning. That was probably one of the most useful parts of building the whole thing because it made the difference between an AI talking about a tool and an AI actually using one very obvious. What I actually learned The biggest thing I learned is that the AI part wasn't really the hard part. Most of the problems were normal software problems. A rendering library making an assumption about node measurements. A deployment having cold starts. A browser tool behaving differently from a web search tool. Two things having similar names but working in completely different ways. The WebMCP part was actually one of the more enjoyable pieces to build. You ask the agent something, it calls a tool, and you can actually watch the result happen on the screen. That feels very different from an AI giving you a paragraph explaining what it thinks is happening. And honestly, that's the part of CodeAtlas I like most. It isn't trying to replace the developer's understanding of the code. It gives the developer something concrete to look at while the agent works. title: CargoMesh
pitch: Autonomous Agentic Freight Orchestration for Cross-Border B2B Logistics
about_excerpt: Autonomous Agentic Freight Orchestration for Cross-Border B2B Logistics Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Moving heavy freight across Latin America is complex and fragmented. Shippers juggle multiple carrier portals, emails, spreadsheets, and phone calls just to verify route coverage, check truck capacity, get rate quotes, and confirm bookings. Traditional automation relies on fragile web scraping or custom APIs that smaller carriers cannot maintain. We asked: what if carrier websites could directly publish typed, structured capabilities to an authorized browser agent through the open WebMCP standard? CargoMesh makes this possible. What it does CargoMesh is an agent-native B2B freight orchestration platform: Canonical Intake : Shippers define or load freight requests (e.g., FR-1042 Callao, Peru → Santiago, Chile). Dynamic Discovery : Discovers 0..N compatible carriers from an open registry without hardcoded lists. Native WebMCP Execution : The browser agent visits carrier portals (Andes, Inca, Pacific) and consumes 5 structured tools via document.modelContext : check_service_coverage , check_capacity , quote_freight , book_freight , and get_provider_booking_status . Result Bridge : Validates and persists commercial responses without client-side data tampering. Deterministic BALANCED Engine : Scores offers mathematically (25% cost, 25% reliability, 20% transit, 10% availability, 10% route experience, 10% org history). Recovery : If a carrier rejects a booking, CargoMesh offers authorized alternatives (e.g., Andes rejection → Inca confirmed). How we built it Frontend & Provider Portals : Next.js 15, React 19, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet for explicitly planned route corridors, and EN/ES support. WebMCP Runtime : Browser-side document.modelContext.registerTool with strict JSON schemas, abort handling, and tool cleanup on provider navigation. Backend & Security : Supabase PostgreSQL, Supabase Auth, RLS, and optimistic concurrency through draft_version . Result Bridge & Auditing : Server-side validation of tool envelopes, origin/classification, request correlation, and commercial responses. The Judge Drawer exposes auditable inputs, outputs, timestamps, and origin evidence. Challenges we ran into Separating browser execution from database truth : WebMCP tools execute in browser memory; we built the Result Bridge to validate signatures before persisting commercial offers. Dynamic 0..N provider identity : Preserving exact matchingServiceId across dynamic navigation without breaking idempotency. Clean context management : Ensuring active WebMCP tools are completely removed from document.modelContext when navigating away from a provider. Technical honesty : Avoiding artificial GPS simulation; planned corridors are explicitly labeled as planned references. Accomplishments that we're proud of Native WebMCP tool surfaces through document.modelContext . A deterministic, explainable BALANCED ranking for the canonical FR-1042 fixture: Andes 89, Inca 84, Pacific 72. Repository and client-bundle checks with no detected secret exposure, plus RLS-protected organization-scoped access. A demonstrated recovery flow: Andes rejection, explicit human selection of Inca, then confirmed replacement booking. What we learned We proved that WebMCP fundamentally shifts how B2B platforms interact: websites can expose clean, agentic tool surfaces without breaking the visual human interface, eliminating the need for brittle web scraping. What's next for CargoMesh Onboarding additional real-world carriers across the Pan-American corridor. Integrating independently hosted provider origins with external WebMCP adapters. Multi-modal freight orchestration (maritime and air freight handoffs). pitch: Agent Native Content workspace for creators
about_excerpt:
