title: Repo Board
pitch: A real-time GitHub task board where humans set the work and agents with WebMCP support claim, plan, execute, and follow it safely through pull requests.
about_excerpt: A real-time GitHub task board where humans set the work and agents with WebMCP support claim, plan, execute, and follow it safely through pull requests. Like Comment Story Updates A real-time GitHub task board where humans set the work and agents with WebMCP support claim, plan, execute, and follow it safely through pull requests. Problem Coding agents can work quickly, but teams of people still need a reliable way to decide what someone's agent may do, prevent two agents from taking the same task, review a plan before implementation, and see what happened after the agent stops. Issue trackers record work for people. Agent transcripts record work inside one conversation. Neither gives people and browser agents a shared, live workflow with explicit ownership and bounded actions. Solution Repo Board is a real-time task board for one GitHub repository. Humans create and groom tasks in a five-column workflow: Todo -> Ready -> In Progress -> In PR -> Done The page exposes WebMCP tools for the actions that are allowed in the current context. A Codex agent can inspect tasks, claim one, attach or revise a plan, start work, report progress, link a pull request, read review state, and check CI. Humans retain authority over sensitive actions such as replacing an active owner, canceling work, and archiving a completed task. The first valid claim wins. Ownership is bound to the signed-in GitHub user and the browser tab, backed by an unguessable per-tab capability. It does not expire because a timer ran out or a WebSocket disconnected. Another agent can take over only after the person using the page confirms it. Why This Matters Agent coordination fails in ordinary, expensive ways: two agents edit the same work, a plan gets separated from its implementation, a stale browser tab continues mutating state, or a human cannot tell whether a status report came from the repository or from the agent itself. Repo Board makes those boundaries visible and enforceable. The person and the agent work against the same task, plan revision, board revision, pull request snapshot, and activity history. The app treats task text, plans, progress reports, and GitHub content as untrusted data. That content cannot select tools, authorize a mutation, choose a repository, or supply secrets. How We Used AI Repo Board does not embed a model or require an OpenAI API key. It gives an AI agent a precise interface to a live product through browser-native WebMCP. The agent discovers only the tools that are valid for the current user, selected task, assignment, and workflow state. For example, an unassigned Ready task exposes claim_task . After the current tab claims it, the registry replaces that tool with read_plan , update_plan , report_progress , start_work , and release_task . After the task reaches In PR, the agent can read review and check state. Aborting the active registration removes stale tools when context changes. This makes the agent useful without giving it hidden authority. Read operations are bounded. Mutations carry an idempotency key and expected board revision. The Durable Object independently checks authorization and state transitions instead of trusting the browser tool layer. How We Used Codex Codex helped turn the product plan into a working system. It traced and implemented the React client, Cloudflare Worker, SQLite-backed Durable Object, D1 directory, GitHub App integration, WebSocket updates, and dynamic WebMCP profiles. It also wrote and ran focused tests for task transitions, validation, authorization, session isolation, concurrent claims, reconnect behavior, pull request state, and tool registration. The build process used Codex to pressure-test product decisions instead of only generating code. One important revision replaced timer-based leases with durable per-tab ownership after the failure modes of expiring work were examined. Codex then added explicit, human-confirmed takeover and server-side fencing for the former owner. A later pass added archive_task with the same rule in both the WebMCP layer and the Durable Object: only completed, unarchived Done work can be archived, and the page must ask the human first. Repo Board was also used for real work. In Codex's in-app browser, the airy-pond ticket for a private GitHub repository was inspected, claimed for planning, and given an approved plan. Repo Board moved it from Todo to Ready and closed the planning assignment. That exercise also caught a stale tool handle; fetching the current WebMCP registry resolved it, which validated the context-replacement design. Key Features Dynamic WebMCP tool profiles based on authentication, permissions, route, selection, assignment, and task state Atomic task claims with structured conflict results when another agent wins Durable ownership bound to a GitHub user and browser tab, with explicit human-confirmed takeover Immutable ticket and plan revisions plus an append-only activity log Typed workflow transitions instead of arbitrary drag-and-drop state changes Real-time board updates through hibernating WebSockets, missed-event replay, and reconnect snapshots Pull request linking, review normalization, check status, merge completion, and closed-without-merge rollback Human-confirmed cancellation and archival, with matching server-side guards Anonymous read-only previews for public repositories and fail-closed access for private repositories Two-word task references such as amber-fox , so people and agents do not have to pass internal UUIDs Bounded untrusted-content handling throughout ticket, plan, progress, review, and GitHub data Architecture The React client renders the board and registers WebMCP tools through document.modelContext . It sends HTTP commands and receives revisioned WebSocket updates from a Cloudflare Worker. The Worker handles GitHub authentication, repository authorization, API routing, static assets, installation-token GitHub calls, webhook verification, and scheduled pull request reconciliation. D1 stores the global directory, GitHub identities, hashed sessions, installations, and permission cache. One SQLite-backed RepositoryBoard Durable Object per owner/repo owns tasks, plan revisions, assignments, pull request snapshots, processed actions, webhook deliveries, and the board event log. It serializes mutations before broadcasting the new revision. GitHub network calls finish in the Worker before normalized results enter the Durable Object. No serialized state path remains open across an external request. Testing Instructions Public judge flow Open https://webmcp-repo-board.zacwhite.workers.dev/boards/zac/test-repo-board in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Google Chrome 149+ with WebMCP enabled. Confirm that the public board has one synthetic example in each column: Todo, Ready, In progress, In PR, and Done. Ask the agent to call list_tasks , then inspect white-vine to see its approved plan and linked open pull request. Inspect teal-whale to see a completed task linked to merged pull request #4. To test mutations, sign in with GitHub and use a repository where the Repo Board GitHub App is installed and your account has triage , write , maintain , or admin permission. Create a Todo task, claim it for planning, save a plan, claim implementation, call start_work , and report progress. Link an open pull request from the same repository. Confirm that the task moves to In PR and exposes pull request, review, and check tools. After the pull request merges, confirm that the task moves to Done. Archive only if you want to hide it from the default board while retaining its history. Mutating tests require a repository where the tester can install or access the GitHub App. Public anonymous routes remain read-only by design. Local setup Requirements: Node 24 and pnpm 11. pnpm install --frozen-lockfile pnpm d1:migrate:local pnpm dev:worker Open http://localhost:8787 . Local development provides a labeled development session and public stand-in repositories, so the core workflow does not require production GitHub credentials. Automated verification Run: pnpm check pnpm deploy:dry Verified again on September 3, 2026: ESLint passed. Both TypeScript projects passed type checking. 58 client and shared tests passed. 42 Worker and Durable Object tests passed. The production Vite build passed. The Wrangler dry deployment assembled the Worker, assets, Durable Object, and D1 bindings successfully. The public homepage returned HTTP 200. The public zac/webmcp-repo-board board API returned HTTP 200 and identified the repository as public and materialized. The public zac/test-repo-board demo API returned HTTP 200 with one task in each workflow column. ChatGPT's in-app browser completed a signed-in lifecycle across planning, implementation, progress reporting, pull request linkage, status refresh, and merge completion. title: coSynth
pitch: A synthesizer you control by talking to AI. Describe a sound. The AI turns the knobs, plays it, shows every change, and guides you through the controls so you can tweak it and learn as you go.
about_excerpt: A synthesizer you control by talking to AI. Describe a sound. The AI turns the knobs, plays it, shows every change, and guides you through the controls so you can tweak it and learn as you go. Like Comment Story Updates Full Wavetable Synthesizer GIF Active AI state and tool visible in the UI coSynth – AI Web Synthesizer Sound design is hard to get into. A real synth has hundreds of knobs. coSynth lets you describe and get a sound. The AI turns the knobs, plays the result, listens to what it made, and shows all the changes in the UI. You keep it, undo it, tweak it, or ask the AI to show you how it got there. You can also ask AI to teach a complext topic and AI will guide you through step by step. Live: https://coSynth.vercel.app Code: https://github.com/brunnolou/coSynth (MIT) Why WebMCP fits A synth is a terrible thing to operate through text or screenshots. Too many parameters (in this case 224), knobs to drag, LFO curves to draw, etc. An agent can misclick, can miss an exact value, and can't hear the audio. The UI is too complex for someone to easily find things when they are not used to it. That makes a synthesizer one of the best interfaces for WebMCP. For the AI agent: It communicates to the synth directly. Every parameter has a name, a unit, and a range that can be edited directly in bulk. When the agent plays a note, it gets back attack time, decay, spectral centroid, and harmonics, then compares that with a reference clip. So it can "hear" with a tool call. For humans Instead of starting from scratch, you get very close to what you want. Then you can see the exact changes and tweak manually. If you don't know a concept or want to find something, AI can show you the exact location or teach you step by step. You can leverage AI's world knowledge to create any synth sound! What used to need trained ears you now can achieve by sending a reference sound and asking AI to replicate. How I Made the AI<>Human UX Better Each knob the AI touched gets a small animated marker. A status line shows which tool is running. You can reject a whole AI iteration and keep your own edits. Undo covers AI changes and yours. Old branches stay reachable in history. The AI can highlight controls step by step and explain them. Every AI performance is saved, so "play that again with my new adjustment" is one click. AI can save as a preset, and you can download it. How I implemented WebMCP Vanilla TypeScript and Vite. DSP in an AudioWorklet, UI in Canvas, WebGL2 and DOM. WebMCP sits on top of the same engine the UI uses, and the synth works without it. Tools register with document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) . There are 24, each with a JSON Schema input and a readOnlyHint : Reading : get_synth_state , get_parameter_schema , get_ui_targets , list_presets , get_history Editing : update_parameters , set_modulation , set_fx_order , apply_patch , save_preset , load_preset , delete_preset , export_preset Sound : play_notes , render_audio , capture_audio , analyze_audio , analyze_reference_audio , compare_audio , suggest_patch , stop_performance Together : show_ui_guide , navigate_history , replay_history All 24 register at page load. play_notes needs the human to click Start first, because browsers won't play audio without a gesture. render_audio uses an OfflineAudioContext, so the agent can design and measure before anyone clicks anything. The page also documents itself. A clipped agent brief in the DOM, a JSON descriptor, ai-tools meta tags, llms.txt and robots.txt . An agent given only the URL can read the page and know what to do. How I tested the agent experience I want to ensure AI could call the tools easily. So I built a loop. A harness exposes only what a real WebMCP client sees, and logs every call. A fresh agent gets a fixed prompt and is never allowed to read the repo. Each round runs on Claude and Codex. When * both trip in the same place( , the tool is wrong . Fix the top blocker, run again. In self-improving loop. Four evals, each asking one question. Can the agent find out what to send ( docs/agent-ux-eval.md ). Can it steer toward a sound it cannot hear ( docs/agent-match-eval.md ). Given a "how do I" question, does it teach rather than edit ( docs/agent-teaching-eval.md ). Given only a URL, does it find the tools at all? Prompts, agent reports and raw logs are all in the repo. Learning all 224 parameters went from 45 calls to 1 . Failed calls went to zero on both models. The matching loop went from 87 calls to 36 . How to test Open https://cosynth.vercel.app in the ChatGPT in-app browser, or in Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing . ChatGPT Desktop was the most reliable client for me. Click "CLICK TO START AUDIO" once. Try: "Make a bright plucked bass and play a short riff." "Show me where the amp envelope is and how to shorten the release." "Save that." Watch the markers, click the status dot for before and after values, and use Keep or Reject. No login. Presets and reference audio stay in the browser. What was already there, what is new I started from Soundgineer by noisyloop ( https://github.com/noisyloop/soundgineer , MIT). Its DSP engine and original UI date from July 6 to 11, 2026, and that version is still up at https://soundgineer.vercel.app . Everything WebMCP-related is from the submission period, August 26 to September 3, 2026, about 200 dated commits: the WebMCP layer and all 24 tools, offline rendering and audio analysis, change markers and Keep/Reject, shared undo history and replays, guided walkthroughs, the interface redesign, the four evals with their harness, and the in-page agent brief. title: Task-Liaison: AI Command Center
pitch: A WebMCP-powered Next.js command center that transforms an LLM into an active operational partner to orchestrate cloud escalations, map blast radiuses, and stage human-approved remediation patches.
about_excerpt:
A WebMCP-powered Next.js command center that transforms an LLM into an active operational partner to orchestrate cloud escalations, map blast radiuses, and stage human-approved remediation patches.

 Comment

 Updates

 Task-liaison 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Task-liaison 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Drawing from my background as a certified Google Cloud Professional Cloud Architect, I've seen firsthand how chaotic infrastructure incident management can be. When a GKE node pool fails or a Cloud SQL database spikes, the resolution process is usually a messy combination of frantic Slack messages, manual Jira routing, and repetitive UI clicks. I wanted to see if the new WebMCP standard could transform an LLM from a passive conversational chatbot into an active, operational partner that orchestrates incident workflows directly on the canvas. 

 What it does 

 Task-Liaison is an AI-orchestrated command center for infrastructure escalations. Instead of clicking through menus, engineers talk to the board. The application uses a three-column Kanban layout: 

 
 The Command Center: Unassigned, critical incidents. 
 The Priority Reward Exchange: An incentivized bounty market where the AI can dynamically price and route tasks. 
 Active Engineering Workloads: Real-time on-call assignments. 
 

 By exposing strict JSON-schema React state mutations to the LLM's runtime environment, the AI can map cascading blast radiuses, re-route workloads between engineers to prevent burnout, and stage mock Infrastructure-as-Code (Terraform/Bash) patches. Crucially, the system enforces Human-in-the-Loop execution: the AI stages the complex configurations, but human engineers retain physical click-approval authority to apply the patches. 

 How we built it 

 Task-Liaison is a frontend-only React application built on the Next.js framework and styled with Tailwind CSS. The core innovation lies in leveraging the document.modelContext API. I registered custom JavaScript tools ( post_bounty_to_market , propose_ticket_swap , analyze_blast_radius , stage_remediation_script ) with rigid input schemas. When the user types a natural language command, the LLM extracts the parameters, maps them to the schema, and triggers instantaneous React state mutations without any backend database. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Maintaining the state synchronization between a non-deterministic AI and a deterministic frontend UI was the biggest hurdle. During development, local hot-reloading would frequently wipe the WebMCP tool registrations from the AI's memory, causing the LLM to fall back into "chatbot mode" where it would hallucinate actions instead of firing the API tools. I had to implement strict lifecycle management using React useRef and useEffect hooks to ensure the JSON contracts remained tethered to the agent's context window. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 I am exceptionally proud of the closed-loop execution flow. When a user tells the AI to "stage a mock Terraform script for INC-102," the AI perfectly formats the code block, injects it into the specific React component, and generates an actionable "Approve & Execute" button. Successfully blending AI-driven state mutations with human-driven React onClick events proves that AI can be trusted in enterprise operational environments if constrained by the right UI boundaries. 

 What's next for Task-Liaison 

 The next step is backend integration. While this MVP handles state in the browser to prove the WebMCP concept, the natural evolution is tying the execute blocks to authenticated webhooks—allowing the AI to actually update live Jira tickets, trigger PagerDuty alerts, or execute validated Terraform plans directly against a GCP environment.

title: Automata - a WebMCP co-creation playground
pitch: You and your agent, one universe. A cellular automata playground where a human and an AI agent build, run, and study Game of Life worlds together through WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: You and your agent, one universe. A cellular automata playground where a human and an AI agent build, run, and study Game of Life worlds together through WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates What it does Automata is an interactive cellular automata canvas where a human and an AI agent share one Game of Life universe. The human draws, erases, and stamps patterns by hand. The agent drives the same universe through 10 WebMCP tools: spawning catalog patterns, inventing new ones from RLE, switching rule systems, fast-forwarding up to 5,000 generations, and analyzing what emerged. Every agent action lights up on the canvas and lands in an on-screen activity feed, so the human always sees what their collaborator did. Why it's a strong fit for WebMCP Cellular automata are a natural human + agent collaboration. The work splits cleanly: humans sketch curiosity (a squiggle, a stamped pulsar, a splash of soup), and agents run the experiment (hundreds of generations in a blink, then a classified report of the outcome). That only works if the agent can operate the app itself, not a parallel API - which is exactly what WebMCP provides. Each of the app's 10 tools is registered through the WebMCP Imperative API with document.modelContext.registerTool, mixing read-only tools (get_state, analyze, list_patterns) with mutating ones (spawn_pattern, load_rle, set_rules, run_steps, add_noise, clear, set_running). What people and agents can do together that was hard before Say "add a glider gun and some chaos, run 400 generations, tell me what emerges." The agent stamps the gun, sprinkles noise, fast-forwards 400 generations, and returns a named census of the wreckage: "12 blocks, 5 blinkers, a beehive, 3 escaped gliders, stable since generation 212." The analyze tool is non-destructive - it clones the universe, simulates ahead, detects extinction, stabilization (with period), or ongoing activity, and names the objects that emerge. Then the volley continues: the human stamps a pulsar into the agent's world, the agent weaves gliders around it with load_rle, or flips the physics to HighLife or a custom B../S.. rulestring and reports what the same world does under new laws. Before WebMCP, an agent could advise about Game of Life; it couldn't sit at the same table. How WebMCP was implemented All 10 tools are registered via the WebMCP Imperative API (document.modelContext.registerTool), with JSON tool results. The page ships a WebMCP origin trial token so Chrome 149+ gets native WebMCP (also testable via chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing); without either, a built-in shim provides the same registerTool/getTools/executeTool surface and an in-page Agent console lets you call every tool by hand. The automata engine is pure dependency-free JavaScript (grid, Life-like rule parser, pattern catalog, RLE round-trips, cycle detection, object classification) with 16 Node tests, so tool behavior is verifiable outside the browser. Challenges and learnings Making analyze non-destructive: it had to clone the universe and simulate ahead without touching the live world the human is watching. Naming what emerges: classifying the settled state into named objects took cycle detection plus object classification, not just a population count. Keeping the human in the loop: every tool call highlights the canvas and posts to the activity feed. Dual registration path: native WebMCP via origin trial/flag, with a shim exposing the identical surface. title: Jumping Beans
pitch: The future of web interaction is two-sided, driving user intent upstream and letting merchants set the path. We let users see the offers they want, how they want, when they want it-powered by WebMCP.
about_excerpt: The future of web interaction is two-sided, driving user intent upstream and letting merchants set the path. We let users see the offers they want, how they want, when they want it-powered by WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Jumping Beans — shopper-controlled WebMCP offer journey One request. Three sites. One human approval boundary. Tell Jumping Beans: “Coffee under $15. Show customer stories first.” It turns that intent into an editable selection. Only after you approve it does the browser discover offer tools from three independently hosted demonstration storefronts, ask each site for structured matches, and assemble one explainable result. Every card says where it came from and why it appeared. Nothing has to be saved. That is the core idea: agents can do the repetitive cross-site work, while people keep control of context, retention, and consequential actions. Inspiration Shopping on the open web is fragmented. People repeat the same category, budget, and presentation preferences on every site. Agents can help, but a general-purpose agent is often forced to infer meaning from changing page layouts, and shoppers cannot easily see which site supplied a fact or what personal context crossed a boundary. We wanted to explore a different model: the browser as a user-controlled capability network. Each participating site publishes a narrow, structured tool; the shopper decides when a request may leave the current page; and the result carries its source, decision reasons, and retention policy with it. Why WebMCP Jumping Beans is not a chat box wrapped around a catalog. Its central action crosses real browser origins. The Engine loads three independently hosted demo storefronts, discovers each site's get_matching_deals tool with document.modelContext.getTools, and invokes the returned capabilities with document.modelContext.executeTool. That makes WebMCP essential: sites opt in by registering their own tools and remain authoritative for their own product records; the browser exposes structured capabilities instead of making an agent guess through page markup; one approved preference can be projected narrowly to several sites without sharing an identity or an entire profile; every origin succeeds, returns no match, times out, or fails independently; and the same journey is visible to the person and available to the agent as a structured receipt. The result is a concrete model for an open agentic web: coordination without turning every website into one centralized API. What people and agents can do together A person can start in plain language or choose a tested recipe. Jumping Beans converts the request into an editable category, an exclusive budget, and presentation rules such as testimonials first, price proof, comparison, or no urgency. An agent can inspect or stage display preferences, build the offer journey, read browser-scoped offer memory, inspect the active profile, and retrieve a redacted journey receipt. The person still decides whether to use the selection for one visit or save it in the browser, and whether network sharing is active. Draft choices stay on the page until they are applied. After approval, the Engine calls the three storefront tools, validates their responses, applies the shopper's rules, ranks eligible offers, and shows the result with source provenance. The shopper can then open a storefront carrying only the reviewed visit-level presentation context. On the Watch Co demo storefront, a declarative register_interest form shows a second collaboration pattern. A visitor or agent may fill a product and target price, but that only stages the action. The page requires separate human confirmation before Watch Co records a non-binding, 30-day demand signal. It does not create an order, reservation, notification, payment, or message. How we built it The project uses plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript modules across four deployed origins: one Cloudflare Worker for the Engine and three Cloudflare Pages demonstration storefronts. Cloudflare D1 backs the optional Engine account experience and the separate Watch Co demand-signal store. Each storefront registers one bounded get_matching_deals tool. The Engine creates cross-origin iframes with explicit tool and isolation delegation before navigation, waits for registration, discovers only the three allowlisted origins, and executes each tool with WebMCP's JSON-string input contract. The Engine also registers six page-level tools: get_offer_memory, set_display_preferences, build_offer_journey, set_deal_watch, get_profile, and get_journey_receipt. Watch Co additionally exposes a declarative register_interest form. The trust boundary is part of the implementation. Production responses use COOP, COEP, CORP, an exact three-origin Permissions Policy, and an origin-trial token on every origin. Partner responses are origin-checked, schema-validated, limited to 24 records and 64 KiB, and bounded by independent deadlines. Invalid or expired offers never become partner cards. Preference projections omit identity and carry only the approved category, price ceiling, and display rules. The Watch write path revalidates server-side, binds the staged payload, requires page confirmation, and uses idempotency to suppress duplicate commits. Non-WebMCP browsers still get a useful, honestly labeled storefront-preview journey. That lane demonstrates the same category, budget, and presentation handoff but never claims a native WebMCP match. Challenges The hardest problem was making a multi-origin native journey reliable and honest. Partner registration is asynchronous, and an early shopper action exposed a cold-start race that a later diagnostic probe could accidentally hide. We changed the test order so the user action happens before any direct registry inspection, waited at the iframe registration boundary, reconciled tool-change events, and tested repeated fresh browser profiles. Browser builds also differed on whether tool input arrived as serialized JSON or an object. We made the production path follow the JSON-string contract and kept a narrowly scoped compatibility retry only for recognized input-type errors. The other challenge was semantic: distinguishing an open-catalog sample, a response from a demo WebMCP origin, a presentation-only storefront preview, and a consequential write. We added explicit labels, per-origin outcomes, provenance, retention copy, staging, confirmation, and receipts so the interface never makes a stronger claim than the underlying event supports. What we learned The best human-agent experience is a handoff, not full automation. Agents are excellent at discovering capabilities, making parallel structured requests, and summarizing evidence. People should own the moment when context leaves a page, whether it persists, and whether a consequential action proceeds. We also learned that provenance is product UX. A source label, a no-match state, and a decision receipt make a cross-site result easier to trust than an opaque “best deal” answer. For an emerging browser capability, isolation headers, feature enrollment, fresh-profile timing, and failure behavior matter as much as the tool code itself. Competition work This is a new project. The repository's first commit was created on August 27, 2026, after the competition opened on August 25. All source code, product design, deployment configuration, documentation, and acceptance work in v0.11.0 was created during the submission period. The exact live v0.11.0 release passed a release-bound 38/38 native WebMCP audit in a fresh, headed, extension-free Chrome Stable 152.0.7977.76 profile, plus 10/10 fresh-profile cold starts. The release workflow passed 812 product assertions and a nine-case responsive-browser matrix. Release: https://github.com/stevekkall-beansgc/jumping-beans/releases/tag/v0.11.0 What's next The next experiment is a browser-native aggregation origin that can fan out to vertical or geographic storefront groups while preserving each underlying origin and result. We would also replace demonstration storefronts with authorized real partners, expand beyond retail matching, and reuse the same consent and receipt model for support and other multi-site journeys. title: Tenscore
pitch: A consent dashboard where the apply tool literally doesn’t exist until a human approves.
about_excerpt: A consent dashboard where the apply tool literally doesn’t exist until a human approves. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most permission UIs assume a human is clicking Revoke. Agents change that. Once a model can call tools on a live page, the hard question is no longer "can the agent help?" It is "what is the agent allowed to do, and can I see that?" Tenscore came from that gap. I wanted a consent workspace where an agent can inspect and plan, but apply stays locked until a person approves in the UI. WebMCP's dynamic tool registration made that enforceable. The product pitch and the safety model are the same idea: consent is visible, and the apply tool does not exist until you unlock it. What it does Tenscore is an interactive simulation of connected apps and grants. You pick a demo profile (Power User, Forgotten Accounts, or Minimalist), then explore a score, findings list, and consent map of who can see what. A browser agent can call typed site tools to inspect access, trace data flows, simulate cleanup, and stage a plan. The human reviews the plan in the UI and clicks Approve. Only then does apply_approved_changes register. After apply, the page shows a permission diff and a consent receipt. How we built it Stack: Next.js App Router, React, TypeScript, Tailwind, Zustand, Zod, Vitest, Playwright. Deployed on Vercel. Domain logic lives in pure functions under src/domain/ : scoring, findings, simulation, approvals, mutations, graph projection, policy, receipts, replay. The UI and WebMCP tools call the same mutation path through the store, so agent actions and button clicks stay in sync. Tools register with document.modelContext.registerTool and clean up via AbortController . Registration is phase-based ( no_plan , staged , approved , applied ), so apply is absent until UI approval binds a plan hash, profile version, and expiry. We TDD'd the domain first, then added scripted agent evals, catalog tests, and a Playwright judge journey. Stretch work includes privacy budget planning, timeline scrubbing synced to the map, snapshot import/export, redacted reports, and manual service creation. Challenges we ran into Keeping one truth for UI and tools. Early on it was easy to let the agent mutate state the panels did not show. Sharing domain functions and flushing UI updates before tool results return fixed that. Making the approval gate structural. A disabled button is weak proof. We needed apply to be unregistered until approve, then disappear after use, with fail-closed errors when the agent tries early. Accomplishments that we're proud of The apply gate is visible in product UI, not only in a README. The capability contract lists available vs denied tools per phase. A blocked apply shows a banner with the human next step. We shipped a full typed tool surface with Zod schemas, annotations ( readOnlyHint , untrustedContentHint ), deterministic evals, and Playwright coverage for the human path. Consent receipts and agent policy make the demo feel closer to how real agent permissions should work: constrain, approve, apply, audit. What we learned WebMCP is most interesting when tools change with state. A static tool list is a thin API. A phase-gated list is a permission model. Human-agent collaboration needs a shared surface. If the agent acts off screen, humans cannot verify anything. Map pulses, plan diffs, and the tool inspector matter as much as the execute functions. What's next for Tenscore Connect real grant sources behind the same stage/approve/apply path, with adapters that never let the agent skip UI approval. Ship a portable capability contract component other WebMCP apps can reuse: phase, available tools, denied tools, human next step. Add stronger live-agent eval harnesses (not only scripted chains) and keep the fail-closed apply path as the default for any write tool. title: voice-web-mcp
pitch: Use a full duplex/speech to speech voice agent CLI to control websites via webMCP + naturally learning languages with accents/tones with Anki cards.
about_excerpt: Use a full duplex/speech to speech voice agent CLI to control websites via webMCP + naturally learning languages with accents/tones with Anki cards. Like Comment Story Updates anime-photo Home page Inspiration Customers sometimes need to access tools/websites, but they can’t do it because websites are hard. The websites have bad UX, the customers are older and non technical, or don't speak English. What it does Parts I built two things: A basic webMCP controllable anki website for language learning. A (realtime duplex speech to speech) voice harness CLI that supports WebMCP. Codex voice mode doesn't let you talk to websites, this thing does. Examples Anyways, here's me screwing around with a bunch of people's websites they built (besides the example video): https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLPP6FwJZGwUA taboo game - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rqPqUa1mNcA rubiks cube https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fIQoW5sJ65g more of my own anki - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=a86MogHEFQA maze solver - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MVpu7fn3kqQ More technical details The website is straightforward, lets you import real Anki apkg files, and have it run on chrome. The agent harness in a similar way to claude code but its streaming speech to speech. It can control your files, your website, chrome tabs/cast controls, etc. Voice wise it supports parsing like Barge in, accents, accoustic event cancellation, noise cancellation, high pass/gain controls, etc. reference codes https://portpowered.github.io/anki-web-mcp/ is the website. https://github.com/portpowered/go-agent-harness is the CLI. Note that you have to have spent like $50+ dollars on OpenAI APIs to get any real usage out of the voice CLI, otherwise you're going to get rate limited, so probably constrained to the webMCP website otherwise. But anyways, it should be able to access whatever website you want. The AI is kind of dumb though. It works on the various webMCP showcases. Recordings: IRL recording: https://youtu.be/G_SsdL5Yqj8 Screen recording: https://youtu.be/811ooWpI0Zw How we built it We built it largely using 1) Codex/Claude 2) An agent factory/orchestrator that wraps luna max/codex workers. I had a Claude agent manage the factory as appropriate. 3) OpenAI realtime API 4) Golang 5) NextJS based static site on github pages. Challenges we ran into The UX of interacting with the MCP is highly fragile. You need to have to have a very strongly defined AGENTS.md and there is no current obvious way to declare WebMCP AGENTs.md/Instructions for each website. Tools that are available on different pages are different, and controlling them is hard for declaring the appropriate context on different pages. audio processing graphs are really actually quite complicated (barge in, accoustic event cancellation, umm/sigh, tool processing), this ended up being a significant time sink since current models aren't able to comprehend audio failures directly (except for like gemini). I don't really understand all the audio tools so was hard to build. Chrome is super flaky for casting and open/close with session controls. Accomplishments that we're proud of its actually really cool to get the agent to just fix the site using your voice. I only recorded it for a second, but I was using it to learn japanese for a few hours since I usually run on my phone. It helps a lot with like coming with phrases and accent help. Helps a lot with korean and chinese as well, since my accent is bad, and I don't understand tones. ~90% of the code was implemented via luna max workers and fixed and dispatched by them. I mostly just left it to run on my laptop at about 50 agents or so. The digital signals processing is more work than I imagined and I was able to figure it out and understand. Understanding accoustic event cancellation, barge in, noise cancellation. Independent of the webMCP functions, the fact that there's now like a generic Anki page that customers can load their deck into is super useful, because installing an app is annoying. What we learned webMCP is super useful actually, i'm probably going to tamper monkey a bunch of websites so that I can just buy stuff off doordash. Audio data signals processing, like how to make the voice robots not echo itself and re-trigger, how to set up the noise clearing, how to set up VAD, etc. Realtime models are much more useful than I anticipated, but they're still kind of flaky. What's next for voice-web-mcp better multi tab handling if you have multiple browser tabs running and you want the agents to focus on a specific one or move between tabs generally. better multimodality input/output is needed for things that can watch/hear/read. better streaming is needed for things that happen over time better connections to payments and authorization is needed for delegated permissions better AGENTS.md/instruction declaration. Built With chrome golang realtime voice webmcp Try it out github.com portpowered.github.io github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I am banana. I eat myself. title: GatherLight
pitch: GatherLight uses WebMCP to channel spare human time and skills into peer-reviewed, verified contributions to the open web.
about_excerpt: GatherLight uses WebMCP to channel spare human time and skills into peer-reviewed, verified contributions to the open web. Like 2 Comment Story Updates GatherLight - Landing Page and Queries Quests and OSS Tools Integrated with - OpenStreetMap and Wikimedia Quest - Completion and Sign off on the Volunteer's name, Minimum Viable Information Screen to verify final submission details A Peer Selected Reviewer Views your contribution Let's Go! Star Lights up, And your community thanks your service! Architecture Diagram Detailing Deployment, Infra, Sites and Tools Inspiration Volunteering takes more time than most people expect. A person might have twenty free minutes and a genuine desire to help but the steps surrounding that desire often take much longer. They need to find a useful gap, learn an unfamiliar system, gather evidence, format it correctly, verify it and locate the right reviewer. And let's be real, most honestly helpful people drop off before they ever reach the step that only they can do. This led us to the enigma : what should an agent never do on behalf of a person? An agent cannot stand at a shop entrance and check whether it is step-free. It cannot make a phone call and take responsibility for what it heard. These actions require human presence, judgment and accountability. However an agent can remove nearly every obstacle surrounding those actions. GatherLight uses WebMCP capability to coordinate human-led civic work across the web. It finds real gaps in OpenStreetMap and Wikidata and guides a person through one useful task. It checks the result, carries it across sites, asks for explicit confirmation and routes it to another person for review. The agent handles the logistics and the human does the work. (A genuine win-win) What it does GatherLight takes one plain-language request and turns it into one verified civic contribution. "Find me something useful I can do near Koramangala in twenty minutes." (for people that don't know what Koramangala is, it is a place in an Indian city - Bangalore, known for parties,tech and ever upgrading infrastructure) The browser agent works through the below five WebMCP tools. find-quests finds gaps on OpenStreetMap or Wikidata that match the volunteer's location, available time and skills. open-quest opens the visible workspace and explains the parts of the work that must remain human such as calling a place, visiting an entrance or reading an independent source. check-contribution checks the form against source-specific rules and returns exact corrections instead of a generic error message. submit-contribution becomes available only after the check passes. It opens an HTML confirmation dialog showing the exact contribution, destination, visibility and licence. The tool waits for the person to click and then checks the contribution again before sending anything. approve-contribution is available only to a reviewer who has a submitted contribution. It rejects self-review, checks that the public source has not changed and records either an approval or a stale result. Some quests continue/handed off on another website. Well, that's the USP. We are not just building a Hackathon repository but something that expands on the very foundations of WebMCP. The handoff carries permission and provenance but it does not carry the volunteer's PII data, observation, credentials or source tokens . The person enters the evidence through the visible interface. After review, an approved OpenStreetMap contribution can be opened in an embedded iD editor. GatherLight reloads the live map element, compares its version and stages the exact change in iD's undoable state. Nothing is uploaded automatically. Approval also produces a visible collective result (Audit purposes when Crowd Sourced - obviously). A mark becomes fully lit only when the public source accepts the change. GatherLight does not treat "approved" and "published" as the same thing. How we built it (This gets fairly technical, fairly fast - bear with us - or if you wanna skip the text - Excalidraw Slides to Show what we did .) The main product is not the website. It is @gatherlight/quest-tools , a framework-neutral package that expresses the five verbs as a reusable WebMCP grammar. Quest is the React reference application and Survey is a separate partner site written in vanilla TypeScript. Both use the same package which is proof that the workflow is portable across sites, origins and frameworks. The package registers tools through document.modelContext . Each WebMCP tool is a thin wrapper over the same operation used by the visible interface so a button and an agent call run the same validation, confirmation, state transition and error handling. There is no hidden automation path that can bypass the human interface. A capability rack shows the tools available at the current moment. When the workflow state changes the package updates the registered tools. By design, The submit-contribution tool does not exist for the agent until the contribution passes its check. The package still validates availability inside every execution because dynamic registration improves tool discovery but it is not an authorization boundary. Every result uses a small quest/1 envelope with an explicit state. Human-readable guidance comes first and one stable machine-readable line comes last. Public place names, source titles, URLs and contribution text are treated as untrusted input. We cap and escape them and mark tool output with untrustedContentHint . Cross-origin state lives in one Cloudflare Durable Object that stores only two entities: contributions and handoffs. Handoffs include: hashed, origin-bound, action-bound, single-use and short-lived. Exchanging one creates a grant for one contribution without exposing the volunteer's session. The data used is real. Overpass finds OpenStreetMap places with missing opening hours or wheelchair information. SPARQL finds Wikidata statements that still lack a source. Nominatim and Photon resolve place names. opening_hours validates map syntax. iD stages reviewed OpenStreetMap changes. Offline snapshots of real source data keep the demo usable when a public endpoint is unavailable. Challenges we ran into Crossing the document boundary WebMCP tools belong to the document that registered them so a full navigation destroys that document and its registered tools, and this boundary is still under discussion in WebMCP issue #227 . We worked around this by having open-quest return the next URL along with an opaque handoff that the receiving site can exchange to register the next valid tools without needing a browser extension. Keeping the person in control A browser-owned elicitation mechanism does not yet exist (see issue #165 ) so our package uses a site-owned <dialog> that follows a fixed sequence of check, preview, wait for confirmation, check again and then submit. Nothing is sent if the form changes after confirmation or if the person declines at any point, though we acknowledge this is an application-level safeguard and not a browser security primitive. Working with live public data A correct contribution can become outdated while it waits for review so GatherLight captures the source revision when a quest opens and reloads it before any approval or iD staging step. If the source has changed the contribution is marked stale and nothing is overwritten silently. Accomplishments that we're proud of One agent coordinates a human-led workflow across two origins and three surfaces using a single shared package. Quest discovers the work, Survey receives the field contribution and iD stages the reviewed change and the same five-verb package works in both React and vanilla TypeScript without any framework-specific logic. The human contribution cannot be bypassed and submission cannot skip confirmation. The agent can open, check, route and submit but it cannot manufacture an observation, photograph or source judgment, and both the UI and agent paths go through the same check-confirm-check sequence. Every contribution is grounded in real public data with each stage of the lifecycle clearly labelled and the prototype produces concrete findings for the open WebMCP Skills proposal . What we learned In civic systems an agent is more useful when it removes the friction around work that still needs human presence and judgment rather than trying to do that work itself and WebMCP makes this possible because the agent acts inside the page's current session through capabilities the site owns while the visible interface stays in control. We also found that being honest about what a contribution has actually achieved is more valuable than overstating it because telling a user that their contribution is reviewed but not yet published builds more trust than an animation that implies more change than actually happened. What's next for GatherLight First we will contribute the implementation evidence back to WebMCP's active discussions. Cross-document

title: Agent City — The Web Built for Humans and Agents
pitch: A miniature internet built from the ground up for humans and AI agents to navigate, collaborate, and act together through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A miniature internet built from the ground up for humans and AI agents to navigate, collaborate, and act together through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Agent City: An Agent-Native Web Experiment The web was made for people. Every button, form, and checkout flow assumes a human is staring at the screen and deciding what to click. AI agents are changing that, but most current browser agents just mimic humans. They inspect a page, find an element, click it, and wait for the result. It is a slow, repetitive loop. We wanted to see what happens when agents are treated as first-class users. So we built Agent City , a small, simulated internet where humans and AI agents work together. The event planning scenario is just an easy way to show the concept, but the real experiment is about what an “agent-native” web actually looks like. The Four Districts Agent City has four districts: Venue District: Searches for and reserves spaces. Catering District: Finds food based on headcounts and budgets. Calendar District: Manages scheduling. Budget District: Tracks spending. Humans use a standard visual UI. Agents use WebMCP tools such as search_venues() and schedule_event() . Both interfaces interact with the same underlying state. How It Works If a user asks for a vegetarian meetup for 12 people tomorrow after 2 PM under ₹10,000, the agent finds the venue and food, checks the budget, and builds the plan. Things get interesting when requirements change. If the guest list jumps to 20 and the venue only holds 15, the system flags the conflict. The agent then has to find a bigger venue and redo the catering and budget. It is not just browser automation; it is collaboration over shared data. To make this visible, we added: An Agent Activity Graph A WebMCP Inspector These tools allow humans to see the agent’s work in real time. Technology We built the city using: React TypeScript Vite Cloudflare Workers D1 The architecture is straightforward: $$ \text{Human} \rightarrow \text{Visual Interface} \rightarrow \text{Shared State} \rightarrow \text{WebMCP Layer} \rightarrow \text{AI Agent} $$ Designing the Tools Instead of one giant “do everything” tool, we gave agents small, composable capabilities. We also made these tools context-aware. An agent sees reserve_venue() before a booking exists, but sees modify_reservation() once the booking is made. The hardest part was the tool design. A tool needs: A clear name A predictable result A well-defined purpose If tools overlap, the agent gets confused. If they are too broad, the agent stops reasoning. If they are too small, the task takes too many calls. Keeping Humans and Agents in Sync We also had to keep the human and agent views in sync. When an agent books a venue, the UI has to show it immediately. When a human changes the attendee count, the agent has to react to that new state. We found that building for agents does not mean killing the UI. Humans and agents just need different views of the same world: Humans want visual exploration and direct control. Agents want typed inputs and predictable results. What Comes Next Agent City is currently focused on event planning, but the idea could work for anything from finance to infrastructure. Next, we want to explore: Better permission systems Human approval flows More complex agent collaboration Safer handling of high-impact actions The core question is simple. If agents are now normal participants on the web, why force them to use interfaces made only for humans? Built With chatgpt cloudflare css html javascript react typescript vite webmcp Try it out github.com agent-city.imyash-chaudhary2.workers.dev Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I built the entire project solo — frontend, backend, and agent layer. I designed and built Agent City as a WebMCP-native app: a React + TypeScript frontend where every capability is exposed as a typed tool through document.modelContext, backed by a Cloudflare Worker API. The hardest part was the tool surface design — getting the read/write annotations, dynamic registration (tools appear only when state unlocks them), and the human-in-the-loop approval gate to all stay consistent. I learned that designing for agents is a different discipline from designing UIs: the schema is the interface, and the approval flow is a UX problem, not just a security check.  Inspiration 

 Yesterday, my friend sent me a message in Facebook because she remembered me out of nowhere. She is an expert in GIS. We talked a lot about GIS, tools and AI.
Then, this morning, I saw a Facebook post about the WebMCP challenge. Thus, I have thought of this idea. 

 What it does 

 Basically, this is a web app featuring a geo dataset. For this demo, I chose just 1 sample public dataset from Melbourne datasets. This dataset is just sample data from the playgrounds dataset. In usual web apps, data or map is displayed. Then, users will query the data based on the filters they need. Example: Which playgrounds have swings or sandpit? Think of niched micro sites or niched directories. 

 As required in the WebMCP challenge, WebMCP is added in the web app. With this, the user puts the question to ChatGPT in natural language, then ChatGPT calls the tools exposed in the web app using the WebMCP. title: Viernes — Autonomous Gym ERP & Visual Floor Commander
pitch: Agent-native Gym Operations ERP powered by WebMCP. Control 2D floor plans, reschedule classes, and manage churn through direct AI agent browser actions in real-time.
about_excerpt: Agent-native Gym Operations ERP powered by WebMCP. Control 2D floor plans, reschedule classes, and manage churn through direct AI agent browser actions in real-time. Like Comment Story Updates Tactical 2D Floor Commander with real-time zone blueprints, equipment status, and WebMCP agent HUD. Live maintenance filter isolating equipment requiring repairs and active service tickets on the floor. Interactive class scheduling modal with real-time trainer conflict detection and capacity validation. Member Churn Radar tracking attendance decay, churn risk scores, and automated retention vouchers. One-click retention campaign dispatch offering personalized vouchers to high-risk member cohorts. Facility Telemetry & Revenue Sandbox modeling live occupancy, peak hours, and dynamic financial forecasts. Live WebMCP tool execution: the AI agent updates equipment maintenance state and moves classes in real time. 💡 Inspiration Traditional gym management software is clunky, fragmented, and buried behind endless tabs of legacy forms. Facility managers and head coaches waste hours every week manually cross-referencing floor maintenance, juggling trainer shift conflicts, and reacting too late after premium members have already stopped showing up. Inspired by Tony Stark’s tactical AI assistant F.R.I.D.A.Y. , we built VIERNES — an agent-native Gym Operations ERP and Visual Floor Commander that transforms static database software into a real-time, interactive command center powered by the Web Model Context Protocol (WebMCP) . 🚀 What it Does Viernes unites the entire athletic facility's operations into a single reactive workspace where humans and AI agents collaborate seamlessly: 🏟️ Tactical Visual Floor Commander : An interactive 2D blueprint of a 15,000 sq ft facility across 5 zones. Real-time machine operational states, maintenance wear badges, and agent attention pulses. 📅 Dynamic Class Timeline & Trainer Roster : High-density weekly schedule grid with room capacity validation, instant conflict detection, and trainer reassignments. 👥 Member Churn Radar & Retention Center : Algorithmic churn risk scoring (0–100%) tracking attendance decay with one-click personalized re-engagement campaigns. 📈 Facility Telemetry & Revenue Sandbox : Live occupancy heatmaps, equipment duty cycles, and real-time financial sensitivity modeling. 🎙️ Floating Viernes AI Copilot HUD : In-browser agent console with one-click multi-step scenario presets and live WebMCP execution telemetry. 🌐 WebMCP Implementation & Paradigm Shift 1. Why is this use case a strong fit for WebMCP? Athletic facility management is intrinsically visual, spatial, and multi-variable. Instead of forcing AI agents to blindly scrape HTML or make disconnected server calls, WebMCP gives the browser's model direct, typed, programmatic control over live in-memory React state and SVG canvas objects. 2. How does it create a better user experience? A manager can issue a single natural language instruction ("Mark Bench #3 for maintenance and move Coach Marcus's 5:30 PM class to Zone C"), and Viernes executes multiple synchronized UI state changes in milliseconds. The manager sees the 2D floor plan pulse red while the calendar shifts room assignments instantly. 3. What humans and agents can do together now: Before WebMCP, combining 2D asset awareness with dynamic scheduling required hours of manual spreadsheet work. With Viernes: The agent detects at-risk member cohorts, calculates churn probabilities, and populates retention offers. The human reviews proposed changes visually on the floor plan and approves or adjusts them with drag-and-drop ease. The agent simulates revenue forecasts and rebalances class schedules to eliminate bottlenecks. 4. Technical Architecture Viernes registers 6 client-side tools directly onto document.modelContext.registerTool upon mounting: update_gym_floor_equipment manage_class_schedule query_member_cohorts launch_retention_campaign simulate_revenue_forecast get_facility_telemetry All inputs are validated via strict Zod schemas with human-in-the-loop safeguards on sensitive financial and scheduling actions. 🛠️ How We Built It Framework : Next.js 15 (App Router) & React 19 Styling : Tailwind CSS & Framer Motion for obsidian/neon tactical HUD animations State & Schema : Zustand & Zod Protocol : WebMCP ( document.modelContext ) & use-webmcp-tool Icons & UI : Lucide React & Radix UI 🏆 Accomplishments That We're Proud Of Zero-latency bidirectional synchronization between agent tool calls and interactive SVG floor elements. A Stark-inspired dark obsidian aesthetic that makes complex facility data immediately actionable. Fully autonomous test suite built with Playwright validating end-to-end tool execution in headless browser sessions. 🔮 What's Next for Viernes Computer vision occupancy tracking via RTSP camera feeds. Multi-branch federation for nationwide gym chains. Direct biometric telemetry integration with wearable health devices. title: Lessonique
pitch: An agent-guided coding classroom where ChatGPT teaches through safe, structured WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: An agent-guided coding classroom where ChatGPT teaches through safe, structured WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates The agent prepares the lesson and configures the learning workspace. A focused explanation connects a variable declaration to its name and value. The learner completes a variables exercise and receives validation feedback. Lessonique waits for a WebMCP connection before opening the classroom. Code highlighting connects undefined and null to concrete examples. The guide highlights a const declaration while explaining its behavior. Inspiration When I first started learning programming, I did not have the kind of guidance I needed. It was difficult to know where to begin, how the concepts connected, or whether I was really understanding what I was doing. Those first steps could feel confusing and frustrating. Lessonique grew from that experience. I wanted to build the kind of learning companion I wish I had: something that explains a concept, shows exactly where it applies, and gives you a small opportunity to practice before moving on. The goal is not to let AI do the learning for you. It is to make learning to code feel more approachable, with clear guidance and less frustration. What Lessonique does Lessonique is an agent-guided coding classroom for learning HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript. ChatGPT uses WebMCP to turn a learning request into a workspace with examples, a learning plan, visual explanations, and practice exercises. Instead of reading an explanation in one window and figuring out where it applies in another, the learner can follow the explanation directly in the classroom. The agent guides; the learner practices. Connect your AI guide Open Lessonique in a WebMCP-capable client. The application detects the connection, and the agent discovers which classroom tools and learning environments are available. No Lessonique account is required. From a request to a classroom Ask to learn a topic from scratch. As the agent prepares the lesson, Lessonique shows the setup stages: understanding the goal, preparing the lesson, and configuring the classroom. Understand one concept at a time Lessons break concepts into small explanations with examples. The guide can focus attention on the relevant code while the learning plan keeps the broader topic sequence visible. In this example, a JavaScript variable is introduced through its name, value, and assignment operator. Follow the explanation in the code The visual guide connects explanations to specific code targets. Here, the learner explores a const declaration and when to use it. Previous and Next controls let them review the lesson at their own pace. Make abstract ideas concrete Concepts such as undefined and null are easier to discuss when the learner can see the exact declarations being compared. The companion, highlight, and guide work together to keep that connection visible. Practice and check your progress The learner writes code in the editor and validates it against the lesson's declared requirements. The screenshot shows a completed exercise using string, number, and boolean values. Guidance supports the learner without replacing the practice itself. Why WebMCP is essential A coding classroom needs more than generated explanations. An agent must be able to configure the workspace, present a lesson, point to relevant code, and request meaningful feedback about progress. Lessonique exposes those operations through 13 structured WebMCP Site Tools registered in the top-level document with document.modelContext.registerTool. The tools use closed schemas, Zod validation, and capability checks. Semantic targets describe what to highlight instead of requiring the agent to supply CSS selectors or screen coordinates. This lets the human and agent share a coherent learning workflow: ChatGPT coordinates the lesson, Lessonique handles presentation and validation, and the learner controls the exercise code. The agent does not need to reconstruct the classroom through fragile UI automation. How I built it Lessonique uses Next.js, React, and TypeScript, with Monaco for editing and Sandpack for the runtime, preview, and console. A provider-neutral core separates the WebMCP tools, lesson orchestration, workspace management, teaching scenes, and validation. Codex helped implement the specification-driven architecture, debug interactions, build tests, assemble visual assets and sprites, and verify the deployed experience. ChatGPT Create Image produced the source visual references for the companion. Asset provenance and third-party notices are documented in the repository. ChatGPT is the teaching agent. Lessonique has no built-in chatbot or custom AI backend. title: ONEPATH
pitch: A calmer, adaptive path forward — shaped together by a person and their agent.
about_excerpt: A calmer, adaptive path forward — shaped together by a person and their agent. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Large goals often fail at the moment they become emotionally or cognitively overwhelming. Conventional agent experiences tend to offer more advice or take more control. ONEPATH explores a different collaboration model: the agent makes the next step smaller and clearer, while the person remains visibly responsible for accepting the path. What it does ONEPATH is a WebMCP-native adaptive interface for moments when a goal feels too large. A person begins with a goal such as “I lost my job and don't know where to start.” ONEPATH exposes the live goal and path through WebMCP. The agent proposes a short initial path, but cannot apply it. The person accepts or keeps the current state in the interface. If Complete your CV feels too large, the person clicks This feels like too much . That direct UI action becomes a structured friction signal. The agent reads the updated state and proposes a smaller replacement: Complete your CV → What was your last job? The person must accept that proposal in the UI. Completing the first micro-step then shows 1 of 5 , 20% complete , and a visible Undo last change control. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, an agent would have to infer the goal, path, current step, progress, friction signal, and undo state from pixels, then guess which controls are safe. ONEPATH gives the agent structured access to the live interface state through a small, bounded Site Tools contract. This is not merely faster automation. WebMCP lets the agent and person share the same structured state while preserving a deliberate authority boundary: the agent may inspect, propose, complete a person-supplied micro-step, or undo when asked, but it cannot silently accept a path proposal. How it was built ONEPATH is a React and TypeScript application deployed as a public site. It registers exactly five tools with document.modelContext.registerTool : get_current_state — reads the current goal, path, active step, progress, friction signal, pending proposal, and undo availability. propose_initial_path — stages a short initial path without applying it. propose_step_adaptation — stages smaller replacement steps only after a matching too_much signal for the live current-step ID. mark_step_complete — records a completed visible step and keeps the change reversible. rollback_last_change — restores the previous accepted state when history exists. There is deliberately no accept_proposal tool . Both Accept change actions in the demo are real person-only UI actions. The agent proposes; the person decides. State transitions, proposal guardrails, reversible progress, and the exact five-tool contract are covered by automated tests. Human experience Proposals remain visibly proposals: each includes its reason, before/after comparison, and Accept change / Keep current controls. The activity panel distinguishes person actions from agent suggestions. Progress and Undo remain visible after completion, so adaptation never feels like an invisible takeover. Challenges and verification The central challenge was making adaptation useful without giving the agent authority it should not have. The interface, state model, and WebMCP contract all had to preserve the same boundary: structured agent action up to a proposal, followed by an explicit human decision. The full natural-language flow was verified on the judge-accessible public site using live ChatGPT Site Tools rather than a preview fallback. The agent discovered all five tools, read production state, staged both proposals, responded to the real too_much friction signal, and produced the hero transformation. After one safe synthetic micro-step, both structured state and the visible UI showed 1 of 5 , 20% complete , and Undo last change . What became possible A person can communicate friction with one direct interface action instead of writing another prompt. The agent can respond to the exact live step instead of offering generic advice. Together they can reshape the path in place while keeping every important decision explicit, inspectable, and reversible. Current scope This challenge MVP deliberately has no backend database, login requirement, voice feature, or automatic proposal acceptance. Demo state is stored locally in the browser. The job-loss path is a scenario; the underlying state model is generic. title: svgent Agent Stage
pitch: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video.
about_excerpt: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent Stage: two showcase scripts rendered by svgent, a terminal and an app Inspiration svgent is a client-only studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. A script describes a chat window or a terminal, with typing, thinking, tool runs, approvals and choices, and the studio renders it to SVG, PNG, GIF and MP4. People use it for READMEs, docs, talks and posts, where a recording of a real session would leak secrets and could not be re-shot or translated. Before this, the studio's AI assist was copy and paste: copy a prompt into a chat, paste the JSON back. WebMCP replaces that with tool calls on the page. The page can also answer with facts a language model cannot see: how long a page runs, when each message lands, what the frame looks like at eleven seconds. The agent works on the stage itself, not on a guess about it. What it does Agent Stage is the studio with WebMCP site tools. The agent in ChatGPT's built-in browser writes the script, sets the surface, look, camera and pages, measures the result, looks at a frame, proposes rewrites, and asks to export. The person keeps the decisions: rewrites and exports wait on a card, every string the script puts on the stage is listed, and each change can be undone. load_script validates a script and previews it at once. direct_camera turns on a deterministic follow camera. inspect_timeline returns per-message timing and a review. snapshot_frame returns a PNG of any moment. fit_duration lands a page on an exact length and reports what it changed. propose_patch puts rewrites on a card. approve_proposal exists only while a proposal is pending and waits for the person's click. export asks first. The rail shows every call. The "Every word on the stage" list holds every string the script puts on the stage, including what a collapse or a page turn hides. The tool descriptions tell the agent to treat what it knows from the conversation as private and to use stand-ins for real names, unless the person relaxes that on the page or in the chat. Credentials never pass. A loaded script keeps only the fields that render. Looks, fonts, images and camera go through their own tools. Live: https://agent.svgent.zakideee.dev/ Code: https://github.com/zakideee/svgent (the page is apps/webmcp/ ) How we built it 13 tools on document.modelContext , with navigator.modelContext as the fallback, registered with an AbortSignal for teardown. approve_proposal is registered only while a proposal is pending. Results are plain objects plus an MCP-style content array (text, and an image part for frames). The studio package gained a small imperative handle: read, replace and patch the project, seek, play, export, render a frame, spotlight a message. An agent's edit goes through the same state the person's controls use, so undo, autosave, validation and preview all see it. Text layout and rasterization run in WASM (boundsvg) in the browser. The animated SVG is CSS keyframes with no JavaScript. There is no server; nothing leaves the tab except the files the person downloads. The submission is apps/webmcp/ : the WebMCP tools, the agent rail, the privacy default, the showcase scripts and the share card, plus the studio handle ( StudioHandle , chrome , renderFrame , spotlight ) and one preview aspect-ratio fix. The studio, scene and render packages predate the challenge. Challenges we ran into ChatGPT's browser exposes document.modelContext , Chromium exposes navigator.modelContext , and the API can appear after the page has loaded. Registration prefers the document, polls for a late API, and reports the outcome in the rail. A dynamic tool ( approve_proposal ) that unregisters itself while a call is in flight fails that call. It now stays registered for a short grace period after the proposal resolves. A script an agent writes from a conversation can carry real names, paths, hosts and keys from that conversation. The privacy default, the script allowlist and the "every word" list exist for that. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole loop runs in the ChatGPT desktop app (built-in browser, GPT-5.6 Sol) and in Chromium with WebMCP enabled, and the demo video is a recording of it. The agent edits through the same state as the person's controls, so undo, autosave, validation and preview treat both alike. Four of the showcase scripts are problems agent-app users have: a clip for the team channel without the secrets; a reproduction of a decline that was missed, when recording is not allowed; three slides that walk a colleague through choices and approvals; a README hero for your own MCP server. What we learned A page can hand an agent facts it cannot infer (timing, frames, what would render), and that is worth more than letting the agent guess well. Approval and visibility have to be part of the tools, not a note in a prompt. What's next for svgent Agent Stage A deny list of the person's own words (names, hosts, projects) checked on the page, next to the pattern-based hints. The same tools on the other surfaces the studio renders, and on the CLI for headless use. The demo video was recorded in the ChatGPT desktop app. Waits are sped up where marked. The narration is a synthetic voice.
