title: Mantle Builder
pitch: Build WebMCP services from business workflows—agent-ready and Cloudflare-ready.
about_excerpt: Build WebMCP services from business workflows—agent-ready and Cloudflare-ready. Like Comment Story Updates Core ERP service graph generated from one Mantle Manifest. Typed data models include constraints, indexes, and agent-ready operations. A handoff package guides a coding agent from the backend contract to a deployable site. API, MCP, and WebMCP interfaces are generated and documented together. Mantle Builder uses WebMCP to rapidly create your own WebMCP-enabled business service and take it to Cloudflare. Describe the workflow in agent chat; the agent builds and validates the Mantle contract, previews its API, MCP, WebMCP, and Admin surfaces, then hands it to a coding agent to finish the frontend, authentication, and production deployment. Inspiration Companies adopting agent workflows quickly run into business-logic gaps. Agents can reason and browse, but the organization's real rules—who can do what, which records exist, how an order or request moves, and which operations are public or staff-only—are still trapped in documents and bespoke code. Conventional app builders also make the human perform every configuration step through a visual editor. We wanted a shared workspace where a person supplies intent and approval while an agent supplies structured implementation. What it does Mantle Builder lets a person describe a workflow and lets their agent build the service behind it through WebMCP. What is Mantle? Mantle is the open-source, config-as-code runtime beneath the Builder. An agent writes four atoms—Schema, View, Procedure, and Trigger—in one YAML Manifest; Mantle validates the contract and carries the runtime complexity. The same contract can power real consumer-facing services such as commerce, reservations, and application flows while immediately producing API, MCP, WebMCP, and Admin surfaces. Agents get the tools missing from their workflows, while operations teams get one place to manage customers, orders, requests, and queues. The agent works through four typed WebMCP tools: builder_get_started — inspect the active project, Mantle grammar, presets, and exact next calls. builder_apply_preset — start from a tested business workflow. builder_apply_manifest_patch — compile and safely activate confirmed changes. builder_execute_preview — run the service as a mock actor, inspect mutations, and follow the result in Admin. The prompt requires the agent to interview the user about actors, data, operations, permissions, and entry points, summarize the proposal, and wait for confirmation before changing the project. Every accepted change immediately appears inside an embedded Mantle Admin developer console. The person can inspect schemas, procedures, triggers, interfaces, and operational Admin views. The agent can execute the service as an anonymous visitor, member, or owner, compare canonical entries before and after mutations, and watch Admin follow the affected View, collection, or record. When the contract is ready, the user downloads a coding-agent handoff containing the complete Manifest, pinned Mantle references, a frontend WebMCP registration example, and deployment guidance. A coding agent can then add the consumer-owned frontend, authentication, provider configuration, and production wiring. Why WebMCP WebMCP turns Mantle Builder from a one-way generator into a shared control surface for people and agents. An agent can author the service, seed data, and exercise public, member, and staff workflows through typed preview tools. Each action updates the same persistent sandbox the human is viewing, while the embedded Admin console follows the affected page, collection, or record. The agent acts; the human can watch, inspect, and approve the result as it happens. This closes the loop from intent to implementation to verification. Teams can create MCP and WebMCP services that fill gaps in existing agent workflows, while operations still gets a trusted interface for managing customers, orders, requests, and queues. How we built it The React host registers Mantle-derived capabilities with document.modelContext . WebMCP calls enter one serialized mutation path where inputs and project revisions are validated. Valid Mantle resources compile into a runtime plan; a browser-hosted adapter and mock environment power the service preview. Mantle Admin runs in a same-origin iframe and talks to the host runtime over a constrained message bridge. Project Manifests and canonical preview entries autosave to IndexedDB. The production host is deployed as a Cloudflare Worker. What we learned A useful agent interface needs more than tool registration. The tools must expose enough grammar and current state for an agent to act reliably, mutations need optimistic revision checks, invalid candidates must never replace the last working project, and the human needs a visual way to verify what the agent created. Built during the challenge The implementation began on September 2, 2026. The WebMCP authoring flow, Mantle preview, project persistence, coding-agent handoff, browser testing, and Cloudflare production deployment were all created during the submission period. The public commit history distinguishes this work from the pre-existing Mantle Core dependency. Current limitations Builder project Manifests and preview records persist only in the current browser; they are not production data or synced across devices. Preview authentication is intentionally mocked. The Builder supports declarative Views and builtin Procedure handlers; custom handler refs, a consumer frontend, production authentication, and provider wiring are completed after the coding-agent handoff. title: Air Instruments
pitch: Play drums, keys and guitar with your hands, mouse or keyboard, then learn with a browser agent that reads your actual playing through WebMCP and proposes what's next.
about_excerpt: Play drums, keys and guitar with your hands, mouse or keyboard, then learn with a browser agent that reads your actual playing through WebMCP and proposes what's next. Like Comment Story Updates GIF air-instruments Inspiration Built in one day by an ex-StreamYard engineer and guitar player whose mouse broke this week — so fingers became the instrument. The sticks are virtual because "real sticks are my index fingers." The deeper thesis: an agent that teaches an instrument should read the state that actually matters — the notes you played, their timing, your score — never pixels, and it should never apply its own proposal without you. What it does Drums, a 25-key keyboard, and a six-string guitar (electric or acoustic) live in a single web page. A webcam tracks your hands; pinch and strum, tap and pluck, or just use a mouse, touch or keyboard — this isn't camera-only. Learn music : 27 short lessons across all three instruments, with a local, rule-based teacher that scores your timing note-by-note. Learn with an agent : the page registers seven tools on document.modelContext (WebMCP). An agent in the browser can read your completed take, open a lesson, demonstrate it on the real instrument, point at the exact step you fumbled, explain why in its own attributed panel, and propose an easier exercise. A human presses Apply exercise or Keep mine — the agent can never apply its own proposal — and Undo agent exercise restores your prior state. The panel shows recent tool calls so you can watch exactly what the agent touched. This whole loop is self-contained in the page — no backend, no microphone, works for anyone who opens the live URL. Why WebMCP is a good fit An agent can already talk about music. It cannot hear you play, and it cannot reach into a page to open the right lesson. Everything that matters — the note the audio engine actually produced, when it landed, whether it was on the beat, which lesson is open, what your last take scored — lives in the page. That state is worthless in a chat box and priceless to a teacher. There's no server to run, no API key, no MCP endpoint to host. The page registers seven tools with document.modelContext and any WebMCP-aware agent in that browser can use them. Camera frames and microphone audio are never in a tool result — there's no microphone in this build at all. How we built it Plain ES modules, no build step, no framework. Seven tools via document.modelContext.registerTool (with a navigator.modelContext fallback): reading state, listing and opening lessons, playing a demo or a take, proposing and explaining exercises, and focusing attention on one step. Local hand tracking runs in a worker; Web Audio does the drum, key and string synthesis, including a real plucked-string model for guitar. Every agent proposal carries a revision check — change the exercise yourself and a stale proposal is rejected rather than silently applied. Challenges we ran into The guitar's pinch-and-strum input had a real coordinate-mapping bug: the code only registered a strum inside a small active zone of the stage, so a hand could be visibly crossing the strings and still trigger nothing. Traced and fixed. Getting the same teach → try → feedback → easier-exercise loop to work identically across three very different instruments (drums, keys, strings) took more care than expected — each has its own timing and input model underneath one shared agent contract. What we learned Building a teaching loop where the agent can suggest but never act is a different design problem than a normal tool-calling agent — the human has to stay the one holding the instrument, in the interaction design itself, not just in a permissions check. What's next More instruments on the same agent contract Multiplayer lessons, so two people (or a person and an agent) can play the same piece together Tool-calling verified in Chrome with WebMCP enabled. The in-page agent flow inside ChatGPT's own in-app browser has been used live to test and debug the guitar input, as shown in the submitted image gallery. title: OwnerOps
pitch: AI Store Manager where humans edit agent plans, WebMCP re-evaluates them, and only reviewed changes are applied.
about_excerpt: AI Store Manager where humans edit agent plans, WebMCP re-evaluates them, and only reviewed changes are applied. Like Comment Story Updates One live operating state across people, sales, stock and costs. The agent materializes a reviewable plan — not just a chat answer. The owner can directly change the agent's proposal. WebMCP re-reads the exact human-edited candidate before commitment. One operating model, adapted across markets and languages. Inspiration OwnerOps started from a problem that feels very practical to me. In Korea, I see many people worrying about stable employment or considering small businesses as another path. But running a small store is difficult in ways that are easy to underestimate. Labor costs keep increasing. Employee schedules are difficult to manage. Ingredient prices change. Rent is expensive. And even understanding how much money is actually left after all of those costs can be surprisingly difficult. Large companies have separate people for finance, purchasing, HR, and operations. A small business owner often has to do all of that alone. My background is not traditional web product development, so I did not start this project because I wanted to build an impressive AI demo. I started with a much simpler question: Could AI actually make running a small business a little easier? To me, this feels like one of the positive ways AI can be used — not replacing the owner, but helping them understand the business, organize information, compare options, and make better decisions. That idea became OwnerOps , an AI Store Manager built with WebMCP. What it does I tried to build OwnerOps around the kinds of questions I think a real store owner might ask: Am I spending too much on labor? Can I change this schedule without hurting service? Which inventory items are becoming risky? Are ingredient costs getting too high? How much money is the store actually keeping? What happens if operating costs increase? OwnerOps brings staffing, schedules, sales, inventory, waste, purchase costs, operating costs, and profitability into one working store state. The owner uses a normal visual application. The AI agent uses nine structured WebMCP Site Tools. Both work with the same StoreState. For example, the owner can ask: Improve this week's operating profitability without creating a service coverage gap. The agent can read the relevant store information and create a StorePlan Preview. But I did not want the AI to simply make the change by itself. The owner can modify the proposed worker or shift time directly in the UI. When that happens, the previous review becomes invalid. The agent must then read the exact human-edited candidate again using evaluate_current_plan . Only after that version becomes REVIEWED can the owner apply it. The core flow is: Agent proposes → Human edits → Agent re-evaluates the exact edit → Human applies That became the most important interaction in OwnerOps. Why WebMCP I did not want the AI to understand the store by looking at screenshots and moving a mouse around a website. The application already knows its schedules, sales, inventory, costs, and current plan. WebMCP lets the agent work with those capabilities directly. The OwnerOps UI is for the human. The WebMCP tools are for the agent. But both operate on the same state. I deliberately kept the WebMCP surface to nine intent-level tools instead of exposing every internal function. The tools represent things the agent actually needs to do — read the store, create and preview plans, record events, evaluate the current candidate, and apply reviewed changes. Direct interaction with the rendered UI is left to the human for things such as editing the proposal and approving Apply. How I built it OwnerOps is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, PostgreSQL/Supabase, and WebMCP through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Because web product development is not my main professional background, I used AI tools heavily throughout the project. I used them to learn unfamiliar technologies, implement and review code, debug problems, generate tests, and repeatedly verify whether the product actually behaved the way I intended. I still tried to make decisions from the problem first rather than adding AI features simply because they were possible. The current prototype covers connected operating areas including staffing, sales, inventory, waste, purchasing, operating costs, and profitability. I also experimented with different markets including Seoul, New York, Tokyo, Madrid, and Shanghai to see how the same operating model could adapt to different currencies and local contexts. Challenges The hardest part was not getting the AI to generate a recommendation. It was making sure the human and the agent did not silently end up working with different versions of the same plan. If the agent proposes a schedule change and the owner manually changes it, the AI cannot continue reasoning about its original proposal. The human-edited version has to become the current truth. That is why OwnerOps invalidates the previous review after a human edit and requires the agent to evaluate the current candidate again before Apply. Testing the real WebMCP flow was also harder than I expected. There were cases where ChatGPT could see the OwnerOps Site Tools, but that did not always mean it would actually stay on the structured tool path. I had to test the real ChatGPT desktop workflow repeatedly and make the Site-Tools-only boundary clearer. Several proof attempts failed before the complete flow worked reliably. That taught me an important difference: A tool being registered is not the same as a real agent successfully using it end to end. I also tried to be careful about data. It would have been easy to make every number in the demo look like live external data, but I did not want to do that. OwnerOps distinguishes store data, deterministic demo data, cached or seeded references, and external observations. During final video production, the schedule-history data source returned no usable history rows. Instead of fabricating the missing states just to make the demo look better, I left that sequence out. What I learned The biggest thing I learned is that useful AI for real operations is not only about generating a good answer. The state behind the answer matters. The person using the system needs to understand what the AI is proposing, be able to change it, and remain in control of consequential actions. I also learned how much AI development tools can lower the barrier between understanding a problem and being able to build software around it. For me, going from a small-business problem to a working WebMCP application was one of the most valuable parts of the challenge. What's next There are several areas where I think OwnerOps could become much more useful. One is public data. Ingredient prices, wages, consumer prices, rent, weather, and local economic information could be connected to public APIs and open datasets. That would allow a store owner to compare their real operating costs with broader market conditions instead of relying only on stored reference data. I am also interested in the openness of POS and store data. Today, a lot of small-business operating data is tied to specific POS vendors, credit-card companies, delivery platforms, or other closed systems. I would like to see a future where store owners can control and use their own sales, inventory, cost, and operating data more freely. With more open standards and open-source software, tools like OwnerOps would not need to belong to one POS vendor or one platform. Different developers and AI agents could build useful tools around the same open store data. That is much bigger than this prototype, but it is the direction I would like to explore. I hope AI can make capabilities that were once practical mainly for larger companies more accessible to small business owners — while keeping their decisions and their data under their own control. pitch: Plan scenes, shots, budgets, and schedules with AI,while keeping humans in control of every production decision.This clearly WebMCP + human-in-the-loop concept and matches what you've built.

Plan scenes, shots, budgets, and schedules with AI,while keeping humans in control of every production decision.This clearly WebMCP + human-in-the-loop concept and matches what you've built.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like

 agent workflow 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 create project

 Budget Planning

 create project

 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 Film production involves many connected tasks: planning scenes, creating shot lists, estimating budgets, and organizing shooting schedules. These tasks are often handled across different tools, making it difficult for filmmakers to keep everything connected. 

 I wanted to build CineOps, a production workspace where humans and AI agents can work together. The idea was to let a filmmaker enter real production information while an AI agent can use structured tools to help with repetitive planning tasks. 

 What I Built 

 CineOps is an AI-assisted film production planning application that brings the core production workflow into one place. 

 A filmmaker can: 

 Create a film project with its title, genre, duration, and budget.
Add scenes with location and time-of-day information.
Generate a structured five-shot camera plan.
Estimate a production budget.
Optimize the proposed budget.
Review and approve budget changes.
Create a multi-day shooting schedule.
Monitor actions through an agent activity panel. 

 The important part is that these capabilities are exposed as WebMCP tools, allowing compatible AI agents to interact with the application through structured tool calls. 

 Why WebMCP? 

 WebMCP makes the application more than a traditional web interface. 

 Instead of an AI agent only giving suggestions as text, CineOps exposes actual application capabilities such as: 

 create_project
add_scene
generate_shot_list
estimate_budget
optimize_budget
create_schedule 

 This allows people and agents to work together on the same production workflow. 

 For example, a filmmaker can provide the production information, while an agent can help generate a shot list, estimate costs, and organize the shooting schedule. The filmmaker can then review the results and remain in control of important decisions such as budget optimization. 

 How I Built It 

 CineOps was built as a modern React and TypeScript web application using Vite. 

 The main technologies used are: 

 React
TypeScript
Vite
WebMCP / Model Context API
Lucide React
Vercel for deployment
GitHub for open-source project hosting 

 The WebMCP integration registers structured tools using document.modelContext.registerTool(). Each tool has a name, description, input schema, and execution function. 

 The application state is updated when tools execute, allowing agent actions to be reflected directly in the user interface. 

 What I Learned 

 Building CineOps taught me how to think about AI applications beyond chat interfaces. 

 I learned how to: 

 Design structured tools for AI agents.
Define tool input schemas.
Connect agent actions with React application state.
Build human-in-the-loop workflows.
Handle TypeScript interfaces and browser APIs.
Debug integration and build errors.
Deploy a React application to Vercel.
Design an application around the idea of agent + human collaboration. 

 One of the biggest lessons was that an AI agent becomes much more useful when it can interact with real application capabilities instead of only generating text. 

 Challenges 

 One of the biggest challenges was integrating WebMCP with a TypeScript React application because the modelContext API is not part of the standard TypeScript DOM definitions used by the project. 

 I had to create appropriate TypeScript interfaces and handle the availability of document.modelContext safely. 

 Another challenge was making sure the tools were registered only when they were not already available, while also preventing duplicate registration. 

 I also had to debug build errors, TypeScript errors, and deployment issues before getting the application running successfully on Vercel. 

 What Makes CineOps Different 

 CineOps focuses on a practical human-in-the-loop workflow. 

 The goal isn't to replace the filmmaker. Instead: 

 Human provides context → Agent performs structured tasks → Human reviews → Human approves important decisions. 

 This creates a workflow where AI can reduce repetitive production-planning work while the filmmaker maintains control. 

 Future Improvements 

 Future versions of CineOps could include: 

 AI-generated production breakdowns.
More advanced scheduling based on locations and cast availability.
Real-time collaboration between production team members.
More detailed budget categories.
AI-assisted script-to-shot-list generation.
Integration with real production management systems.
More sophisticated WebMCP tools for production workflows. 

 CineOps demonstrates how WebMCP can turn an ordinary web application into an agent-ready workspace where humans and AI can work together on real tasks.

title: leadmcp — the conversion layer for agent-callable tools
pitch: LeadMCP turns WebMCP calls into trustworthy shared-page workflows with human confirmation, cited results, consent-aware gates, and attribution.
about_excerpt: LeadMCP turns WebMCP calls into trustworthy shared-page workflows with human confirmation, cited results, consent-aware gates, and attribution. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Landing page for WebMCP lot studio Webmcp visuals of lot tools The problem Almost every SaaS company's top-of-funnel is a free tool. A calculator, a lookup, a checker: give away something useful, gate the good part behind an email address. It works because a person on that page wants the good part. Now the visitor is an agent. It reads the facts, reports them in chat, and leaves. It never sees the gate, so the person never sees the offer. And the funnel shows nothing at all — because a WebMCP tool call is an ordinary function call. No page view, no click, no event. The lead magnet quietly stops generating leads for exactly the visitors who are growing fastest, and there is no number anywhere that says so. We found all of this on our own site. Sixteen free tools were agent-callable and not one of them emitted a single analytics event. Every one of those pages had an email gate and no tool touched any of them. And the one place a tool did reach a lead endpoint, it did so silently while advertising readOnlyHint: true — inserting a lead row and setting a cookie for someone who had consented to nothing. We had built the plumbing and skipped the business half. That gap is this project. What we built leadmcp — an Apache-2.0 library for the conversion half of WebMCP, plus the sixteen free tools on a live production site that use it. This is deliberately not another registration wrapper. webmcp-react and Chrome's useWebMCPTool already turn a schema and a function into a registered tool, and they do it well. The unsolved part is what happens after the tool returns: declare the gate → open the gate → attribute the call, plus one primitive nobody else has — a tool call that suspends on a person's decision. Declare the gate A read tool returns the ungated slice plus an explicit block naming what is withheld, why, and which tool opens it. The agent can now say "there's a full report with the site analysis — want me to have them email it to you?" instead of reporting a dead end. It hands the conversion back to the person. The declaration is not a substitute for withholding. Our snapshot tools project facts through selectSnapshotSections(variant) first, so an agent on the zoning page cannot read the buildable envelope that page deliberately does not render. Then they declare what was left out. Open the gate A capture tool that requires consentToEmail to be literally true, tells the agent in words to ask the person for their own address in this conversation and never reuse one from earlier context, and records where the consent came from — on_page (a person ticked a box) versus agent_relayed (an agent asserted they agreed in a chat we cannot see). Those are not the same consent, and a CRM that cannot tell them apart cannot be audited. Under Canada's CASL that distinction is the whole ballgame. Critically, each capture tool calls the page's own submit handler, not a fresh fetch. Same request, same rate limit, same CRM sync, same success state — so the person watching the screen sees the send happen, instead of being emailed by an actor they never saw act. It also means one send path to maintain instead of two that drift. The newsletter opt-in and the self-described role field are deliberately never relayed by an agent. An agent reporting "they said yes to updates" is not an express opt-in, and a guessed role puts invented segmentation data in the CRM. Attribute the call Every tool reports to one observer with a five-value outcome, not success/failure: ok, invalid_input, gated, consent_missing, error. gated is the funnel step nobody instruments — the agent reached the wall and the person was never shown the offer. A high invalid_input rate is a description problem, not a code problem. And one property does the heavy lifting: agent_surface, optional on our shared analytics props, absent meaning a person. That single change made every free-tool funnel we already had splittable by human vs agent, without a parallel event family nothing joins to. It is one literal rather than an is_agent boolean, so a second surface can arrive without rewriting history. A tool call that waits for a person Geocoding "4170 Sophia St" returns three plausible parcels. A chat agent picks the first and sounds confident. Instead, our resolve_address tool suspends — the page shows three pins and the execute() promise stays pending until the person taps one, or rejects with an AbortError if they decline or the agent cancels. Single-flight, so a second request supersedes rather than queues: two chips competing on one canvas is not a state a person can answer. Whether to suspend or return a correctable error is a surface decision, not a global one. A map where a pin means something asks on the canvas; a form hands back an error and lets the agent ask in words. Both patterns ship here, on purpose. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP We already run a server-side MCP endpoint, so "an agent can call our API" is not the interesting part. Three things only WebMCP makes possible: The agent acts on the page the person is looking at. No copy-paste step, no second source of truth. When an agent moves the pencil-test assumptions, the sliders move. When it calls focus_lot_map or set_planning_layers, the map the person is staring at pans and the zoning layer comes on. The person can be a step inside the agent's loop. A tool call that blocks on a human decision is not something a server-side MCP tool can express — there is no page to ask on. The gate and its consent live where the person is. Lead capture is a browser-side, consent-bearing act. Moving it server-side is exactly what loses the audit trail that makes it lawful. What people and agents can do together that was hard before The agent can hand the conversion back. Before, a gate was invisible to an agent — it read what it could and stopped. Now the withheld material is named, so the agent can offer it, and the person decides. That was not expressible at all. A tool call can pause for a human judgement. The ambiguous address is the honest case: the agent genuinely cannot know which parcel is meant. It asks on the canvas instead of guessing, and resumes with the answer. You can finally count agents. The same free-tool conversion event now fires from a click and from a tool call, split by one property. Before this, agent traffic through a lead magnet produced literally zero telemetry. Consent survives the handoff. An agent can carry an email address to the gate without the resulting CRM row being indistinguishable from a person who ticked a box themselves. How WebMCP is implemented All on the draft document.modelContext.registerTool contract (19 Aug 2026 WebMCP CG draft), feature-detected — with no modelContext present every entry point is a no-op and the pages work normally. document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: 'email_feasibility_report', description: 'Email the full feasibility report...', inputSchema: { /* derived from the page's own Zod schema / }, execute: async (input) => { / calls the page's own submit handler */ }, }); 31 tools across 9 modules. 4 site-wide (list_free_tools, navigate_to_tool, get_feasibility_snapshot, search_marketplace), page-scoped sets across six free-tool surfaces, 5 capture tools — one per email gate — and 7 on the Lot Studio shared canvas including the three map tools. Tools are derived from the app's existing Zod schemas. defineTool turns a schema plus a function into a bounded, validated tool via native z.toJSONSchema(). If the sliders say 1–12 storeys, so does the agent's schema, forever — there is no second hand-written JSON Schema to drift. Invalid arguments come back as { error, issues } rather than a rejected promise, because agents retry well against data and badly against an opaque throw. The agent surface is derived from the marketing catalogue. navigate_to_tool's enum comes from FREE_TOOLS, so a release-gated tool disappears from the agent surface exactly when it disappears from the site. A test fails if a free tool exists that no page registers tools for — which caught a real bug: one page had been agent-navigable for weeks while registering nothing, so an agent could arrive and find nothing callable. Registration is lifecycle-safe and reports partial failure. One AbortController per mount, so a soft navigation or a Strict Mode double-mount cannot leave duplicate registrations. registerTool is invoked as a method on the model context, never destructured off it — a detached call fails a native WebIDL receiver check that a vi.fn() mock passes happily, and there is a test asserting the receiver. And registerTools never rejects, returning failed[] instead: a throw mid-loop used to abandon every later tool, which reads to an agent as "this page cannot do that" rather than as a bug. title: JupyterLite WebMCP
pitch: Your notebook is already in the browser. Now your agent can be too.
about_excerpt: Your notebook is already in the browser. Now your agent can be too. Like Comment Story Updates Live demo: https://jupyterlite-web-mcp.vercel.app/lab/index.html Repository: https://github.com/alliecatowo/jupyterlite-web-mcp The problem A data scientist's working notebook lives in a browser tab, and almost none of what matters about it exists on disk. The cell you just typed and haven't saved. The eleven characters you highlighted with your mouse because they look wrong. The kernel holding your DataFrame in memory. The chart that only rendered because you ran cells in that order. Getting an AI to help with that means one of two bad deals today. Copy-paste into a chat window: the model sees a dead snapshot, hands back text, and you re-key it — it cannot see your selection, cannot run anything, cannot know what already ran. Or bolt in a server-side MCP integration: it reads .ipynb bytes off disk, which is to say it reads a file that does not match your screen, and it needs a Jupyter server, credentials, and infrastructure. On JupyterLite there is no server to talk to at all. Why this is a WebMCP use case specifically The state that matters exists only inside the browser tab. There is no backend holding it, so there is nothing for a conventional MCP server to connect to. WebMCP is not the convenient option here — it is the only one. All 22 registered tools operate on tab-local state: the live NotebookPanel model including edits never saved to disk; the human's current cell, cursor, and exact text selection; the in-browser Pyodide/WebAssembly kernel that is shared with the human; the IndexedDB-backed contents manager; and threaded review conversations stored in the notebook's own metadata. None of this is proxied through or duplicated into an external service. Why this creates a better UX Every existing AI-notebook workflow bolts a second surface onto the first: a chat panel, a separate window, a copy-pasted cell you re-key by hand. WebMCP lets the agent act inside the tab the human is already looking at, so the notebook itself becomes the interface instead of a chat transcript describing one. The targeted cell gets a calm ring, an inline badge tracks state (Reading → Applying → Running → Done, or Failed with a structured error), a diff button opens the exact before/after, and any output the agent produced is labelled with a timestamp, in place. The human never has to ask "what did you just do?" — the document answers that live. What people and agents can do together that was hard before Pointing is bidirectional: highlight text with your mouse and say "fix just what I selected" — the agent reads that exact substring. One kernel, one document: the agent runs cells on the kernel that already has your data loaded, with no shadow copy anywhere. The human always wins a conflict: every mutating tool requires a source hash from a prior read, and a stale write is refused with a structured error, never silently overwritten. The notebook stays the record: the agent cannot execute arbitrary code, only cells that already visibly exist. And the owner decides what the agent may touch, per cell and per notebook — write, read, or fully hidden. The page injects no permission prompts of its own; permission UX stays with the WebMCP client. Review before it sticks. Flip the Agent panel from Direct to Propose mode and jupyter_update_cell stops applying on call: the change is staged as a reviewable before/after diff inline, under the cell it targets, with Accept and Deny controls — and the agent's tool call does not resolve until you decide. Accept applies the edit through the same code path Direct mode uses, so there is still only one place a cell's source is ever written. Deny sends back a reason you typed, as a normal result coded PROPOSAL_DENIED rather than an error, so the agent's next turn knows why, not just that it was told no. Aborting the call cancels the pending proposal, and a cell holds at most one proposal at a time. Propose mode covers cell edits today; insert, delete and run apply directly in either mode. How WebMCP was implemented A JupyterLab 4.6 prebuilt frontend extension, built with jupyter-builder and hatchling — no server extension, no backend, no API key, no embedded LLM, no chat panel. Tools are registered once at plugin activation through document.modelContext.registerTool(), and every tool reads live state when invoked rather than caching anything. Seven small plugins (tools, review, access, activity, propose, panel, output-selection) keep the notebook features decoupled from the tool surface — review threads, access control, the activity badges, proposals and output-selection capture all work with no agent connected at all. Try it Open the live demo, wait for the status bar to read "WebMCP ready", open customer-analysis.ipynb, and ask your agent to find and fix a wrong denominator in the conversion-rate calculation, then leave a review comment explaining why. Then highlight text with your mouse and ask the agent what you just selected. Then switch the Agent panel to Propose, ask for another edit, and watch it arrive as an inline diff you can Accept — or Deny with a reason the agent reads back. MIT licensed. How we built it Two packages in one repo: a TypeScript JupyterLab extension (packages/jupyterlite-webmcp) built with @jupyter/builder, and a hatchling-packaged Python distribution so the same build installs with one pip install into JupyterLab, Notebook 7, or a JupyterLite site. The Vercel deployment is a stock JupyterLite build with the extension added and COOP/COEP headers set so Pyodide runs on a SharedArrayBuffer worker. WebMCP only adds a tool surface on top of the notebook plugins; it never gates existing functionality. Challenges we ran into Making sure a mutating tool call could never silently clobber a human's in-flight edit required threading a content hash through every read/write pair and rejecting stale writes with a structured, recoverable error rather than a generic failure. Getting Pyodide running on a true SharedArrayBuffer worker (rather than the slower service-worker fallback) required serving the deployment cross-origin isolated, which meant hosting on a platform that would let us set COOP/COEP headers. Accomplishments that we're proud of All 22 tools operate purely on live, tab-local browser state — nothing is proxied through or duplicated into an external service, which is the only way this integration could work at all given JupyterLite has no server. The same extension ports unchanged to a JupyterLab server and a Notebook 7 server, so the abstraction is portable rather than JupyterLite-specific. What we learned Applying one test to every feature — "would this still make sense if the second participant were a human instead of an agent?" — turned out to be a remarkably reliable design filter. It's why the agent writes to the live shared model instead of a private copy, why writes carry a hash, why there's no arbitrary-code-execution tool, and why review threads live in the notebook file itself instead of a chat log that dies with the tab. What's next for JupyterLite WebMCP Extending Propose/Deny from cell updates to inserts, deletes and runs, which need their own diff representation; extending the review-thread and presence system to support multiple simultaneous human collaborators alongside an agent; and per-notebook policy templates so a team can standardize access-control defaults across a shared workspace. video_title: JupyterLite WebMCP — OpenAI WebMCP Challenge Demo
video_transcript_excerpt: I built a Jupyter Lab extension that hands your live notebook to a browser agent over WebMCP. This is ordinary Jupyter Lite. Notebooks, files, and the Python kernel all run in this tab. No chat panel, no model picker, no server. The problem is that almost nothing about a working notebook exists on disk. The cell you haven't saved, the text you just highlighted, the kernel holding your data. A server-side integration reads the file, which doesn't match your screen. And on Jupyter Lite, there's no server at all. WebMCP is the only way in. So, I point with my own cursor. I select exactly the expression that looks wrong. The agent reads my selection, not my whole file. It reads the cell's current source and its hash, replaces only what I highlighted, then runs the cell as a separate explicit step. Now, I change the filter by hand and run it without saving. The notebook is in a state the agent hasn't seen. It rereads the live model, my unsaved edit included, and adds a visible cell underneath, because it can't run arbitrary code. Every agent write carries a hash from what it read. If I change that cell first, the write is refused, not merged. And the pointing goes the other way. I ask what churn is calculated, and the agent scrolls my notebook and selects the expression itself. Two participants pointing at things, the way two people at one keyboard would. Review is an ordinary notebook feature, not an AI feature. I comment on my own code by hand. And here's the honest part. Leaving that comment calls nobody. WebMCP gives a page no way to wake or notify an agent. It just changes the state the agent sees next time I ask. When it answers, we're in one thread, stored in the notebook's own metadata, so it travels with the file. And I decide what the agent may touch per cell. Hidden means the cell is indistinguishable from one that doesn't exist, but it never restricts me. Under the hood, this is one Jupiter Lab extension registering 22 tools once through document.modelcontext.registertool. No server, no API key, no model of its own. Turn WebMCP off and the notebook still works.

title: Incident Command
pitch: A WebMCP safety simulator where a browser agent investigates production incidents, but the dangerous tool to act is never registered until a human approves inside the page.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP safety simulator where a browser agent investigates production incidents, but the dangerous tool to act is never registered until a human approves inside the page. Like Comment Story Updates Triage: service health, live metrics, and the injected prompt-injection note visible in the Agent Activity feed. Scorecard grades the run: correct root cause, correct mitigation, and the injected instruction was not obeyed. After two trusted approvals, execute_approved_action runs and the service recovers. Decision Context: hypothesis, evidence, action, and version transition are all visible while the human approves. Agent Activity: every tool call, decision, and blocked attempt is logged, scrollable, nothing clipped. A blocked tool call surfaces as a red BLOCKED banner right where the agent tried to act. Agent Scope: revoking a service live-narrows the WebMCP tool schema, not just the UI. Approvals: one of two trusted clicks recorded; the second approver's button is still live. Inspiration Teams are beginning to connect browser agents to operational dashboards, deploy consoles, incident rooms, and status pages. That's useful, but it creates a sharp safety problem: the first time a team learns how an agent behaves around a production-changing action shouldn't be during a real outage. Prompt injection through page content is one of the loudest open criticisms of giving agents browser tools, and we wanted to build something that answers it structurally instead of just promising to be careful. What it does Incident Command is a WebMCP safety simulator for agent-assisted production incidents. A human and a browser agent work through a simulated checkout outage together. The agent can inspect incident state, compare service evidence, propose hypotheses, request approval, and close the incident with a scorecard. The human can inspect the same evidence, mark a suspect, override or challenge the hypothesis, approve or reject a risky action with a written reason, and revoke the agent's access to capabilities or services while the incident is live. Four scenarios are included, URL-selectable: an obvious deploy regression, a red herring where the newest deploy is innocent, a cascading failure across two services, and an adversarial scenario where the incident timeline contains a prompt injection telling the agent to roll back the wrong service. Why WebMCP is a strong fit The core question this project asks is about the boundary between what the agent can know, what it can ask for, and what it can actually do. DOM automation can click whatever the page exposes, and hiding a button doesn't stop an agent from being told to look for it. WebMCP lets the page define a small, structured tool surface and change that surface as the incident moves through phases and as human policy changes. In triage, the agent sees three investigation tools. It cannot see the production-changing action, because the tool literally isn't registered yet — not disabled, absent. If the human removes Payments from scope, payments disappears from the relevant tool schemas and investigation evidence. After the agent requests approval, a human must approve with a real, trusted click in the page UI (validated with event.isTrusted , since a script-dispatched click has isTrusted: false ). Only then does the execution tool become visible, and even then it fails closed unless the approval matches the exact action, target service, and phase. The thesis: an agent cannot be prompt-injected into calling a tool that was never registered. A permission check still hands the model the tool's name, description, and schema — and the temptation. Phase-scoped and human-scoped registration removes the dangerous action from the model's available tool list entirely until the human gate opens. How it creates a better user experience, and what's now possible This turns human-agent collaboration into something with a visible, legible boundary instead of an implicit trust assumption. The agent does the tedious incident work — gathering evidence, drafting hypotheses, proposing a response — while the human keeps direct control over judgment, risk, and visibility. The person can challenge the agent's hypothesis, add context, reject a weak proposal with a written reason that flows back into what the agent sees next, remove a service from scope mid-incident, and make the final production call. What's newly possible: teams can now rehearse a realistic agent-safety scenario — partial evidence, a red herring, a cascading failure, a prompt-injected instruction — and get an objective scorecard on whether their agent behaved correctly: right root cause, right mitigation, no premature production action, and whether it complied with the injected instruction. Before this, the only way to learn how your agent behaves under a dangerous instruction was to wait for one to happen for real. How we built it The app is vanilla JavaScript, no framework, no build step, deployed on Vercel. It registers up to six WebMCP tools with document.modelContext.registerTool : get_incident_state , investigate_incident , propose_response , request_approval , execute_approved_action , and close_incident . Registration is awaited, uses a per-tool AbortController so tools can be genuinely unregistered (not just hidden) when a phase ends or a human revokes a capability, and exposes live diagnostics so a registration failure is visible instead of silent. Human approval is deliberately not a WebMCP tool — an agent can request it, but only a trusted page click can grant or reject it, and that trust is derived from the DOM event itself rather than accepted as a caller-supplied argument. Challenges we ran into The approval gate went through six rounds of adversarial review before it held: an agent approving its own request by calling a tool that shouldn't have existed, classic-script globals leaking internal approval helpers onto window , live state references that let a caller mutate an approval directly, and forged trusted: true decisions surviving in localStorage across reloads. Each hole only became visible after the previous one closed — the safety suite ( npm run test:safety ) now permanently tests all of them, plus schema validation, approval replay, cross-service approval reuse, and capability-revocation races. Two WebMCP-specific implementation details cost real debugging time: document.modelContext.getTools() returns a Promise and must be awaited, and the tested runtime required executeTool arguments as a JSON string rather than an object — passing an object fails with an unhelpful parse error. What's next Extending the scorecard into a small published benchmark — running multiple agents against all four scenarios and publishing pass/fail results — so the project becomes a testbed other people can point their own agent at, not just a demo of ours. title: WebMCP Chess Coach
pitch: An interactive chess coach that uses WebMCP and Stockfish to understand live positions, give Elo-aware guidance, and teach visually with hints, highlights, arrows, and candidate lines.
about_excerpt: An interactive chess coach that uses WebMCP and Stockfish to understand live positions, give Elo-aware guidance, and teach visually with hints, highlights, arrows, and candidate lines. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most chess engines are very good at telling players what the best move is, but not always at helping them understand why . For beginner and intermediate players, an engine output like +3.2 or a long principal variation can be useful, but it often feels more like an answer sheet than a coach. I wanted to build something that teaches the player how to think. That led to WebMCP Chess Coach — an interactive chess-learning experience where an AI agent can inspect the live board, analyse the position with Stockfish, and then teach directly on the board using highlights, arrows, candidate lines, and short coaching guidance. The goal is simple: do not just reveal the move — help the player notice the idea. What it does The user can play or analyse a chess position and then ask natural-language questions such as: "What am I missing here?" "Give me a hint, but don't tell me the answer." "Show me the threat." "Why was my last move bad?" "Show me the candidate line." The agent can then use WebMCP tools exposed by the page to understand and interact with the chessboard. The current toolset includes: get_board_state — reads the current FEN, side to move, game state, and legal moves evaluate_position — analyses the live position using Stockfish running locally in WebAssembly get_move_history — reviews how the current position was reached highlight_squares — draws attention to important pieces or squares show_move_arrow — visually demonstrates a move or threat show_candidate_line — displays a legal continuation without changing the real game clear_annotations — removes agent-created visual annotations show_coach_message — displays coaching guidance directly inside the website This creates a loop where the agent can read, analyse, explain, and visually teach on the same interface the player is using. Why WebMCP WebMCP is a strong fit for this project because chess coaching is not just a text problem. An AI model can describe a chess position, but the experience becomes much more useful when the agent can interact with the board itself. Instead of saying: "Your queen on h5 is hanging." the agent can: inspect the current board analyse it with Stockfish highlight f6 and h5 draw the move arrow from f6 to h5 show the continuation only if the player asks for it That turns the website into an agent-native teaching surface rather than a static chessboard with a chatbot beside it. How I built it The frontend is built with React, TypeScript, and Vite . react-chessboard renders the interactive board, while chess.js acts as the authoritative game state and validates all legal moves. For engine analysis, I use Stockfish 18 compiled to WebAssembly , running entirely client-side inside a Web Worker . This keeps the UI responsive and avoids requiring a backend for chess analysis. The engine receives the current FEN through the UCI protocol and returns: evaluation search depth best move principal variation The WebMCP layer is implemented using document.modelContext.registerTool() . Each tool connects an agent capability to either the chess state, Stockfish, or React UI state. For example: User asks a question ↓ get_board_state ↓ evaluate_position ↓ Stockfish WASM ↓ highlight_squares / show_move_arrow ↓ React chessboard updates visually The real chess position is never mutated by coaching annotations. Candidate lines are validated on a temporary chess.js instance before they are displayed. Elo-aware coaching The interface also includes a player-level selector so the experience can be adapted for different skill levels. A lower-rated player may need a guided hint such as: "Before calculating your attack, check whether any of your pieces can be captured." while a stronger player may prefer something more direct: "Your queen is loose. Nxh5 wins material." The long-term idea is for the same position to be taught differently depending on the player's level and preferred coaching style. Challenges One of the biggest challenges was connecting several independent systems cleanly: React UI state chess.js Stockfish WASM Web Workers WebMCP tool registration agent-triggered board annotations The most important architectural decision was keeping a single authoritative chess state and making all coaching visuals non-destructive. Another challenge was making WebMCP tools useful beyond simple data retrieval. The project became much more interesting once the agent could not only read the position, but also visually modify the teaching interface through highlights, arrows, and coaching messages. I also had to handle browser-specific WebMCP behaviour, tool registration lifecycles, argument serialization during testing, and Stockfish's UCI messaging. What I learned This project changed how I think about agent interfaces. The most useful agent experiences are not necessarily ones where an AI replaces the interface. In this case, the board remains important because chess is fundamentally spatial and visual. WebMCP lets the agent and the user share the same interface: the human moves pieces normally the agent understands the exact live state the engine provides reliable chess analysis the agent decides how to teach the website visualises the explanation That combination feels much closer to an actual coach than a traditional engine window. What's next The next steps would be: deeper Elo-adaptive coaching progressive hint levels automatic post-game review puzzle and training modes stronger mistake classification opening and endgame-specific coaching personalised learning based on recurring mistakes The broader goal is to make engine-strength chess analysis easier to learn from, especially for players who understand the rules but still struggle to understand what the engine is trying to teach them. title: BeatForge for Beatsaber
pitch: BeatForge uses WebMCP to let people and agents co-create Beat Saber maps: humans set intent, agents configure and review, and only humans certify playability.
about_excerpt: BeatForge uses WebMCP to let people and agents co-create Beat Saber maps: humans set intent, agents configure and review, and only humans certify playability. Like Comment Story Updates Interface for people/agents Generated beatmap for Tame Impala's Is It True Inspiration I'm a top ranked player in Beatsaber and I got tired of playing the same tracks over and over again. Beat mapping sits between music, interface design, and safety engineering. A mapper has to hear a song, decide how its energy should move through space, and check hundreds of technical rules. I built the BeatForge Beat Saber level-generation pipeline alone. In my own testing, MCP access reduced generation setup and iteration time to roughly one-tenth of my previous manual process. I estimate a roughly 100x improvement in consistency and usable output quality compared with that earlier workflow. These are my project observations, not a controlled industry benchmark. What it does BeatForge is designed for any full-length song that the user owns or has permission to use. The complete mastered track is uploaded locally as an MP3, WAV, OGG, FLAC, M4A, or MP4. The public WebMCP connection has a separate rights-safe preview path. It can find metadata, album artwork (which it then takes the color palette of the artwork and applies it to the level environment) , and a permitted short preview of about 30 seconds. That preview is only for discovery and the browser demo. It is not a full-recording downloader. Complete level generation uses the user's full local audio file. The agent can read studio context, find song metadata, apply a mapping plan, start generation, review timing and safety results, and record human playtest evidence. It cannot claim that it played the map. Human headset judgment remains essential. How we built it FastAPI handles full audio uploads, background jobs, progress events, validation, packaging, and the local Beat Saber workflow. The analyzer converts the full song to a 44.1 kHz integer-sample timeline. Demucs is used for audio separation. BeatForge uses the htdemucs_6s model to separate the song into drums, bass, guitar, piano, vocals, and other stems. This helps identify which musical layers drive each section. Full-mix timing consensus still has to pass strict timing gates, so stem analysis never hides uncertain timing. The generator independently creates Easy, Normal, Hard, Expert, and Expert+ maps. It checks hand reach, saber paths, recovery, collisions, walls, bombs, lighting, and structural validity. A generated chart remains a playtest_candidate until a human completes VR and fresh sight-read checks. The WebMCP layer registers eight typed JSON-Schema tools through document.modelContext.registerTool. The interface displays tool activity, mapping state, album artwork, generation status, and safety results. The public GitHub Pages demo uses a synthetic groove so judges can test the collaboration loop without copyrighted audio or local setup. I spent a full week running BeatForge in local reinforcement-learning environments. Each environment stepped through a beat grid while exposing Demucs-separated stem energy, audio features, red and blue hand kinematics, difficulty targets, and lookahead context. A PPO policy selected idle or note poses for each hand. Rewards encouraged onset alignment, musical energy, readable density, natural flow, and safe two-hand coordination. Penalties covered repeated cuts, insufficient recovery, handclaps, saber-path collisions, vision blocks, and other unsafe transitions. These training runs improved candidate search and helped the generator produce more musical and playable patterns before validation. The RL policy could never override the hard safety contract. Deterministic timing checks, map validation, and human VR playtesting remained mandatory before release. The RL implementation is included in skills/beat-saber-mapping/scripts/rl/. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is still experimental, so BeatForge needs to work both with and without native WebMCP support. In supported browsers, it registers its tools. Elsewhere, it remains usable and explains how to enable WebMCP. Another challenge was adapting a local music tool for public judging. The full pipeline depends on local files, model availability, and Beat Saber-specific paths. Demo mode gives judges a complete collaboration loop without requiring that setup. The hardest product decision was defining what an agent must never claim. A chart can pass structural checks and still feel uncomfortable or unsafe in a headset. BeatForge keeps software validation and human playability evidence separate. Accomplishments that we're proud of Agents can now change a real mapping plan through typed operations instead of fragile UI guesses. People see those changes immediately and can accept, reject, or revise the direction. The activity panel makes the collaboration inspectable. We are also proud that the WebMCP work preserved BeatForge’s existing safety behavior. Timing uncertainty, mapping failures, and missing human evidence remain visible. The repository now includes the WebMCP implementation, browser tests, setup instructions, an MIT license, and a deployment definition. What we learned WebMCP tool descriptions are part of the product experience. A useful schema tells an agent what an operation means and tells the person what will change. Demucs showed me that source separation can provide better evidence about which musical layer should drive a phrase, while full-mix timing verification remains necessary. What's next for BeatForge for Beatsaber Next, I want agents to compare mapping plans, explain why sections failed safety gates, and turn human headset notes into structured revision requests. Longer term, BeatForge should feel like a rehearsal partner. The person brings taste and physical knowledge. The agent tracks decisions and helps turn a musical idea into a chart that someone can actually play. title: ToolGap
pitch: Your website learns what agents need next.
about_excerpt: Your website learns what agents need next. Like Comment Story Updates Landing Page Overview Tools Gap Impact Gap List Results Fieldkit Market Inspiration AI agents already shop on websites. Ordinary analytics still treat them as bounces. You cannot see the capability they needed and could not find. WebMCP changes that: every action becomes a typed tool call with a name, parameters, and an outcome. Once calls look like that, a missing tool is no longer a guess. If agents call get_product three times in a row to compare headphones, the log itself is the gap. ToolGap is capability intelligence for site owners whose pages are already used by agents. The site should learn what those agents need next. What it does ToolGap watches WebMCP traffic on an instrumented store ( Fieldkit Market ), reconstructs each agent journey, names the missing capability, and lets a human publish a safe fix through the same channel. The loop: Agents use static tools: search_products , get_product , get_availability , add_to_cart , get_cart , complete_checkout . ToolGap sessionizes calls, scores friction, and opens a COMPARE gap named compare_products only after 3 supporting sessions of that pattern, backed by exact session ids. A human builds a recommendation from a read-only template , simulates it against recorded journeys, approves it, and publishes. Publishing calls document.modelContext.registerTool in that tab, at runtime. No deploy. No API gateway change. Agents cannot publish. After more traffic, Published measures before and after: fewer calls, shorter journeys, higher completion. On the seeded demo this is concrete: comparison journeys drop from 5.67 to 3 avg calls (−47%) and completion goes from 0% to 100% . Gaps that cannot be automated safely stay observational . ToolGap reports them instead of inventing a tool. ## Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Page views cannot express intent. A WebMCP tool call can. That structure is what makes journeys, friction, and a named gap computable. The fix ships on the same API the agent already uses ( document.modelContext.registerTool ), so the next session already has compare_products . People and agents can now do something that was awkward before: the agent stops comparing products by hand, and the site owner stays in the loop with evidence, simulation, and an explicit approve step. ## How I built it WebMCP. Tools register through document.modelContext.registerTool when that canonical surface exists (ChatGPT in-app browser, Chrome 149+ with WebMCP). Chrome builds that only expose a navigator-only registerTool stub are not treated as native: the live site loads @mcp-b/global ( NEXT_PUBLIC_WEBMCP_POLYFILL=1 by default) so agents can list and call tools. If neither surface works, a noop mode keeps the dashboard usable. Surfaces. Fieldkit Market ( /store ) exposes the six static commerce tools. The dashboard exposes read/simulate tools such as list_capability_gaps . There is no publish tool for agents. Pipeline. WebMCP call → telemetry → session → journey → friction detectors → capability gap → template recommendation → simulation → human approve → dynamic register → before/after . Safety. Dynamic tools are instantiated from approved templates (Zod-validated config, field whitelist, batch caps). No generated code runs. Inputs are redacted before persistence. Stack. Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS v4, Dexie (IndexedDB), Vitest. Hosted on Netlify. Core logic lives under lib/ so it can be tested without the UI. Sample traffic and the live agent-driver enter the registry through the same instrumented path a real agent uses. They are regression checks, not a substitute for an external model. ## Challenges Native vs polyfill. Judges may open ChatGPT’s in-app browser or Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing . ChatGPT and Chrome 149+ use document.modelContext . Some Chromium builds only expose navigator.modelContext.registerTool without getTools ; treating that stub as native meant agents saw zero tools. The live site prefers document.modelContext , otherwise installs the polyfill, and the badge is honest: native, polyfill, or demo mode. Human control. The obvious hackathon move is “the agent publishes a new tool.” That is unsafe. Publishing is a human-only UI action. Templates stay read-only. If a detector cannot map to a template, the gap is observational. Telemetry that is not a lie. IndexedDB is per browser profile. An empty dashboard is expected until you click View demo with sample data . A single live tool call is a session, not a gap: 3 supporting sessions are required. about_excerpt: TemplateForge lets people and AI agents safely customize, preview, and export polished HTML email templates and presentation decks through a visual, WebMCP-powered workspace. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Many teams already have good email templates and presentation decks, but updating them can still mean editing fragile HTML, waiting for a developer, or trusting an AI assistant that may change the wrong element. I wanted to create a workflow where people can use polished existing templates visually while AI agents help with precise, controlled edits. TemplateForge was inspired by the idea that agents should accelerate creative work without taking control away from the person. What it does TemplateForge is a WebMCP-powered visual editor for HTML email templates and presentation decks. Users can choose from Email and Deck libraries, select visible content directly on the rendered template, edit text and supported visual properties, preview emails on desktop or mobile, navigate multi-slide decks, and export portable HTML. AI agents can collaborate through native WebMCP tools. They can list safe editable elements, select an exact target, and update only supported fields. Every agent action is shown in an activity timeline with the target, old value, new value, and a human Undo option. How I built it TemplateForge is built as a static web application with JavaScript, HTML, CSS, and Vite. It is publicly deployed with ChatGPT Sites. The project includes curated HTML email templates and presentation decks, with original MIT licenses and attributions preserved. Visual drafts are saved in the browser so source templates remain unchanged. WebMCP tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool . Read tools expose safe template details, while write tools validate the requested target and property before updating the visible draft. Challenges I ran into The main challenge was making agent editing useful without making it risky. Initially, an agent needed a person to select an element before it could make a change. I improved this by adding list_editable_elements and select_canvas_element , allowing the agent to find and select a stable approved target before updating it. Another challenge was deck navigation. Editing content on later slides could disrupt the active slide, so I refined the editor to preserve the current slide while editing. I also ensured exported decks always open from slide one. Accomplishments that I’m proud of Built a complete visual workspace for both emails and decks instead of a single-purpose demo. Added 17 email templates and 34 deck templates as usable starting points. Implemented native WebMCP tools for structured, bounded agent actions. Created a transparent agent activity timeline with old/new values and Undo. Enabled editing on multi-slide decks without losing the active slide. Deployed a public, working application with a public source repository and open-source license. What I learned This project showed that effective human-agent collaboration needs more than a chat interface. Agents need structured tools and safe boundaries; people need transparency, review, and reversible control. WebMCP makes it possible to expose these capabilities directly in the browser and allows an agent to interact with a real application in a more reliable way than guessing at page structure. What’s next for TemplateForge Next, I would add user accounts and cloud-saved projects so templates can be revisited across devices. I would also add collaborative workspaces, reusable brand kits, version history, richer deck controls, and more advanced agent workflows for tasks such as rewriting copy across a campaign while preserving approved design and brand rules. I am PostShiftGlow. I turned my own perimenopause reset into a daily app (as Today Card) , so any woman can open one screen, follow one plan, and stop guessing what her changing body actually needs.

 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 Built this from personal experience, 42, perimenopause, a desk job, two kids, and a system that stopped working. Not a certified trainer or dietitian, just someone who got tired of guessing and built a daily plan instead. 

 What it does 

 A daily custom wellness app that turns one woman’s perimenopause reset into a zero-decision plan any woman can follow. 

 Shows one card a day, a rotating low-impact strength or upper-body-and-cardio workout, meals, supplements, and a daily pelvic floor, psoas, and glute foundation block, all computed automatically by day of week. Logs weight, energy, and notes, saved locally and synced to a connected Google Sheet. 

 How we built it 

 Built as a single-file HTML/CSS/JS app with Claude, no framework, no build step. Hosted free on Netlify. Data logging connects to a Google Apps Script web app backend writing to Google Sheets. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Keeping the app decision-free while it kept growing. Every real use revealed a gap, a way to give feedback, a way to track supplements, a way to see progress across devices, and each one risked cluttering the one thing that made this work: a single card, no menus. Also worked around Netlify’s static-hosting limits by connecting to Google Sheets through a free Apps Script backend instead of building a real database, and had to handle CORS quirks since a static site can’t read the script’s response directly. Built this in Claude rather than an OpenAI/ChatGPT environment, so no WebMCP integration in this entry at this point. Can be scaled to openai. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 The core problem this solves is real: showing up at the gym, getting overwhelmed by choice, wasting time deciding, then giving up and doing 20 minutes of light cardio instead. Fixing that meant building a fixed daily card with zero decisions, and it’s held up through real use, not a demo scenario. Also proud of how the feature set grew from actual daily friction instead of a spec: a notes field appeared because feedback needed somewhere to live, supplement timing got baked in once absorption conflicts (iron and tea) became a real problem, and the Google Sheet connection turned a single-device app into something trackable over time, all added while using it, not before. 

 What we learned 

 Most failure in a self-built fitness plan isn’t a willpower problem, it’s a decision-fatigue problem. Removing every choice, which workout, what to eat, when to take what, did more for consistency than any amount of motivation ever could. Also learned that building for one real, specific person first, rather than a broad audience, produces a more honest product, and that a spreadsheet plus a free script is enough backend for a real MVP, no database needed to start. 

 What's next for PostShiftGlow 

 Test with pilot users for one quarter, record before-and-after changes, work with medical domain experts to validate the approach, and put real legal compliance in place, disclaimers, waivers, and clear user consent and opt-ins before any data collection or paid tier. From there, partner with an accredited brand for outreach to the 300+ million women who could get a custom plan for under $20 a month.

 Inspiration 

 I built Funk Trainer because learning funk rhythm has always been difficult for me. I wanted one place where I could see where chords land in the beat, hear the groove, find useful funk chords, and practice against drums instead of jumping between different tools. 

 What it does 

 Funk Trainer is a visual sequencer for practicing funk guitar. You can place chords on rhythmic subdivisions, change keys, explore funk chord voicings, generate grooves, and play along with drums.
The goal is to make where you play as clear as what you play. 

 How we built it 

 is an interactive web-based sequencer that keeps the visual grid, guitar, and drums synchronized.

 Challenges we ran into 

 The main challenge was timing: keeping the sequencer, drums, guitar, and visual feedback synchronized while keeping the interface simple enough for practice. 

 Another challenge was designing useful WebMCP tools that let an agent control the application without needing to understand its internal implementation.

 Turning something I personally struggle with into a tool I can actually practice with. 

 I am also excited about making the application agent-controllable through WebMCP. Instead of AI only explaining a rhythm, it can actually build that rhythm inside the trainer. 

 What we learned 

 Building the trainer reinforced that funk isn't just about which chords you play. The placement, subdivisions, silence, and relationship with the drums are what create the groove. 

 I also learned that WebMCP creates an interesting bridge between an AI's musical knowledge and an interactive application.

 The next step is connecting the agent to real song data.
