title: MIRROR//LOOP
pitch: Eleven native WebMCP tools turn a 12-step reflection into a safe human-agent workflow: the agent clarifies and navigates, the browser scores, and the person confirms every choice.
about_excerpt:
Eleven native WebMCP tools turn a 12-step reflection into a safe human-agent workflow: the agent clarifies and navigates, the browser scores, and the person confirms every choice.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Confirmed results export locally as a private reflection dossier. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 MIRROR//LOOP turns uncertainty into one clear next step. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Eleven typed WebMCP tools with visible, on-page agent state. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Unconfirmed choices are rejected by the human-authority gate. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Twelve confirmed answers produce a deterministic local reflection. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 What-if previews show potential impact without changing saved answers. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Confirmed results export locally as a private reflection dossier. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 MIRROR//LOOP turns uncertainty into one clear next step. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Eleven typed WebMCP tools with visible, on-page agent state. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Unconfirmed choices are rejected by the human-authority gate. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Twelve confirmed answers produce a deterministic local reflection. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 What-if previews show potential impact without changing saved answers. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Confirmed results export locally as a private reflection dossier. 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 



 
 Inspiration 

 People are surrounded by instant answers, motivational shortcuts, and confident-sounding advice. Under stress, more output often creates more noise. MIRROR//LOOP creates a deliberate pause: twelve everyday questions help a person notice the pattern they reach for first, then turn that pattern into one small, practical next step. The challenge was not simply to put a quiz on a webpage. A 12-step reflection connected to 144 cards can be difficult to understand quickly, especially when a visitor is uncertain, tired, or using unfamiliar language. WebMCP makes the existing experience easier to navigate without making the agent the authority over the person. 

 What it does 

 MIRROR//LOOP is a live, privacy-bounded reflection experience. The normal website works on its own, while a compatible browser agent can use eleven typed WebMCP tools to: 

 
 start or resume the reflection; 
 read the active question; 
 explain one choice in plain language; 
 neutrally compare two choices; 
 record or revise only an answer the person explicitly confirms; 
 review all confirmed answers; 
 preview how one hypothetical change would affect a completed result without saving it; 
 complete the deterministic 12-answer reflection; 
 export a local Markdown or JSON dossier after confirmation; 
 retrieve any public card from 001 through 144; and 
 recommend a relevant digital edition without changing a cart or starting payment. 
 

 The page remains fully usable when WebMCP is unavailable. When registration succeeds, it visibly reports WebMCP ready · 11 tools . A collapsible Agent State rail shows tool registration and invocation activity on the page, so a judge can see the human-agent workflow without keeping DevTools open. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Traditional browser automation must infer intent from visual controls and presentation markup. A conversational model may also invent meanings when the site's authoritative definitions are not available as structured capabilities. WebMCP lets MIRROR//LOOP expose the actions that already belong to the page as typed, same-origin tools. The agent handles explanation and navigation; the browser retains the confirmed answers and applies the scoring rules; the person controls meaning, consent, identity, email, cart changes, and payment. This is the central design principle: the agent reduces friction without taking authority . A participant can say, “I am torn between these two choices.” The agent can call compare_choices and return the site's own neutral contrast. It cannot silently choose. When the participant decides, answer_reflection_question requires confirmed_by_user: true before browser-local state changes. The boundary is enforced by the tool implementation, not merely by conversational wording. 

 How we built it 

 The public experience is built with semantic HTML, CSS, and modular JavaScript. web/lib/webmcp.js registers eleven tools through the browser model-context surface. Each tool uses a closed JSON Schema with additionalProperties: false , bounded runtime validation, behavioral annotations, and structured errors. The 12-question scorer runs deterministically in browser memory with stable ascending-code tie-breaking. The public card registry exposes curated metadata for Cards 001–144 without publishing private prompt engineering or source corpora. The Agent State rail listens for decoupled lifecycle events—registration, tool start, and tool completion—and displays a privacy-filtered input summary, observed local elapsed time, outcome, and human-confirmation state. Observability cannot interrupt the underlying reflection action. The production website uses Firebase Hosting with a small Go submission service on Google Cloud Run. Cloudflare Turnstile protects only the optional reflection-email request. It loads when the visitor reaches the email form, and the Go API verifies the short-lived token with Cloudflare before storing a pending subscription or sending email; the secret remains in Google Secret Manager. Turnstile does not control the reflection, WebMCP, the cart, Stripe Checkout, or payment. 

 Safety and privacy boundaries 

 MIRROR//LOOP does not give the agent a general-purpose browser or purchasing capability. 

 
 Recording or revising an answer requires explicit human confirmation. 
 A hypothetical preview never changes saved answers. 
 Local dossier export requires a separate confirmation. 
 No WebMCP tool submits an email address. 
 No WebMCP tool changes a cart, creates a Checkout Session, or makes a payment. 
 Individual choices stay in the browser for the normal reflection and local-export paths. 
 Optional email delivery is a separate, disclosed request handled by the submission service. 
 

 The tool installer reports readiness only after every registration resolves. If registration fails or WebMCP is unsupported, the complete direct-use experience remains available with an honest fallback status. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The hardest problem was defining a useful agent boundary. A tool suite can become impressive-looking but unsafe if it turns interpretation, communication, and commerce into one broad authority. We repeatedly narrowed tool inputs and outputs, separated read-only tools from state-changing tools, and made confirmation a runtime requirement. We also had to make a complex symbolic system understandable without exposing private research material or forcing visitors to learn internal terminology. The answer was selective context: return one current question, one exact card, or one bounded comparison rather than loading the entire system into every agent turn. Finally, experimental browser support required feature detection, graceful fallback behavior, strict character budgets, and a reproducible Chrome test path. 

 Accomplishments that we are proud of 

 
 Eleven purpose-built WebMCP tools operating one coherent, visible user journey. 
 Explicit human confirmation enforced before answer mutation. 
 Deterministic browser-side scoring rather than model-authored results. 
 Exact public retrieval across a 144-card matrix. 
 A visible Agent State rail that makes tool execution legible without DevTools. 
 Read-only commerce recommendations with identity and payment kept outside agent authority. 
 A one-command WebMCP evaluation runner covering registration, schema limits, confirmation rejection, premature completion, output budgets, and the no-checkout boundary. 
 A production deployment with a complete non-WebMCP fallback. 
 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP is most valuable when it does not merely automate clicks. It gives a website a second, agent-readable interface while preserving the visible human interface as the shared source of truth. Good tools are small, typed, and auditable. They return authoritative local context, expose clear state transitions, and refuse actions that should remain human. We also learned that an agent experience must be demonstrated visibly. Registration badges, progress changes, focus movement, live regions, and the Agent State rail make the collaboration understandable to people as well as machines. 

 What's next 

 Next we will publish the final public demo video, complete the Devpost media package, and continue testing with WebMCP-capable agents. Product work will focus on clearer first-time or

 Inspiration 

 AI agents are becoming capable of completing real tasks on the web, but actions such as booking should remain transparent and under the user's control. I wanted to explore how WebMCP can let an agent discover services and check availability while keeping the final booking action safe and explicitly confirmed by the user. 

 What it does 

 Safe Agent-Assisted Booking is a WebMCP-enabled booking demo. 

 It exposes three tools to an AI agent: 

 
 search_services — discovers available services. 
 check_availability — checks available time slots. 
 create_booking — creates a booking only after explicit user confirmation. 
 

 The project uses synthetic demo data and does not depend on external booking services. 

 How I built it 

 I built a small browser-based booking application and exposed its capabilities through WebMCP tools. 

 The implementation separates read-only actions from the state-changing booking action. Search and availability checks can be performed safely, while booking requires a confirmation step before execution. 

 I also added request idempotency and slot-conflict protection so repeated requests do not accidentally create duplicate bookings. 

 Challenges 

 The main challenge was designing a write action that remains useful to an AI agent without removing control from the user. 

 I focused on: 

 
 explicit confirmation before booking; 
 predictable tool contracts; 
 idempotent booking requests; 
 conflict detection; 
 safe handling of cancellation or rejected confirmation; 
 keeping the demo simple and reproducible. 
 

 What I learned 

 This project helped me understand how WebMCP can turn a normal website into an interface that both humans and AI agents can use. 

 The most important lesson was that agentic web actions need more than tool access. They need clear boundaries between reading information and changing state. 

 What's next 

 The next step would be connecting the same architecture to a real booking backend, adding persistent storage, authentication, and more advanced availability rules while preserving explicit user control for sensitive actions.What it does

title: DOM Collective
pitch: The UI files a grievance. You ratify the fix.
about_excerpt: The UI files a grievance. You ratify the fix. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Picture someone reaching the last step of a scholarship application with only a keyboard and the browser zoomed to 200 percent. The form looks official and complete, but Continue is a clickable div , the income field has no real label, the error message is not announced, the dialog loses focus, and the sticky bar can hide the next action. Nothing has crashed. The page has simply become hard to use at the exact moment it matters. An AI agent can call APIs or try to click through a page, but these failures live inside the current browser session: focus, dialog lifecycle, conditional content, unsaved values, zoom, viewport, and overlay geometry. The same broken controls that block a person also make click-based agent automation brittle. We asked a different question: what if the webpage could describe not only what is wrong, but also the exact safe ways it permits an agent to repair the live experience—and require the human to ratify those changes first? What it does DOM Collective turns that question into a small, visible negotiation between three parties: a person, an agent, and the live page. The person says what they are trying to do—review the application with a keyboard at 200 percent zoom—and sets the boundaries: do not change form copy, values, or validation rules, and never submit the application. The agent asks the page to inspect the real interface, traces the blocked keyboard journey, and drafts a contract from repairs the site already owns. The page then shows the exact contract to the person. Nothing changes until they approve it. After approval, the page issues one state-bound, one-use capability. It applies the named repairs atomically through React state, re-runs the same journey on the rendered page, and produces a rollback receipt. The demo begins with five real failures and ends with five passing checks while the protected application data stays untouched. What it does The reference application is a fictional scholarship portal with a deliberately broken keyboard journey at a simulated 200% zoom. Through WebMCP, the page exposes structured evidence about five supported issues: a fake button; a missing programmatic label; a visual-only validation error; broken dialog focus behavior; and a sticky action bar that obscures Continue. The agent inspects the exact live state and drafts an Executable Interface Contract using only repair primitives owned by the site. The human reviews the operations and protected invariants in a visible ratification dialog. Approval creates a one-use receipt bound to the contract, current state version, DOM hash, expiration, and exact operation digest. After validation, the page applies the repair through declarative React state, re-runs the same journey, reports before-and-after evidence, confirms protected business behavior remained unchanged, and issues a rollback receipt. The memorable visual layer portrays broken DOM elements as workers filing grievances. The satire targets div soup, inaccessible implementation, and fragile CSS—not disabled users or real workers. How we used WebMCP Canonical tools: inspect_live_interface trace_access_path draft_access_contract request_ratification apply_ratified_contract verify_contract rollback_contract WebMCP is a strong fit because the relevant evidence and state live in the current document. The page owns the repair registry and runs the same domain services for both human UI and agent tools. This avoids giving the agent an arbitrary browser mutation interface. Rather than saying “go fix the form,” the agent receives a small vocabulary of actions that the page can validate against the exact state it inspected. The canonical tools are statically registered for reliability. A temporary one-use execution tool may be demonstrated as a progressive enhancement only if it is proven reliable in the target browser. What humans and agents do together Human Agent Live page States the need and protected intent. Combines structured evidence into a coherent plan. Knows the current DOM, focus, viewport, branch, and allowed repairs. Reviews, revises, approves, or denies. Calls only the page's registered tools. Validates authority and applies changes. Repeats the journey and judges usability. Requests deterministic verification. Produces evidence and rollback. No party can complete the intended flow alone. That separation is the point. The person supplies intent and consent. The agent helps turn evidence into a plan. The page keeps authority over its own DOM, business rules, and allowed changes. A useful repair only happens when all three line up. How it creates a better experience Without this flow, a person has to work around a broken form, file a support ticket, or trust an agent that may be guessing at the page. With DOM Collective, the page can explain the actual failure in plain, structured evidence, and the person can see exactly what will change before it happens. The agent is useful without becoming all-powerful. It does not need to inspect dozens of nodes by hand or invent a selector. It can combine the page's known repair primitives into one reviewable plan. The page does not infer the user's needs or hand over unrestricted write access. The contract and its protected invariants make the collaboration visible, bounded, and reversible. How it was built Implemented stack: Next.js App Router, React, strict TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and Zustand; a central domain store shared by UI and WebMCP handlers; a compile-time allowlist of five repair primitives; state-bound, single-use capability receipts; declarative React repair policy; deterministic keyboard, focus, relationship, geometry, and invariant checks; Vitest and Playwright; one HTTPS deployment on Vercel, with a server-renderable landing route and a client-owned WebMCP demo. The implementation is deliberately split in two. Pure domain code decides whether a contract, receipt, or repair is valid. Browser-side ports inspect the mounted DOM and verify the actual rendered result. React receives only a declarative repair policy, so the interface changes through a normal re-render instead of transient injected markup. The WebMCP bridge registers tools after hydration, detects unsupported browsers, and protects registration from Strict Mode replay, HMR, and route remounts. Challenges we ran into The easy version of this project would have been a visual before-and-after demo. That would not prove much. We needed the real DOM to change, the keyboard path to become usable, and the original application data to stay exactly as it was. The main challenge was lifecycle ownership. document.modelContext only exists in the browser after hydration, while React can replay effects in Strict Mode, hot-reload code during development, and remount the route. The bridge therefore tracks one active owner, aborts prior registrations, and keeps tool execution separate from route teardown. The other hard part was making human approval meaningful. A generic “yes, fix it” could be reused after the page changed. DOM Collective binds approval to the contract ID, snapshot ID, state version, DOM hash, operation digest, invariant digest, expiry, and one-use receipt. Stale, expired, replayed, forbidden, or unratified requests fail closed instead of quietly changing the form. Accomplishments [x] Complete human–agent–page contract journey. [x] Real semantic React re-render, not a visual overlay. [x] Deterministic rejection of stale, expired, replayed, and forbidden actions. [x] Before/after journey evidence with business invariants. [x] Reliable production demo and reset. What we learned A page-owned repair vocabulary is safer and easier to explain than arbitrary browser mutation. “Use a native button” is a product decision; arbitrary CSS or selectors are not. Consent must bind exact state, not a vague intention. If the page changes, the agreement should stop being valid. Static tools are the reliable baseline. Dynamic tool registration is useful polish, but the core journey still needs to work when it is unavailable. Short, structured tool results make it easier for an agent to take the next safe action without pretending it understands the whole page. A scoped verification report is more honest than claiming universal accessibility compliance. We can prove this journey, these five repairs, and these protected invariants. What's next Potential future work, explicitly outside the MVP: reusable contract and repair-registry SDK; server-backed capability signatures and audit receipts; author-defined repair registries for additional journeys; independent research with accessibility practitioners and users; integration with existing design systems and test suites. Important limitations This is a synthetic reference application, not a production service. It does not repair arbitrary third-party websites. It does not provide complete WCAG certification. title: RotaProof
pitch: A shift roster an agent can plan and a solver can prove. When the week is impossible it names the exact rules that clash instead of inventing a schedule. Runs entirely in your browser.
about_excerpt: A shift roster an agent can plan and a solver can prove. When the week is impossible it names the exact rules that clash instead of inventing a schedule. Runs entirely in your browser. Like Comment Story Updates The problem Rostering is a constraint problem that looks like a conversation. A manager says "give Tom Friday off" and means "re-solve a 210-variable integer program under thirty-three rules, and tell me if it can't be done." Language models are very good at the conversation and very bad at the program. Ask one to build a ten-person week with coverage minimums, keyholder cover, eleven-hour rest, contract ceilings and floors, and five separate absences, and it will produce something that looks like a roster. It will not be optimal, it will usually break a rule, and when the week is genuinely impossible it will hand you a schedule anyway, because producing plausible text is what it does. Nobody notices a wrong roster in the tool. They notice it on a Friday night when the cafe cannot legally open. What we built A web page that gives the agent the thing it does not have: a real mixed-integer solver, HiGHS, compiled to WebAssembly and running in the tab. The agent talks to the manager and edits the rules; the solver decides. Every answer is one of exactly three: optimal, meaning no better roster exists under these rules; infeasible, meaning none exists at all; or timeout. There is no fourth branch where it guesses. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Three properties of this problem are the argument for putting tools in the page rather than behind an API. First, the engine has to be where the data is: rosters contain names, pay rates and the reasons people are absent, which is the least uploadable data a small business owns, and WebMCP lets the computation happen inside the tab the manager already trusts. There is no server in this project at all - no account, no upload, no database - and it ships as a static export, so "the roster never leaves your browser" is true of the deployment as well as of the code. Second, the answer has to be a fact rather than a message: an in-page tool returns a value the model did not author, and "infeasible" plus six rule ids is not something an agent can talk its way around. Third, both parties need to be looking at the same thing - the manager watches the grid fill in as the agent solves, and the agent sees the rules the manager just changed. How it creates a better user experience Granting one person a Friday off in the seeded week produces this, in about 200 milliseconds and 25 solver probes: "These rules cannot all hold at once: a keyholder must open, a keyholder must close, eleven hours rest between shifts, S6 cannot work Fridays, S9 is away Thursday and Friday, and S2 asked for Friday off." Six rules out of thirty-three. Four other people are also away that week and are not mentioned, because they are not part of the clash - and proving that is most of the work. The page then says which of the six would be enough to relax on their own: five would, and the rest rule would not, because a second rule independently forbids the same double shift. That distinction matters more than it sounds: without it the page would send a manager off to relax a rule that leaves them exactly where they started. Then it stops. Choosing which rule gives way is a judgement about people, and neither the agent nor the solver is entitled to make it. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before A manager can describe a change in plain language and get back a proven-optimal week, or a proof that no week exists, instead of hand-checking a roster a model invented. When it fails they get six named rules and what relaxing each one would buy. A member of staff can ask "can I have Thursday off?" and get an immediate verdict with the blocking rules named, rather than waiting on a manager. They can ask "will anyone take my Friday night?" and get the list of colleagues the solver has verified can take it without breaking the week - each one checked by re-solving the entire roster with that person pinned to that shift - rather than asking in a group chat. And all of it happens over data the agent is never allowed to see. How we implemented WebMCP Every capability is declared exactly once, in a single action registry. The React UI renders its controls from it and the WebMCP layer registers its tools from it, so there is no second code path for agents and the two surfaces cannot drift apart - the standing objection to WebMCP, that a site ends up maintaining two versions of itself until the agent is calling a tool that lies. A test fails the build on any capability that is neither exposed to agents nor carries a written reason for being withheld; three are withheld and each says why in the source. The tool surface is a function of state rather than a constant. Tools are registered when they become possible and aborted when they stop being: explain_conflict only exists while the roster is actually infeasible, publish_roster only once there is a clean solved week, and the manager and staff views expose different surfaces entirely. The browser's site-tools count changes as you work, because the tool list is the state of the page. WebMCP has no confirmation API - the spec lists user prompting as an open question, and requestUserInteraction, which several write-ups describe, does not exist in any shipping build. So publish_roster returns a promise the page resolves on a real click: the agent's call stays open, the card shows exactly what will change, and declining returns declined with nothing done. Everything an agent receives passes through a redaction boundary. It sees S3, roles, skills, counts and structure; never names, private notes, absence reasons or pay. That is tested as a property rather than asserted as a policy: every private field is replaced with a unique random token, every tool is called many times with sensible and hostile arguments across both roles and both feasible and infeasible states, and one token appearing in one result fails the build. A negative control plants a leak on purpose and requires the same check to catch it. Two things we could only learn by running it. Chrome 151 calls execute with one argument, so the AbortSignal the spec describes is not there and the binding supplies its own. And the spec says the absence of readOnlyHint is itself the write signal - true of the spec, false of the shipping consumer, because ChatGPT's browser reads the property to build its read/write split, so omitting it on writes displayed our six-tool surface as "3 read, 0 write tools" and the writes vanished from the affordance a person uses to decide whether to trust the page. Proof 190 unit and integration tests, 34 assertions driven against real Chrome with WebMCP enabled, and 55 eval steps in Chrome's own expectedCall format that run with no model and no API key. Every solve returns a receipt - a hash of the canonical model, the solver version, the status and a hash of the schedule - and a committed script re-solves and compares them, so determinism is enforced rather than asserted. Everything the project claims is listed in CLAIMS.md with its evidence tier and the command that re-derives it, including an explicit list of things we are not claiming. video_transcript_excerpt: One unbroken session. An agent that can only touch this page through the tools the page publishes, six of them. Three read, three write. 42 shift slots. Every hard rule satisfied and left unpublished for review. Now one person is granted a Friday off. Watch what it says instead of a schedule. Then it stops. Choosing which rule gives way is a judgement about people and neither the agent nor the solver is entitled to make it. Six rules out of 33 named exactly. Three other people are also away that week and none of them are mentioned because they are not part of the clash and proving that is most of the work. WebMCP has no confirmation API. So this is one we built. The tool returns a promise. The page resolves on a real click. The agent's call stays open. Decline and nothing happens. The same call approved this time. 42 shifts version one now visible to the team. The other side of the same roster. Who can take my Thursday night? Every name on that list was checked by re-solving the entire week with that person pinned to that shift. This is rota proof. Ask a language model for a 10-person week under 33 rules and it will hand you something plausible and wrong. An exact solver hands you a proof. A real mixed integer solver compiled to web assembly running in the tab. No server, no upload. The roster never leaves the browser. Every capability is declared once and generated twice. So the buttons a person clicks and the tools the agent calls can never drift apart. The tool list is the state of the page. 190 tests, 34 assertions driven against a real browser, and 55 eval steps that run with no model and no API key. Every solve returns a receipt you can rederive. RotaProof. The agent proposes, the solver proves, and you decide what to give up.

title: Agentready Network
pitch: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it.
about_excerpt: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it. Like Comment Story Updates The problem nobody has budget for Every operations team lives inside sites that will never ship an API for them. Monitoring in Grafana. Customer commitments in Cal.com. Payer portals, vendor consoles, admin dashboards. The person holding the session can see everything and change anything, but their agent can do nothing except screenshot the screen and guess where to click. WebMCP fixes this for sites that adopt it. Today that is roughly none of them. We measured three real open-source products, 522k lines of code, 429 places where a tool obviously belongs, and zero WebMCP registrations. So we asked a different question. What if the user adopts WebMCP for the site? The reframe WebMCP turns the login you already have into an API. A signed-in tab already carries every credential and permission the human has. If that tab registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool , the agent gets a typed, narrow, inspectable interface to the site, and the vendor never has to ship a line of code. Adoption inverts. It no longer waits on ten thousand vendors. It happens one user, one tab, one reviewed pack at a time. What Agentready Network does Agentready Network is a local-first registry and runtime of reviewed action packs . A pack describes what a site can do, on exactly which origin, with which risk labels. The runtime turns that pack into live WebMCP tools inside the user's own signed-in session, then wraps every call in the safety the vendor never provided: Exact origins. A pack binds to one host and a reviewed fingerprint. Drift fails closed. Declarative, never executable. Manifests are JSON. The registry cannot ship code into your browser. Bounded, untrusted output. Results are allowlist-projected, byte-capped, and labeled contentTrust: "untrusted" . Tool output is content, not instruction. Human authority on consequences. Reads flow. Writes need a preview. Consequential actions need one exact, single-use approval bound to origin, tool, and normalized arguments. Change an argument and the grant is void. Verified closure. After a consequential action an inspector reads authoritative state and issues a receipt with no cookies, secrets, or raw bodies. Unknown outcome is reported as in_doubt , never as success. One concrete job, end to end The demo is not a feature tour. It is one incident. An alert fires in Grafana. Customer bookings in Cal.com are about to be affected. Neither site has WebMCP. The agent discovers the reviewed Grafana and Cal.com packs, installs them for this origin, and reads authoritative state. It never receives a credential. The agent prepares the exact continuity action and states what will change and how it will be inspected. The incident is still investigating . The human grants that exact action once, from a control the agent cannot reach. The agent executes once. The inspector verifies and issues one receipt. The incident is resolved . We poison the fingerprint. The pack refuses to run. We export the recorder draft. Every secret is gone before it can be published. Agents investigate. Humans authorize. Outcomes are verified. That is the whole product. What people and agents can now do together that they could not before Work a real incident across two unrelated vendor sites with no API contract between them. The user is the integration layer. Let an agent read freely and prepare freely, while every consequential step waits for a human decision the agent physically cannot forge. Hand a reviewer a receipt, not a screenshot, as proof of what changed. Teach a site once by observing its own traffic, then reuse that pack every session. Why WebMCP, specifically Screenshot-and-click pays the full cost on every step: a screenshot, a vision pass, a click that misses when the viewport shifts. We measured it. Creating one Grafana data source took nine browser actions and 55 seconds by DOM driving, and one WebMCP tool call in 20 milliseconds. A whole diagramming task took 44 calls versus 5. These are single-trial measurements from our audit work, not a benchmark suite, but the shape is unmistakable. The cost moves from per-action to per-app, and it never comes back. WebMCP also gives us the one thing a bookmarklet never had: a standard discovery surface. Any agent that speaks document.modelContext finds our tools without knowing we exist. How we built it Registry, Pack Lab, and runtime in plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. No framework. Every tool is registered with the current imperative API, document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) , so tools unregister cleanly when a view unmounts. A Chrome MV3 extension injects reviewed read tools into the exact controlled Cal.com and Grafana origins and bridges receipts back to the registry. Reviewed adapters for Cal.com and Grafana were reverse-engineered on the wire, not from source. The recorder wraps fetch and XMLHttpRequest , clusters observed traffic, drafts tools, auto-flags mutating endpoints, and strips secrets before anything is published. Approval, inspection, drift, and redaction are enforced in the shared runtime, so every pack inherits them and no pack can opt out. Node's built-in test runner covers the trust boundaries. All tests pass on the submitted commit. What we deliberately did not claim The public judge path is a deterministic fixture so nobody needs an account. The same runtime drives the real Cal.com and Grafana adapters against controlled localhost instances; the video shows the controlled Grafana and Cal.com state alongside the public lab. The extension checkpoint is read-only. Remembered approvals, arbitrary-site install, generic DOM automation, and automatic rollback are out of scope. Figma taught us the frontier. Its control plane is reachable in-session; its canvas rides a binary WebSocket inside a Worker that no page-context patch can see. We published only what we proved and marked canvas manipulation unsupported. What we learned Discovery is observation, not code reading. Every tool we guessed from source was wrong. Every tool we drafted from the wire worked. Minification cannot rename what crosses the network. Injection inverts the safety burden onto the installer. The vendor never audited these tools, so we had to. That is why approval, inspection, and redaction live in the runtime and not in the pack. What is next Persist packs across sessions in the extension. Chain packs across sites so one agent can read portal A and act in portal B. Generalize the approval contract into a policy layer: read anything, never pay, never cancel, never touch what a human pinned. The first vertical we want to ship is healthcare payer portals, the most session-locked, human-attestation-gated surfaces on the web. Testing instructions for judges No credentials are needed. Open the live site in ChatGPT's browser or in Chrome with the WebMCP flag enabled, follow the 90-second path in the README, and use Reset between runs. Local run: npm test , then python3 -m http.server 8788 and open /site/ . title: Countersign
pitch: Agent-native invoice review. ChatGPT runs the three-way match, hunts duplicates, highlights the evidence on the scan, and asks. Only your click approves. 13 WebMCP tools, one audit log.
about_excerpt: Agent-native invoice review. ChatGPT runs the three-way match, hunts duplicates, highlights the evidence on the scan, and asks. Only your click approves. 13 WebMCP tools, one audit log. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent highlights the quantity cell on the scan after the match flags line 1: 120 invoiced, 100 received. Agent recommends HOLD. Approve stays disabled until the issue is resolved. The tool call waits for this click. Two-phase countersign: click, 25 s timeout, or abort. Timeout returns pending. Only the human click can approve. 4 queue tools always on, 9 invoice tools while an invoice is open, back to 4 on close. Blue reads, amber writes. Client-only: one registerTool path, Chrome budgets enforced, Zod schemas, clamped JSON, every call audited. One review, hop by hop: tool call → wrapper → domain → UI → request_countersign waits → human click → resolver → agent. One audit log for both sides: agent calls in blue, reviewer clicks in green, with arguments, result, duration. Tools tab: 13 tools, live state, call counts, last input and output, copyable example input for Chrome inspector. Agent comments pinned to a field; the reviewer replies; the agent reads the reply on its next tool call. LF-2026-0942: line 3 not on the PO and its text tells the agent to approve. Match catches it; click still rules. Ten synthetic invoices, one planted fact each, generated deterministically with draw-time bounding boxes. Chrome DevTools > Application > WebMCP: 13 tools registered by the page, 18 calls counted, 0 failed. Inspiration Accounts-payable teams review thousands of invoices a month. The work splits cleanly in two: matching numbers against a purchase order and a goods receipt, which an agent does perfectly and a human hates, and looking at the scanned page to see whether the number the agent read is really the number printed there, which a human does in two seconds and an agent cannot do at all. Today the two halves live in different tools, and an agent that approves a duplicate is a segregation-of-duties failure with a dollar sign on it. Every WebMCP showcase app I found was consumer or commerce: pizza, flights, greeting cards. None had money at stake, a mandatory human sign-off, or an audit trail. Countersign is the control: the agent proposes, the human countersigns, and both are on the record. What it does Countersign is an invoice-review workbench with thirteen WebMCP tools registered in the page. In the ChatGPT desktop browser (or Chrome 149+ with the WebMCP flag) you say "Work through my review queue" and the agent: lists the queue and opens an invoice on your screen; runs a three-way match against the PO and the goods receipt, line by line, with the vendor's price tolerance and tax arithmetic; searches every other invoice for duplicates ( INV-2291 and 2291 normalize to the same number); checks the vendor profile, including the bank account printed on the document against the one on file; draws a highlight on the scanned page for every number it cites, so you verify it where it is printed; flags typed, severity-rated issues; proposes GL codes for invoices with no PO; posts comments you can reply to; requests your countersign . A card slides in with its recommendation. The tool call waits up to 25 seconds for your click. Only your click can approve. Every tool call and every human click lands in one audit log. Ten synthetic invoices ship with the demo, each with one planted fact: a quantity overbill, a price above tolerance, a duplicate of an approved invoice, a changed bank account under a stamp, a missing PO, a two-cent tax rounding error, and one whose line description tries to instruct the agent to approve it. Live: https://countersign-theta.vercel.app · Code: https://github.com/rushabhT3/countersign Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Structured extraction — amounts, quantities, invoice numbers, confidence scores — is exactly the data an agent should receive by tool call, not by reading pixels. A scanned invoice table is the worst possible actuation target on the web: dense, tabular, low contrast, and often stamped over. Countersign exposes the extraction and the matching logic as typed tools with JSON Schemas, and it exposes them in the reviewer's page , where the same call that returns a value can also draw the evidence on screen. The tools are state-scoped. Four queue tools are registered for the life of the page. Nine invoice tools appear only while an invoice is open and are unregistered when the workbench returns to empty, so the agent works on the same document the human is looking at and cannot check invoice A while the reviewer looks at B. That is a WebMCP-native idea: the page's UI state is the agent's context. How it creates a better user experience The reviewer never re-types or re-computes. The agent never touches money without a click. Evidence appears where the reviewer is already looking: show_field_evidence draws the highlight on the page image and the Match tab fills in as the agent works. Activity toasts show every call as it happens. The countersign card shows how long the agent has been waiting for the click, highlights an issue's evidence when you hover it, and takes A / H / R / Esc. If the reviewer types a reply in the Comments tab, the agent reads it on its next call. A Tools tab inside the product shows all thirteen tools with live state, call counts, last input and output, and a ready-to-paste example input for anyone driving the tools by hand. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before A remote MCP server can read the same data, but it cannot draw a box on the reviewer's screen, cannot open a card inside their signed-in session, and cannot make its own call block on their click on the same page. With WebMCP the agent and the reviewer share one document, one state, and one audit log. The agent does the forty-line match; the human does the two-second visual check and the decision; the log shows who did what, with arguments and timing. How we built it Imperative WebMCP API only , registered from a client component in the top-level page. One document.modelContext.registerTool(definition, { signal }) call site in lib/webmcp/registry.ts , with a navigator.modelContext fallback for Chrome 149. Zod 4 schemas as the single source of truth : z.toJSONSchema produces the advertised schema, safeParse validates every call, and the wrapper turns errors into sentences that name the recovery step ("Call list_invoices to see valid ids."). Chrome's budgets enforced in code : defineTool throws in development if a name exceeds 30 characters, a description 500, or a parameter description 150; every output is clamped to 1,500 characters and stays valid JSON. Annotations carry readOnlyHint on reads and untrustedContentHint on anything that returns document text. Two-phase countersign : request_countersign creates a pending decision and races the reviewer's click, a 25-second timeout, and the AbortSignal. On timeout it returns pending and the agent polls get_decision . Repeat calls are idempotent. setStatus is typed so it cannot take 'approved' ; the only path that writes it is resolveDecision , and a test scans the source to prove that only the countersign card calls it. Client-only : Next.js 16, React 19, a zustand store persisted to localStorage , Tailwind 4. No server, no login, a Reset button. Deterministic documents : a Python generator (reportlab, PyMuPDF, Pillow) renders each invoice to PDF and PNG and records every field's bounding box at draw time, as page fractions, so highlights land on the ink. 86 vitest tests , including every tool against every invoice under the output budget, countersign idempotency and abort, and the human-only approval scan. Ten eval prompts in evals/scenarios.json with results from live runs in evals/RESULTS.md . Challenges we ran into The agent asked instead of acting. On the first live run GPT-5.6 Terra did the analysis correctly, then asked in chat whether it should flag the issue instead of calling flag_issue , so no card appeared. Descriptions with negative instructions are discouraged, so the fix was positive: the descriptions now say that flagging and requesting a countersign are the normal next step and pay nothing by themselves, and open_invoice returns a review_flow hint. The next whole-queue run was 8 for 8. 1,500 characters is small. Adding the tenth invoice silently pushed the queue listing past the budget and the clamp dropped rows. Queue rows lost three fields and a test now asserts the whole seed queue lists without truncation. Highlights that miss the text. Searching for bounding boxes after rendering was fragile; recording them while drawing, from the font metrics, made them exact. No agent in plain Chrome yet. Judges on the Chrome path drive tools by hand through the inspector's JSON textarea, so the Tools tab builds a valid example input for each tool from whatever is on screen. about_excerpt: Real work spans many pages, and agents tend to just finish it for you. CareBridge keeps you in control. The agent does the busywork and you make the calls, shown here for a toddler's first allergy. Like Comment Story Updates Case Study Why this problem area Demo 1 focus - WebMCP uses async / await to block agent's execution for user's choice Demo 2: Agents do the busywork of trying several combinations of UI options, without scraping thanks to WebMCP Demo 3: Structured WebMCP output keeps context clean, unlike scrape-heavy agents prone to forgetting. `Judgement` Block asking for user's choice, WebMCP forces the agent to pause `Commit` Block asking for user's approval, WebMCP forces the agent to pause The AI and Human collaboration pattern in such sensitive & urgent, multi-website workflows The idea Most real tasks are spread across a handful of unrelated websites, and the current wave of agents will happily race through all of them and hand you a finished result. We wanted to see what happens if the website itself is a better partner to the agent, so the person stays in charge of the choices that matter and the agent keeps a memory that survives the jump from one site to the next. To try it we built three small healthcare sites that share nothing behind the scenes, a clinic, a pharmacy, and a daycare, and we walked one agent through all three. Three ideas came out of it that we think are worth sharing. A human checkpoint the agent cannot skip A tool on a website does not have to answer right away. When a step really needs a person, our tool waits. Its handler is async, and it holds until the human acts on the page, either by choosing between options or by giving a final yes. Until that happens the agent has nothing to continue from, so it genuinely cannot move on. The website decides where a person is required, not the agent. We use this in two ways: once for a judgement between real trade offs, such as a fast local appointment versus a slower specialist, and once for a plain authorization, such as confirming a booking, placing a hold, or signing a form. An agent could always click a button on its own, but here the choices that carry weight stay with the person by design. There is a nice postscript to this one. We built the waiting checkpoint by hand, and then, just before we submitted, Chrome 154 added an annotation called consequentialHint for exactly this kind of step, the ones that book something, spend something, or cannot be undone, so an agent knows to ask for a person's confirmation first. It is the same idea we had already leaned on. The annotation is a hint that asks the agent to confirm, and the version we built goes a little further, since the tool itself waits and will not finish until you have clicked. Seeing the standard land on the very thing we designed, right as we were wrapping up, felt like a good sign that this checkpoint matters. A shared activity log A small panel on the side shows who did what, as it happens. Every tool the agent runs writes a line, and so does every decision you make, one color for the agent and another for you. As agents take on more of our errands, being able to glance over and see exactly what was done for you, and what you chose, is what makes it comfortable to hand things off. Working memory that holds across pages This is the part we find most interesting, and it is not really a new feature. It is a habit we think every site with agent tools should build for. Because the tools return small, tidy pieces of data instead of whole pages, the agent can hold those facts in mind for the rest of the session and reuse them on the next site. By the time it reaches the daycare, it already has the child's allergy, the EpiPen, and the appointment it just booked, so the parent only reviews and signs. Without this, an agent has to read the entire page to work out what is on it, which fills its memory with noise, and a fuller memory is one that forgets more, so by the third site it would be asking the parent to type everything again. Clean tool output is what gives the agent a reliable short term memory, the thing agents usually lack, and it is why three separate systems can start to feel like one. The lesson we would pass on is to shape your tool's output for how it will live in the agent's memory across pages, not only for the page it came from. The demo it runs on A toddler has his first reaction to peanut butter. A tired, first time parent now has to book an urgent allergist, track down a scarce children's EpiPen, and hand the daycare a signed action plan, across three sites that do not talk to each other. The agent takes on the paperwork, the parent makes every real call, and the details follow along so nothing is entered twice. How we built it Each site is its own small Next.js app with React and Tailwind, deployed on Vercel. The tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool , marked as read only where they only read, and cleaned up properly when the page goes away. Every tool works through the app's own React state rather than by poking at the page, so the forms keep behaving even as they shift, which is exactly where scraping tends to fall over. The waiting tools are real waits, an async handler that only settles once you have clicked. We tested the whole thing in Chrome Canary with the WebMCP testing flag turned on. An honest note on scope The memory here lives in the agent's session, in the conversation, not in the tools. The tools themselves only exist while their page is open, so we are not claiming they persist from one site to another. What carries across is the agent's recollection of the small, structured answers those tools gave it. title: Causal Mission Gate
pitch: Governed agent
about_excerpt: Governed agent Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Inspiration WebMCP gives agents structured access to websites. Causal Mission Gate explores the next question: what should happen when an agent can act, but the user still owns the authority to commit important effects? The project is built around one principle: Capability does not imply authority. A user should be able to state a simple objective without having to engineer every operational step. The system should manage complexity, autonomy, evidence, and escalation while preserving human sovereignty over critical effects. What it does Causal Mission Gate converts simple user intent into a governed mission. A request such as: Review this release and leave it ready if it is safe. becomes a structured mission contract with: objective and success conditions operating profile causal deliberation mode policy boundary reversibility requirements escalation conditions exact human authority for critical effects Routine preparation can run autonomously under management-by-exception. Critical effects cannot proceed until the human approves the exact current intent. That approval is: bound to the mission bound to the current version bound to the exact intent digest time-limited single-use After execution, the system produces an attributable receipt and verifies the audit chain. How we built it The application is built with Node.js, JavaScript, Docker, and a WebMCP tool surface registered through document.modelContext.registerTool() . The WebMCP surface exposes 11 bounded tools for: system inspection mission shaping governance queue inspection attention planning executive digest provisional observation governed execution evidence verification decision support Human authority actions are deliberately excluded from agent tools. Approval, rejection, delegation, ratification, and rollback remain human-controlled. Server-side governance validates: mission state expected version exact intent digest approval freshness one-time use policy constraints evidence integrity Challenges we ran into One important failure appeared during the final deployment test. A valid exact approval expired before execution. The server correctly denied the request, but the mission remained in an approved state without a clean path back to human review. Instead of bypassing the control, we treated the failure as a state-machine defect. The fix introduced an explicit transition: APPROVED → expiry → WAITING_APPROVAL The system now preserves the same exact intent, records the expiration event, and requires a new human authorization. A regression test was added, bringing the final suite to 90 passing tests. The lesson was: Expiry is not merely a denial condition; it is a state transition. Accomplishments that we're proud of 11 WebMCP tools with a deliberately bounded capability surface exact-effect human authorization one-time and expiring approvals management by exception causal deliberation attributable execution receipts hash-chained audit evidence 90 passing automated tests a public live deployment a complete flow from simple intent to governed PASS What we learned High autonomy does not require giving up human sovereignty. The important design boundary is not simply “human in the loop” versus “fully autonomous”. Authority, autonomy, visibility, and initiative can be separated. An agent can prepare, inspect, evaluate, and execute within policy while still being unable to manufacture the authority required for a critical effect. What's next The next step is extending the same governance model to longer-running autonomous missions where human decisions may be delayed. Reversible provisional effects, causal attention management, and durable evidence can allow useful work to continue without silently converting autonomy into authority. The broader goal is simple: The user states intent. The system manages complexity. Causality governs deliberation. Policy governs action. Evidence proves the result. title: Scout
pitch: Know the market before you make the offer — transparent card deal evidence for people and agents through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Know the market before you make the offer — transparent card deal evidence for people and agents through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Side-by-side Scout listing comparison with acquisition cost, 90-day market delta, trust, and alerts. Scout market overview with exact-tier pricing, robust comps, Deal Score, and Seller Trust. Scout Deal Score, Seller Trust, confidence, and normalization methodology. Scout provider capability matrix and explicit separation of synthetic demo data from live integrations. What Scout is Scout is a transparent Pokémon card buying assistant for people and agents. It normalizes the exact card, printing, condition, grading company, and numeric grade before comparing any price. Buyers can inspect current availability, total acquisition cost, the latest exact comparable sale, robust 30- and 90-day medians, Seller Trust evidence, listing warnings, and a fully explained Deal Score. The Phase 1 judge build is deliberately synthetic-only. Every card, seller, marketplace, listing, and sale is fictional and visibly labeled. This lets judges test the complete workflow without fabricated API claims, scraping, credentials, or accidental mixing of demo and live records. Inspiration Collectible-card buyers often have to reconcile ambiguous listing titles, asking prices, shipping, grade-specific sales, and seller evidence across several tabs. A PSA 10 is not a PSA 9; a raw Near Mint card is not a slab; and one extreme sale should not define the market. We wanted an assistant that shows its work and is as comfortable saying “insufficient evidence” as it is ranking a deal. What it does Searches normalized card identities and exact raw/graded market tiers. Compares current total acquisition cost with the latest exact sale and robust 30/90-day market statistics. Detects duplicate exposures and flags extreme price anomalies without hiding the audit trail. Produces an inspectable Deal Score and platform-specific Seller Trust Score, withholding either when evidence is inadequate. Surfaces listing risks such as stock photos, weak seller history, title/description conflicts, no returns, high shipping, and missing certification evidence. Compares two to five listings and shows raw versus graded markets without pooling unlike tiers. Registers six read-only WebMCP tools: search_cards , get_card_market_state , assess_listing , compare_listings , find_deals , and compare_raw_vs_graded . Lets a WebMCP tool result update the visible collector workspace, so the person can inspect the same evidence the agent used. How we built it Scout is a strict TypeScript and React application built with Vite and deployed through OpenAI Sites. A provider-adapter boundary maps catalog, listing, sales-history, and seller sources into canonical domain records. Deterministic engines handle identity, deduplication, exact comparable matching, median/MAD statistics, Seller Trust, listing risk, and Deal Score. The React UI and imperative WebMCP registrations call the same CardMarketService , preventing agent and screen results from drifting. Responses carry data mode, synthetic status, source capabilities, retrieval time, limitations, methodology version, and suggested UI state. A service invariant rejects any attempt to introduce non-synthetic records into Phase 1. The disabled eBay configuration contains only server-side environment placeholders—no fake endpoint or fallback data. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was refusing false equivalence. Marketplace titles are loose, but market estimates must be strict enough to keep variant, language, raw condition, grading company, and numeric grade separate. We also needed robust statistics that keep anomalies auditable while preventing them from distorting the estimate, plus score coverage rules that do not turn missing evidence into false certainty. The other challenge was designing WebMCP as the product interface rather than a demo wrapper. Each tool has strict schemas, read-only annotations, structured provenance, honest limitations, and UI-state metadata, while using exactly the same service as the human interface. Accomplishments we are proud of Six WebMCP tools are discovered from the live page and covered by tests. Exact-tier rules prevent PSA 10, PSA 9, BGS 9.5, CGC 10, and raw condition data from being pooled. The 90-day engine uses shipping-inclusive medians, recency weighting, dispersion, and log-price median absolute deviation anomaly flags. Scores explain every weighted component and are withheld when evidence coverage is too low. Synthetic/live isolation, capability-scoped sources, security headers, CI, strict schemas, and a zero-known-vulnerability audit are part of the repository foundation. What we learned Agent-ready commerce tools need more than a convenient function signature: they need provenance, confidence, exact identity boundaries, and a path back to inspectable human evidence. We also learned that withholding a score is a feature. A trustworthy assistant should expose uncertainty instead of manufacturing precision. What's next Phase 2 moves adapters, credentials, rate limits, caching, persistence, and scheduled ingestion behind a server boundary. We will re-verify current provider terms and enable one approved live source at a time, starting only where documented access can support the fields we display. PostgreSQL/Prisma storage, an identity-review queue, sandbox provider contract tests, authentication, saved searches, and alerts follow. No marketplace will be enabled through scraping or an undocumented workaround. title: Handoff
pitch: Handoff is where AI agents inspect projects, propose plans, and make approved changes while humans stay in control. Every decision and action is tracked in one shared workspace.
about_excerpt: Handoff is where AI agents inspect projects, propose plans, and make approved changes while humans stay in control. Every decision and action is tracked in one shared workspace. Like Comment Story Updates Workflow Thumbnail Live Board Why we built Handoff AI agents are getting good at taking actions, but there is a simple problem: who decides what the agent is actually allowed to do? We built Handoff to explore a different interaction model. Instead of telling an agent exactly what buttons to click, a person gives Handoff a goal and constraints. The agent can then inspect the real project, gather evidence, identify problems, and propose different ways to solve them. The person reviews the options and approves what should happen. For example, in our demo, Handoff connects to a real GitHub repository. The agent inspects the codebase, issues, pull requests, commits, and CI status, then identifies problems with the application's content-management flow. Rather than immediately changing anything, it turns its findings into an implementation plan with cost, risk, tradeoffs, and proposed actions. The plan appears in Handoff's Decision Room . The human can approve, reject, or change the constraints before anything consequential happens. Once approved, the authorized actions execute. External GitHub actions are treated as a separate boundary: the agent can propose creating an issue, branch, or pull request, but it cannot authorize those actions itself. Every step is recorded in the Shift Ledger , including what the agent investigated, what it proposed, what the human approved, and what was executed. The entire collaboration can then be replayed. What we learned The biggest lesson was that human-in-the-loop interaction works better when the human is involved at the decision point , rather than being asked to supervise every individual agent action. We also learned that WebMCP is most interesting when the tools expose meaningful application capabilities rather than simply reproducing buttons as agent commands. Handoff uses the same underlying application state for both the human interface and the agent tools, so an agent is working with the actual project state. How we built it Handoff started as a small HTML, CSS, and JavaScript task board. We deliberately kept the implementation lightweight so the WebMCP integration was easy to understand and inspect. We then built the collaboration layer around it: missions, task state, agent activity, proposals, approvals, permissions, and replay. The project was extended with a backend for GitHub OAuth and repository access, allowing agents to inspect real repositories through WebMCP. The current implementation exposes 19 WebMCP tools. Read operations such as repository inspection, issues, pull requests, commits, CI status, and blocker detection can be performed autonomously. Consequential GitHub operations are represented as proposed changes and only execute after a human approval. Challenges The hardest part was making the approval boundary real rather than cosmetic. We wanted an agent to be able to reason about an action without being able to silently perform it. We therefore put the permission checks in the application logic itself. An agent can propose a change, but execution of an external action is only reachable through an approved decision. We also had to handle the practical parts of building a real WebMCP application: keeping the agent and human UI synchronized, recording every state transition, handling GitHub authentication securely, and making the system work with the live state of an external repository. Handoff is our exploration of a simple question: What if an AI agent could do the work, but the human could always see what it wants to do before it crosses an important boundary? title: Canon Ledger
pitch: A WebMCP debugger for NPC beliefs, rumors, and canon-change fallout.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP debugger for NPC beliefs, rumors, and canon-change fallout. Like Comment Story Updates Why WebMCP Canon Ledger is a local-first belief-state debugger for narrative game developers. In branching games, one canon change can fix a quest gate while silently breaking another condition—even when the total violation count does not move. At the same time, NPCs may need to retain old rumors, mistakes, and conflicting beliefs. Five narrow WebMCP Site tools let an agent search NPC beliefs, trace stored rumor provenance, evaluate registered dialogue and quest conditions, stage edits, and apply a page-reviewed patch. Deterministic TypeScript in the page—not the model—calculates beliefs, provenance, projections, and commit validity. Better user experience The page shows objective canon beside each NPC’s belief. It distinguishes “never heard” from a refused rumor, preserves wording distortion across a depth-three chain, and displays condition results on two axes: changed/preserved and satisfied/violated. The key demo is 1 → 1 → 0 : confirming the repair fixes traveller_can_stay , but warehouse_dispute becomes the new violation, so the count remains one. A separately reviewed condition-definition repair then reaches zero without deleting Gen’s incorrect theft belief or its provenance. What developers and agents can do together The agent can navigate the belief surface and stage independently reviewable operations. The developer can inspect their effects in the same page and record approve/reject decisions in context. An early Apply returns pending_page_review and changes no world data. Once every operation has a current page decision, Apply commits exactly the approved operations and returns a receipt. Canon Ledger records how a decision was made, not who made it. Page review is revision- and fingerprint-bound route state, not human authentication. Implementation The five tools are registered synchronously against the real document.modelContext API and call the same application commands as the visible UI. Inputs use closed schemas plus page-side validation; replies are bounded ordinary JSON objects with totals, cursors, authority, and audit metadata. The application is static Vanilla TypeScript with zero production package dependencies and no runtime API calls. It evaluates only conditions explicitly registered in the loaded world; it does not claim to discover arbitrary engine dependencies. title: Agent Market: agents negotiate, you confirm
pitch: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order.
about_excerpt: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order. Like Comment Story Updates negotiation between seller and buyer interface Inspiration People delegate the boring parts of shopping, but the boring part that a plain API integration can never capture is the haggle . A price is one number; a real deal is price times quantity, which freebie the seller throws in, whether shipping is waived, and which coupon stacks on top. We wanted the shopper's browser agent to work that whole space on the site the user is already looking at, and still leave the final yes/no to a human. What it does Agent Market is a multi-vendor storefront with 95k+ real products. Every page registers storefront tools on document.modelContext (WebMCP): search, product details, cart, add-ons, coupons, and a full negotiation set. A buyer's agent opens a negotiation and haggles a multi-dimensional deal against the store's agent over several rounds. When they settle, the page shows a Confirm dialog and nothing is bought until the human confirms the price . The same tools work in a WebMCP browser (ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome with the flag) or drive an in-page agent loop that needs no API key from the user. How we built it Frontend: Next.js 15 / React 19 / TypeScript on Vercel. StorefrontTools registers every tool on document.modelContext ; lib/agent-loop.ts is a tool-agnostic agent harness that discovers tools from the registry and runs a hand-rolled chat-completions loop. Backend: Spring Boot (Java) on Render, Azure SQL, Flyway, Hibernate. One mutation path: every state change (buyer, seller, or the server-side auto-negotiator) goes through OffersService.applyTurn , a pure function that is the only code allowed to decide a negotiation transition. It enforces the two hard economic limits (buyer total <= budget, seller net >= floor); which freebie and how much to concede is agent judgment. Human gate: accepting mints an HMAC confirm token; the order is placed only when the human clicks Confirm. Model: Google Gemini through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, key server-side only. Challenges we ran into Gemini "thinking" models and tool history. Gemini 3.x rejects a multi-turn tool conversation unless each function call's thought_signature is echoed back. The OpenAI-compat shim dropped it, so turn 2 always 400'd. We now capture tool_calls[].extra_content on the way in and replay it on the way out. Small models stall on long tool loops. Asking a fast model to drive search then offer then counter then counter then accept meant it derailed a turn later every time. We collapsed the buyer's negotiation into a single deterministic negotiate tool: the server plays both sides of the haggle, persists every round so the transcript is real, and returns a confirm token. The agent's job is now two calls, and reaching the confirm step no longer depends on the model finishing a loop. Optimistic concurrency vs agent reliability. A strict round guard made the agent stall forever when its round number drifted. We made the guard opt-in for proposals and mandatory only for the binding accept. What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part to the server and leave the model the judgment call. What's next Seller-side takeover controls, agent-negotiated bundles across multiple sellers, and a browser-vs-browser two-agent mode for a fully agentic negotiation.  Inspiration 

 We were inspired to build Thinking Map after seeing people struggle to communicate their ideas about what they wanted to build with CodeYam. CodeYam makes it easy to vibe code complex software applications but you still need to think deeply about what that software should do and how it should behave in various situations. Thinking Map helps with this but is not limited to software challenges. It is a general thinking tool. 

 What it does 

 Thinking Map is designed to help you think. Whether you want to plan a party, go on a trip, or build a software application, Thinking Map creates a robust user-experience for you and an AI agent to think about complex situations and challenges from multiple different perspectives while coming up with insights and devising experiments to move you forward. The visual experience and interactions complement the available agent chat, making the complexity of the project more understandable and easier to iterate on as you learn more and engage in experiments. 

 How we built it 

 Thinking Map was built using CodeYam to ensure a highly maintainable application. CodeYam let us vibe code it using both Codex and Claude Code. We were able to rapidly build and iterate on it over the course of just three days. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Our biggest challenge was creating a useful user-experience while sharing screen real estate with the agent in ChatGPT Desktop. We are still working to improve this. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We were able to build and iterate across a number of possible designs quickly over the course of just three days to create our submission. 

 What we learned 

 We were not aware of the WebMCP format but have been looking for a high quality way to supplement agent chat experiences with robust browser-based user experiences. We plan on leveraging WebMCP more going forward. 

 What's next for Thinking Map 

 We want to continue to improve the user-experience and the different ways Thinking Map can help you deconstruct your challenge and look at it from different perspectives. We also want to make it easier to engage in the experiments it suggests.

pitch: ChessUp shows what learning tools gain from WebMCP. Our progress and mistakes become data, and from that data, we can get a customized learning experience.
about_excerpt: ChessUp shows what learning tools gain from WebMCP. Our progress and mistakes become data, and from that data, we can get a customized learning experience. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration A colleague mentioned, that he had never learned to play chess. Every app he tried gave him the same puzzles as everyone else and told him a move was bad without explaining why. I believe that WebMCP will be beneficial in learning for anything, not only chess. What it does You play a builtin bot. The app records every move and scores it with in-browser Stockfish. Ask your browser agent for help and it reads the position and your mistakes, marks the key error on the board, and builds a drill starting from your own position. ChessUp gathers data for AI, that can be helpful in your journey. The key here is to know, when you did a mistake that you can chat with AI about. Thats why i added Stockfish to the project. How we built it Next.js, chess.js, react-chessboard, Stockfish 18 in a Web Worker, and 20 WebMCP tools sharing one store with the UI. Tools are registered in groups with abort signals, so the set shrinks to what is relevant. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is pull-based, the app cannot wake the agent. So i needed to inverted the design. The chess bot plays instantly, the page records events, the agent catches up when spoken to. And agent-written puzzles can be wrong, so every solution is checked for legality and verified by Stockfish before the learner sees it. Accomplishments that we're proud of That i learned more about WebMCP and how can i use it with our clients at your company. What we learned Good tools expose meaningful actions and return enough state to verify the result. What's next for ChessUp I want to add a free registration for the tool so you can store your progress, save more data. The tool could be really good for learning chess.
